Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant fluctuations in cosmic-ray densities at large scales of around 300 million meters or more. By comparing observed patterns to theoretical predictions, we found that features larger than 100 million meters are not consistent with standard models of the universe. Specifically, we found that cosmic-ray densities exhibit increased values in four non-overlapping areas spanning around 300 million meters each, with data suggesting that these regions likely contain sources of extremely energetic cosmic rays that are separated by distances of at least 4 billion meters. Additionally, we discovered evidence of fluctuations in cosmic-ray directions that are correlated with features in density distributions, a finding that further supports the presence of sources in the universe. By analyzing features in density distributions and their corresponding flux enhancements, we were able to determine that they are primarily caused by cosmic-ray interactions with gas in host galaxies. However, since we are observing extremely energetic cosmic rays, interactions with gas in the galaxies must be confined to a very narrow field of view, likely centered on the direction to the galaxy. By combining data from different features in density distributions and incorporating information about cosmic-ray energies, we were able to identify the presence of sources that are not only located outside our galaxy but also in the nearby M87 galaxy. Interestingly, we found that sources of extremely energetic cosmic rays have a much larger field of view when considering lower energy cosmic rays. By analyzing features in density distributions and their corresponding flux enhancements at lower energy levels, we were able to determine that they are caused by cosmic-ray interactions with gas in host galaxies over a wider angle of about 10 degrees, and that they are more efficient at producing cosmic rays through a process that involves multiple steps. Using this information, we were able to make predictions about cosmic-ray fluxes at different energy levels and angles, and verify these predictions based on data from different experiments. Since we are observing extremely energetic cosmic rays that have traveled long distances, we used data from different features in density distributions and incorporating information about cosmic-ray energies and directions to identify the presence of sources that are located in the nearby M87 galaxy, and also sources that are located in other galaxies that are optically bright. Additionally, we used data from different features in density distributions and incorporating information about cosmic-ray energies and directions to determine that sources of extremely energetic cosmic rays have a high density of matter that is highly magnetic, and that they are also rich in energy that is not carried by light, but we were not able to determine the specific mass or the exact amount

This study explores how certain classical quantum mechanical models can be reimagined using noncommutative operator algebras derived from Lie algebras. We examine specific deformed versions of these models, based on su(2) and su(3) Lie algebras, and discuss their distinguishing features, commonalities, and differences. Our focus is particularly on superintegrable models, those with more general casework, and those exhibiting nonperturbative effects in their classical formulations. We outline initial findings on quantum versions of these models, with an emphasis on observable implications that can be deduced through classical limits. Our work sets the stage for a broader examination of quantum mechanical models based on simple Lie algebras and their fundamental representations. We anticipate that such models will often share key characteristics, including the presence of noncommutative operator commutators that close onto the underlying Lie algebra, a fact that has significant implications for their study. We also outline a strategy for analyzing these systems via classical limits, and the potential for this to be adapted to other areas of theoretical physics. Finally, we note that many open research questions remain in this field. We discuss one promising approach, involving the replacement of spatial derivatives in field theories with suitable deformation-induced operators, and speculate on the implications of this for both pure theoretical considerations and potential experimental interventions. We intend to explore this approach further in a companion paper. With this study, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the subject for fellow researchers and to facilitate the development of our research program. We welcome input, guidance, and feedback from a wider community of experts. In the short term, we plan to proceed with the investigation into quantum mechanical models based on simple Lie algebras, as outlined in this study, and with the proposed field theoretical generalizations in our companion paper. We anticipate that this research will yield valuable insights into the study of quantum mechanical models based on Lie algebras, potentially leading to a greater understanding of both their classical and quantum formulations, and facilitating the development of new approaches to dealing with the singularities that can arise in their classical limit. In the longer term, we aim to investigate further the implications of this research for our broader program, and to consider the potential for it to be generalized to other areas of theoretical physics. We are confident that this research will provide a valuable contribution to this effort, and we look forward to continuing this investigation in the laboratory of ideas that we share. We would like to express our gratitude to this environment for allowing us to explore new ideas

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in classifying tumor cells from whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of publicly available images, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the feasibility of applying FL in a scenario that mimics cross-institutional data collaboration, without compromising model performance. Additionally, we explored the effects of varying dataset size and number of participants in the federated learning setting, which provides valuable insights for designing FL studies in this context. These findings are particularly relevant to the cancer research community, which heavily relies on accurate tumor cell detection and classification. Moreover, our study highlights the success of applying federated learning to a critical biomedical analysis task, while also highlighting potential issues with scaling FL in such scenarios that arise from the need for extensive fine-tuning before achieving optimal results. Additionally, we investigated the role of data quality and quantity within each participating institution, which holds significant value for data-rich fields like biomedical research. Overall, our research offers a clear demonstration of the potential of federated learning to address the data challenges facing biomedical researchers, while also providing a framework for evaluating the effects of dataset size and number of participants in FL settings. This has broad implications for any field that relies heavily on image analysis using deep learning models. In terms of future work, we explored potential avenues for further research that could yield even greater advances in the application of federated learning to biomedical research. These potential advancements could provide a new pathway for smooth adoption of cutting-edge deep learning models across the biomedical sector, while addressing the critical issue of ensuring reliable and accurate analysis of biomedical data across multiple institutions. This study offers a thorough evaluation of the performance of federated learning in a setting that is highly relevant to biomedical research, that can serve as a model for assessing the effects of dataset size and number of participants in FL settings, while also providing a framework that is equally applicable to any field that relies heavily on image analysis using deep learning models. In this study, a high-speed underwater fiber transmission link was tested, and the results showed that a 32GBaud 16QAM signal could maintain an error rate below 10^-3 after traveling 86.1km of fiber. When using a decision-feedback equalizer (DFE), a significant increase in signal distortion and bit error propagation occurred within a 54.8km fiber segment. To address this issue, a novel DFE-NEP algorithm was developed to reduce noise enhancement and improve transmission performance. For the 54.8km fiber link, the new algorithm decreased the bit error rate below 10^-3 and increased the photon energy per bit by 0.5dB, confirming the algorithm's effectiveness in preventing noise propagation and extending the applicability of DFE in fiber transmissions. Scale model trials with DFE-NEP also demonstrated compatible performance with real-time underwater communications. To facilitate further research, an open-source DFE-NEP code is available for download. High-speed underwater communications are crucial for the development of future underwater sensory networks and have significant potential in marine science, navigation, and military applications. These systems will enable real-time data transfer between underwater sensors and their associated base stations over extended distances. One key technology for enabling these communications is the fiber-optic transmission system, which is already proven on land and has been successfully trialed in seawater over long distances. However, one significant challenge in underwater communications is the high level of cross-polarized noise that can cause signal distortion and limit data transfer rates. To address this issue, researchers have explored novel modulation schemes such as polarization-agnostic transmission and WDM transmissions that can operate in conjunction with DFE-NEP. These solutions are shown to significantly improve transmission performance and enable fast and reliable data transfer over long underwater distances. As a result, the scope of underwater communications is set to expand rapidly in the future, enabling real-time data transfer between underwater sensors and their associated base stations over extended distances. Deep learning models with temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) have achieved great success in various time-series analysis tasks. TCNs offer a unique combination of flexibility and computational efficiency by using a different approach to temporal convolution and pooling. However, due to the distinct design of TCNs, this kind of network often requires a significant amount of data to achieve optimal performance, which can result in a substantial increase in training time. In addition, there is a notable gap between the performance achieved by training TCNs from scratch and using a pre-trained model in a few-shot learning setting. In recent years, trimmer-based methods have been proposed to adapt general-purpose networks for time-series data, but these methods have several limitations: they can't handle multiple input feature dimensions, the trimmer itself needs to be trained on a large dataset, and the model typically needs a large amount of data to achieve comparable performance to a pre-trained model. In this research, a new framework called trimming in time (PIT) is presented, which addresses these issues by adapting TCNs to time-series data through a leaner trimmer that can handle multiple input feature dimensions. In our experiments, PIT outperformed all other trimmer-based methods and achieved comparable performance to pre-trained TCNs with only 16 data points. The results show that PIT's performance continued to improve over time, in contrast to other trimmer-based methods which saw a notable decline in performance as the dataset size increased. In particular, with just 64 data points, the model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0292 on the ETAS dataset, a 26.6% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art in few-shot learning studies. In addition to evaluating the method on the ETAS dataset, we also conducted an additional experiment on the Harfard dataset, where PIT outperformed all other trimmer-based methods and achieved a relative improvement of 21.6% over the previous state-of-the-art in few-shot learning studies. In order to facilitate further research, we released the code and models used in this study on the Harfard dataset, which can be found at https://github.com/ghs75/trimming-in-time. This paper classifies finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras over a given field, determining that they are essentially abelian. Specifically, we find that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra can be equated to the direct sum of its nilpotent component and an abelian component, whose dimensions are respectively finite and at most two. Notably, this classification applies broadly, encompassing the specific cases of Malcev and right-doubly linear algebras. We also provide a straightforward definition for the nilpotent dimension of any Zinbiel algebra. Building on this foundation, we derive key properties, including the nilpotent dimension being invariant under algebra isomorphism, as well as its maximum value of $d-1$ for $d$-dimensional algebras. Finally, we explore the implicit growth estimates for the dimensions of specific subalgebras, particularly the one-dimensional subalgebras, whose dimensions form an increasing sequence that mirrors the ordering of the natural numbers. We also establish that the dimension of any one-dimensional subalgebra can be expressed as a sum involving (mutually exclusive) analytic and projective components, arising from the corresponding properties of the underlying Zinbiel algebra. This framework enables us to demonstrate that the dimension of any two-dimensional subalgebra can be determined through a quadratic equation, while also identifying a significant basis involving (distinct) nilpotent and abelian components, that is invariant under the action of the algebra's automorphism group. This definition facilitates a pivotal realization: any Zinbiel algebra can be expressed as the union of its one-dimensional and two-dimensional subalgebras. This essential insight allows us to conclude that these subalgebras are in fact equivalent to the Malcev and right-doubly linear subalgebras previously identified. Ultimately, we leverage this understanding to derive a general formula for the dimension of any one-dimensional subalgebra, while also identifying a specific two-dimensional subalgebra with the simplest possible structure. This specific subalgebra serves as the basis for a broader introduction to the more complex algebras described by the higher-dimensional variational Zinbiel algebras. This framework also enables us to establish that the dimension of the underlying $d$-dimensional Zinbiel algebra can be determined through a higher-dimensional generalization of the specific two-dimensional subalgebra mentioned earlier. Our research examines the transverse flow pattern known as the 'chopper model' or'stream model,' which suggests that initial conditions influence the pattern's development. We studied the model's predictions regarding the fluctuation of the stream angle and flow intensity in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Our data analysis indicated that the stream angle and flow intensity exhibit inherent fluctuations, which align with the 'chopper model.' These findings also provide evidence that the model's'resonance barrier' scenario accurately describes the transition from elliptical to circular collisions at the LHC. We investigated this transition at higher energies with the Au-Au collision at RHIC and discovered that the'resonance barrier' scenario cannot explain the observed shift in stream angle. Instead, we propose that this shift arises from an increase in the fluctuation of flow intensity with rising energy. This interpretation has implications for heavy-ion research, suggesting that experiments should further examine the'resonance barrier' scenario and the fluctuations of stream angle and flow intensity in various collisions. We also suggest that in collisions where the'resonance barrier' is not observed, researchers should look for the possible existence of an 'isotropic barrier' and investigate its relation to jet production and the initial conditions of the quark-gluon plasma. Moreover, we propose that in collisions where the'resonance barrier' is observed, researchers should examine the possible relationship between the stream angle and the production of baryons and antibaryons. Additionally, we suggest that experiments should further examine the 'chopper model's' predictions regarding the stream angle and flow intensity in proton-proton collisions, as well as in collisions at higher energies with the future LHC at 13 TeV. If confirmed by experiments, these findings have the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of the quark-gluon plasma and the fundamental laws of physics that govern its behavior.

The Unified Correspondence Theory focuses on correspondence theory for modal logics by presenting the modal operators as first-order connectives achieving a comprehensive understanding of many modal correspondences. However, it lacks a unified approach for its reverse correspondences. This paper builds upon the Unified Correspondence Theory by providing a reverse correspondence for every entry and exit modality in Intuitionistic Logic, thereby filling the gap in the Unified Correspondence Theory. Moreover, it offers a novel approach for reverse correspondences that combines the patterns found in the Unified Correspondence Theory with additional patterns. This combined approach covers all DLE-Logics by means of a general framework, which is a key contribution of this paper. Additionally, it provides a framework for a correspondence theory that encompasses both positive and negative correspondences. Furthermore, this paper explores a connection between the unified approach and a previous paper on correspondences for Intuitionistic Logic. A further development from this connection results in a corresponding proof for a given Intuitionistic Logic formula, given that the corresponding proof for the same formula in the underlying classical logic is known. This feature, in turn, leads to a corresponding proof for any formula in DLE-Logics when the corresponding proof for the same formula in the underlying classical logic is known. This, in effect, enables the transfer of correspondence facts from classical logics to their intuitionistic counterparts. This paper offers a wealth of corresponding proofs alongside its main concepts. It also provides a way to express the corresponding proofs in the intuitionistic logic by using the existing connectives, which is referred to as the 'weak correspondence'. This concept is more versatile as it allows for correspondence in cases where the corresponding proof in the underlying classical logic involves the modal axiom. This paper proves the limit laws for the weak correspondence, which provides a solid foundation for further research on the correspondence theory of the modal mu-calculus and other fixed-point logics. This is achieved by establishing a connection between the weak correspondence and the modal mu-operator. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these rules, our work aims to incorporate them into the data, expressing potential connections and constraints that are only probabilistically certain. By incorporating the rules' uncertainties, our model can handle functional dependencies that may not hold due to null values or can exist despite apparent inconsistencies. We examine how to revise values to align with these rules, treating them as optimal solutions to a reformulated version of the original problem, which incorporates the probabilities of relationships and constraints. Additionally, our research is supported by an algorithm that employs the framework of tractable embeddings and can handle the complexities of modern large-scale data sets with millions of entries. Our study is complemented by an evaluation using real-world data sets from various domains, which shows that our approach outperforms existing methods in both quality and speed. Furthermore, our study includes a thorough analysis of the theoretical guarantees provided by our model, along with an expansion of our method that deals with multiple tables through inter-table functional dependencies. This expanded version is also evaluated using real-world data sets from various domains, which shows that our approach outperforms existing methods in both quality and speed. This study presents a novel Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregressive model, which effectively manages time-variant relationships among count time series. Our proposed model utilizes a dynamic system approach for modeling connections and incorporates external influences through non-stationary moving averages. We have formulated likelihood-based estimators for TV-AR(p) parameters and established the asymptotic theory for their convergence. Regarding model selection, we developed a criterion that chooses the optimal order and indicates consistency of this choice. Additionally, our results for TV-AR(1) include a representation of the estimated process and a non-asymptotic expression for estimation errors. Exponential and binary transformation of the original data are both explored, and we provide a simulation investigation of our estimators' performance. The benefits of TV-AR models are illustrated through an application to real count time series data from an epidemiological study. Finally, an R package TVPAR has been created to facilitate implementation and computation of TV-AR models. This package is adaptable to various data transformations and offers options for model selection and diagnostic checks. Its application examples include analysis of the referenced epidemiological study as well as analysis of count time series data from financial markets. With wide ranging potential applications, TV-AR models are an valuable tool for analyzing and forecasting non-stationary count time series. These models are particularly useful for epidemiological data analysis, providing unique insights into disease dynamics and facilitating investigation of co-epidemics in scenarios where multiple outbreaks may occur during a single time period. This can be further explored through analysis of binary and exponential transformed data, which is achieved through the R package TVPAR and its adaptation of external diagnostic checks. This package is highly versatile and allows for forecasting and visualization of data, in addition to performing various checks and tests on time series data. This includes customized application of Heijmans and Wesseling's test, which is now accessible through an interface and easily executable on large data sets. This has the added benefit of providing a clear and concise visual representation of time-varying characteristics in data, which can be achieved through the use of a custom function called the variance path plot. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that uses rotation and translation invariance to facilitate seamless adaptation to various object poses. NDFs use Neural Fields to model object presence and pose probabilities across 3D spatial coordinates, achieving both pose and object presence prediction on the Multi-Object Pose (MOP) dataset with exceptional performance. To further enhance the representation's practical applications, we integrate NDFs with Neural Network-based grasping and manipulation components, successfully executing complex tasks by adapting NDFs through iterative refinement and the incorporation of sensory feedback. Our results on the MOP dataset demonstrate NDFs' efficacy in both object understanding and manipulation, showcasing the potential of rotation and translation invariance in Neural Networks to model complex objects and poses. One key improvement to NN-based object understanding representations, NDFs excels in capturing the spatial relationships inherent to objects through their descriptor fields. This is particularly apparent when considering that many objects comprise interconnected components like hinges, handles, and links. By modeling these spatial connections, NDFs enables more effective and precise grasping and manipulation strategies. A notable aspect of NDFs is its descriptor field's ability to capture spatial relationships through pose dependencies, which in turn facilitate the prediction of grasp success probabilities in areas that have not been exposed to the learning algorithm. The SiD (Silicon Detector) Tracker concept for the ILC (International Linear Collider) has undergone a review and revision. The original design consisted of a disk and a forward section with a proprietary 2D silicon sensor, known as the FF-AF (Forward-Fast Forward) section. Following the review, the proposal has been updated to utilize a 3D silicon sensor in both the disk and forward sections. This change aims to enhance the radiation tolerance of the detector without compromising performance. The revised design is expected to operate effectively across a wide energy range spanning from DaVinci to the top mass threshold. The updated SiD Tracker concept is now referred to as the 3D SiD Tracker. The design revisions, along with the motivations for the changes, will be presented in this proceeding. The 3D SiD Tracker's upgraded design, including its magnetic field requirements and preambers' layout, will also be outlined. The detector's predicted performance, obtained through extensive simulation, is set to be showcased, highlighting its capability to accurately identify the mass, charge, and trajectory of particles. The 3D SiD Tracker's simulation results indicate it can efficiently distinguish between jets containing photons, Higgs boson characteristics, top quark properties, and W and Z boson properties, meeting the requirements specified in the SiD Detector Concept Document. The updated design's potential, derived from thorough assessment and testing, has reaffirmed the 3D SiD Tracker's position as one of the most advanced and effective detector designs for the ILC. Furthermore, this proceeding will also detail the progress made in the development of the 3D SiD Tracker's prototype and the planned upgrades to the prototype to include a 2-layer 3D silicon detector in the forward section. The prototype's development aims to validate the revised design's performance and inform the design of the ILC detector. The 3D SiD Tracker's development will contribute significantly to the advancement of silicon detector technology and research in this field. The workshop's findings have highlighted the potential of 3D silicon detectors to enhance detector performance and tolerance in heavy and high-energy environments. As such, the 3D SiD Tracker will likely serve as a benchmark for future detector designs. The development of the 3D SiD Tracker also marks an important step in the progression of silicon detector research, and it is expected that the technology developed within this project will be applied to other detector designs in the future. This study presents a deep learning approach called the Electron Interaction Network (EIN), which automatically generates accurate potential functions for electron interactions in complex atomic systems. Trained on a comprehensive set of data with minimal assumptions, EIN effectively captures the intricate correlations between electrons. We compared EIN to a widely accepted theoretical model called the Configuration Interaction (CI) method, using a simple electron system known as the-stable hydrogenic negative ion (n=1, Z=1). Our analysis showed that EIN and CI produced very similar results, with an average error of less than 0.0005 millihartrees in energy calculations. Conversely, when we used a large amount of data to train EIN on a negative ion with only 1% accuracy, it surprisingly still achieved a very low energy calculation error of less than 0.01 millihartrees. We also discovered that increasing the number of electrons in a negative ion led to a significant increase in energy calculation errors, indicating a need for further research in this area. Overall, our results suggest that deep learning approaches like EIN could be an efficient way to study complex electron interactions in atomic physics. We have made our code publicly available and invite other researchers to contribute and further develop the EIN model. While photometric observations from the sky can be useful for monitoring aerosol levels, they are largely limited due to being heavily influenced by various clear sky perturbations such as cloud fields, dust storms, and volcanic eruptions.  Recent research has expanded the possible use of such observations by integrating them with satellite data, incorporating multiple spectral channels, utilizing refined aerosol models, and developing effective detection methods for identifying and excluding anomalous photometric readings.  This work reviews the advantages of using such observations, discusses the challenges associated with their interpretation, and examines the methods for combining photometric data with other information to improve the accuracy of aerosol assessments.  Certain approaches such as using the angular AOT (aerosol optical depth), multiangular observations, and retrievals of aerosol properties using inversion techniques have been found to be particularly effective in achieving accurate results.  Furthermore, the research has also shown that when properly handled, photometric observations from the sky can be a valuable source of information for the global assessment of aerosol levels in the future, especially with the use of multiple spectral channels and advanced detection methods for anomalous clear sky conditions.  It is anticipated that with the launch of new all-sky spectrophotometric instruments such as the OLI+SWOT and the TROPE-I, we will have improved capability to study aerosols accurately.  This work also discusses the necessary requirements for maximizing the potential of such observations, including the development of more accurate forward models of aerosol interactions with light and robust detection methods for identifying and excluding anomalous clear sky conditions, as well as the incorporation of multiangular observations and all-sky spectral data that will definitely enhance the accuracy of aerosol assessments.  Additionally, the work touches on the fact that such observations not only provide valuable information on aerosol levels but can also be utilized for the retrieval of cloud optical properties and water vapor content in the atmosphere.  This work is a contribution to the International Space Science Institute's ISSI workshop on "Recent Advances in the Understanding of Cloud and Aerosol-Mediated Climate Variability".  I would like to extend my gratitude to the organizers for providing a conducive environment that facilitated the exchange of ideas and the exploration of novel approaches with renowned experts in the field.  This work is also a result of the collaboration between the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and the University of Morocco in Marrakech, Morocco.  I would like to express my appreciation to my colleagues at the University of Morocco for their support and the wonderful hospitality they provided during my visit

Recently, estimating a 6-DoF pose using only point clouds or 2D-3D correspondences has gained significant interest. Our research delves into using feature-based methods for this task, employing a deep learning framework that efficiently establishes correspondences and poses an ongoing challenge in the field. To address this, we introduce a novel, two-stage framework named DeepHMap++ that distinguishes itself from conventional feature-based methods. In the first stage, a dense feature extractor identifies unique features in the source point cloud, while a secondary, cross-stage matcher reinforces correspondences based on combined feature and proximity information. To enhance performance, we propose a new error metric and associated optimization method that minimizes both stage-specific losses, resulting in a compact, efficient, and portable network. Our evaluation experiments demonstrate that DeepHMap++ outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms, surpassing them by a significant margin in terms of accuracy, while requiring substantially fewer parameters. Moreover, our method exhibits superior performance in real-world applications, incorporating data obtained through simulation and real-world scenarios, as well as remote collaboration scenarios involving large-scale indoor environments. The source code of DeepHMap++ has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/kaist-vision/DeepHMap++-pose-estimation. Additionally, pre-trained models and demonstration videos are available at https://kaist-vision.github.io/DeepHMap++-pose-estimation/. We have also published a detailed project documentation, available at https://kaist-vision.github.io/DeepHMap++-pose-estimation/doc/index.html. Continuous performance evaluations are being conducted through an open-source evaluation framework, compatible with cloud services like Google Colab and Amazon SageMaker. The framework, along with DeepHMap++ source code, is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/kaist-vision/DeepHMap++-pose-estimation. The model's code has been optimized for usage within the Open3D framework and is available under the permissive MIT License. We invite the community to contribute their implementations of other 3D pose estimation methods to this repository. We have submitted an extended conference paper detailing our work, which has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2022. Additionally, we have successfully applied our method in collaboration with multiple industrial partners and research institutions. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGLasso) issues. This framework extends the Graphical Lasso model by incorporating a L1 penalty on a block-diagonal matrix derived from a set of regression matrices, enabling researchers to detect non-zero interactions across different datasets. GGLasso leverages the COCO L1 solver developed by dAribot et al. and is available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. The library can be easily installed via pip and is compatible with Python 3.8 and higher. GGLasso offers an user-friendly interface for obtaining the solution paths associated with different penalty levels and the soft-thresholding operator. Additionally, it provides an intuitive method for predicting a new data point based on the estimated model. We demonstrate GGLasso's capabilities using synthetic and real-world datasets, including data from the MIMIC-III clinical database. Furthermore, we contribute Python versions of the examples and tests previously described in the article by Koh et al. published at the NIPS 2007 conference. As open-source software, GGLasso is suitable for third-party contributions. We welcome potential users to submit their own implementations or extensions to the library. With GGLasso, researchers and practitioners can explore and analyze extended graphical Lasso models. We also hope this open-source project may serve as a starting point for further development in this area. Specifically, we leave for future investigation the following aspects: (1) extending GGLasso to accommodate an L1 penalty on a non-block-diagonal matrix, (2) exploring alternative estimators such as the Graphical Lasso with extra nugget parameters, and (3) incorporating data generation capabilities. We have already included an initial attempt at defining data generation capabilities, but this feature is still in its early stages and requires further development. We intend to follow a open-source, collaborative approach to enhancing the library. We have established a GitHub repository for this project where we post issues related to the article, including code examples and tests. We have also created an issue report regarding the data generation feature and encourage anyone with expertise in this area to contribute their ideas. With sufficient support, we plan to present an updated version of this article, covering all aspects discussed above. We have also included the results obtained with the real-world datasets from the MIMIC-III

Numerous applications in physics, chemistry, and materials science rely on molecular dynamics methods to solve complex problems. While Monte Carlo methods offer a complementary set of tools for sampling molecular configurations, their effectiveness is often hindered by the high computational costs of evaluating potential energies for multiple degrees of freedom. To address this issue, we propose a novel hybrid method that leverages the benefits of Langevin dynamics and the simplicity of Monte Carlo steps. By integrating the velocities of particles over short time periods, we transform the configuration integral into a form that can be efficiently sampled using a mixture of deterministic dynamics and stochastic perturbations. The resulting algorithm significantly reduces the necessary computational resources by minimizing the need for explicit temporal integration and still accurately captures intermolecular correlations. Moreover, we demonstrate that our proposed method offers improved configurational sampling efficiency, surpassing that of straightforward Monte Carlo simulations, and apply the algorithm to solve two notable problems: the positioning of a plate in a liquid under pressure and the formation of nanoscale protein-protein associations. The source code of the algorithm is also made freely available for download. High-performance parallelized variants of the method are also introduced and used to tackle even more demanding problems of which one is the placement of multiple plates in a variety of liquids. The algorithms we introduce achieve significant performance improvements, surpassing traditional molecular dynamics methods by several orders of magnitude in terms of computational cost, while accurately modeling real-world processes that involve the movement of proteins and other complex molecules. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on identifying entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our results indicate that our proposed architecture achieves top-performances on actual entity extraction tasks, such as TALC scores, which evaluate the accuracy of extracted entities in conjunction. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/Nested-NER. A specific class of conformal field theories in two dimensions is defined by equations that have been broadly applied, yet surprisingly, many details remain unclear. This uncertainty is where the Euler-Arnold equations come in - a diverse range of second-order partial differential equations that describe the motion of rigid bodies in various environments. These equations can be seen as a combination of the Hall-Anomaly equation, the Benney-Hassanov equation, and the Landau-Lifshitz equation, among others, and their relationship to conformal field theories is revealed through a formal identity that is derived here. This identity demonstrates that many properties of these Euler-Arnold equations can be transferred to the corresponding conformal field theories. In particular, we show that some solutions to these equations will correspond to non-trivial solutions for these field theories, given specific constraints. This connection also allows us to formulate a new conjecture regarding the solutions to these equations, and by extension, the solutions to these field theories, for a specific type known as two-dimensional superfluids. Achieving flawless interaction between humans and robots relies on precise testing of their joint dynamics. Although various methods for robot motion and action space testing exist, there is a lack of a unified framework for assessing the robots' performance in shared tasks with varying objectives. To bridge this gap, our novel machine testing framework is designed to evaluate the robots' ability to complete tasks by making distinctions based on their performance, satisfaction of task constraints, and overall quality of the resulting state. To deal with an infinite pool of potential tests, our system uses a linear programming algorithm to identify the most critical subspaces containing relevant examples, thus efficiently reducing the examination scope while maintaining a strong representation of the underlying performance space. To accommodate changes in performance metrics or task constraints, our system is further capable of regressing the test results to a low-dimensional representation, enabling effective handling of non-linear performance spaces through a linear autoregressive model. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through the development of a testing system for robots working in household environments, using the YCB object set and the Chair-based Task and Motion Planning Benchmark suite as reference examples. By applying our approach to the LB for household tasks, we obtained a significant reduction in test data size (from 512 to 100) while maintaining a nearly error-free test result accuracy of 98.5%. Additionally, our study highlights the advantage of our approach in efficiently handling changes in performance metrics or constraint modifications, also demonstrated with changes to planning benchmarks. Furthermore, our study includes a visualization example of a learned performance space representation using a dataset of 256 samples in the 3-dimensional object orientation space. We investigate the problem of finding rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer games under various information exchanges between players. Our analysis considers three levels of private thinking, where players may have limited knowledge of others' strategic knowledge and potentially even their own, requiring us to integrate extensive smoothness into our analysis. We demonstrate that approximately rationalizable equilibria can be computationally found when players think privately about their own strategies and when there are multiple independent groups of cooperating players, but this becomes NP-complete when players think about other players' thinking. For the latter scenario, we develop a generalized algorithm for finding approximately rationalizable outcomes. Notably, our results apply to broad classes of games that allow for discounting, continuous strategy spaces, and extensive smoothness, contributing meaningfully to the existing body of research on computationally finding equilibria. We further explore the acquisitive version of this problem, where an external agent initiates play and pays other players to induce rational behavior, and discover that it is an NP-complete problem even in simple 2x2 games with private thinking. Building on this, we investigate the application to online advertising, highlighting the challenge of inducing rational behavior in complex multiplayer interactions. Finally, we empirically evaluate the effectiveness of our algorithm both with synthetic data and in real-world online advertising scenarios, demonstrating its capability in finding high-paying outcomes that induce rational behavior. This work contributes a new model for inducing rational behavior in complex multiplayer interactions and provides an efficient algorithm for finding approximately rationalizable equilibria, paving the way for future research in this domain. We found that a 5σ significance for polarization measurement can be achieved with as few as 3 inverse attobarns of integrated luminosity at 14 TeV, or 1.5 inverse attobarns at 17 TeV, assuming the electron and neutrino pair are measured in the forward-backward direction with high transverse energies. Furthermore, with sufficient data, the magnitude of the top quark polarization can be determined, providing valuable insights into the underlying short-distance processes and potential new physics phenomena. This study also highlights the importance of selecting highly polarized top quark events, as well as rejecting background events involving W bosons that are not associated with a top quark. We observed that the top quark polarization measurement can be optimized by minimizing the background fraction, which occurs when the electron and neutrino have similar transverse energies. This occurs less frequently than other high-energy combinations, allowing for a more distinctive low-background sample with a 5σ significance in half the integrated luminosity. This study will guide the development of dedicated analyses for measuring the top quark polarization at future colliders, particularly those involving less common processes like the t-channel. Additionally, it underscores the importance of thorough background studies, control regions, and simultaneous analyses of related processes to uncover the top quark polarization, a fundamental phenomenon that could provide insight into new physics beyond the Standard Model. This study also highlights the importance of considering real and virtual missing transverse momenta, as well as initial- and final-state radiation, in the analysis of top quark polarization, as well as potential new physics affecting the W boson's decay. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in high magnetic fields provide direct evidence for the existence of a long-range order induced by the LaAlO$_3$ layers and offer insights into the spin dynamics within the LaNiO$_3$ layers, suggesting that they behave like an itinerant antiferromagnetic system at low temperatures. Our results also indicate a transition from an intrinsic to a surface-dominated spin lattice relaxation mechanism as the number of LaAlO$_3$ layers decreases, attributed to increased carrier concentration at interfaces. We have further observed an increase in the spin lattice relaxation time in high magnetic fields, a phenomenon more pronounced in the interfaces, where it is thought to result from an alignment of the initial spins within the LaAlO$_3$ layers. These findings are a significant contribution to the understanding of the correlated metallic state in these systems and have important implications for the surface modification of LaAlO$_3$ induced by LaNiO$_3$ layers. Current evaluation sets for conversational systems focus on extended, single-threaded conversations. These sets fail to capture the complex conversation patterns seen in real-world discussions, which are often characterized by multiple branches and divergent topic changes. To address this limitation, we introduce MultiTalk, a large-scale evaluation set consisting of over 25,000 annotated conversation turns. Distinguishing features of this set include conversational branches that explore multiple subtopics and abrupt topic shifts, which require models to naturally navigate between related and unrelated subjects. Moreover, we incorporate contextual connections and contrasting statements to assess a model's ability to grasp contextual elements and maintain coherent thought processes. Establishing a new benchmark for conversational evaluation, MultiTalk is designed to evaluate a model's capacity to engage in natural, high-degree branching conversations. We introduce MultiTalk-Eval, a suite of evaluation tasks tailored to assess various aspects of conversational understanding and generation. This evaluation framework is open-sourced and employs a combination of automatic and human-assisted evaluation methods, including both task-based and reference-free assessments. Our findings demonstrate significant discrepancies between the performance of state-of-the-art models on standard evaluation sets and their limited capacity to handle complex conversation scenarios. We address this issue by presenting a new model, MultiTalk-Model, which leverages a diverse set of child domains to capture underlying relational patterns. This model employs a novel multi-head child selector to navigate conversations involving multiple subtopics and employs a contrastive memory-augmented context encoder to incorporate contextual elements. We showcase its capacity to generate natural, high-degree branching conversations and highlight its superiority over baseline models. The code for MultiTalk-Eval is available at https://github.com/ghulou/MultiTalk-Eval. The model code is available at https://github.com/ghulou/MultiTalk-Model. The evaluation framework code is written in Python and utilizes the following libraries: PyTorch; Transformers by HuggingFace; Numpy; Tensors; and MultiThreaded Processing. We introduce a novel computational method that enables a full N-body simulation in modified gravity models, specifically those involving conformally coupled theories. Our approach is fast and exhaustive, with results equivalent to N-body simulations for the same system. We apply this technique to investigate three distinct scenarios involving conformally coupled gravity: (1) a factor that halves the cosmic constant, (2) a factor that triples the cosmic constant, and (3) a factor that doubles the cosmic constant in the present day. For each scenario, we conduct an N-body simulation and a fast, comprehensive simulation with the same initial conditions, comparing their internal structure at the present day. Our findings support the idea that fast N-body simulations can model N-body systems with similar internal structures at the present day, further demonstrating the feasibility of using fast simulations to explore a wide range of modified gravity models. WorkingWiki retains the core features of MediaWiki that facilitate rich, structured knowledge representation, including tables, lists, and nested pages. Additionally, it offers a range of features that enhance user experience and support for a variety of input methods, such as mouse, keyboard and voice. Through a thorough usability evaluation and a practical application, our project aims to explore the potential of public versions of WorkingWiki that enable community contribution and management. A computational approach has been developed to study the interaction between turbulent flame reactions and acoustic oscillations in combustion processes. By applying a linearized framework, it minimizes heat release fluctuations caused by acoustic waves' impact on flame dynamics, while still capturing the large amplitude effects on combustion acoustics. To model this phenomenon, active flame methods were modified to include negative feedback mechanisms, describing how heat release responds to temperature changes in the combustion process. Additionally, a specified active flame response time was incorporated to analyze how heat release fluctuations are influenced by acoustic pressure oscillations in both closed and open combustion chambers. Numerical simulations based on this model accurately predict the decreased amplitude of heat release fluctuations when acoustic oscillations are induced in a specific frequency range, showing good agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, it was observed that increasing the active flame response time or specific frequency range leads to a larger than expected amplitude of heat release fluctuations. This approach has the potential to be applied to more complex combustion systems while retaining its fundamental principles. We present a novel method to pinpoint specific groups of coupled neurons that are exhibiting synchronized multi-part patterns of activity, known as travelling chimeras, within large-scale heterogeneous networks of coupled neurons. Our method is robust and efficiently detects these dynamic patterns, even in scenarios where a large proportion of the network is composed of randomly connected, noise-making neurons. Additionally, we have developed a complementary technique that flags nodes contributing to the emergence of synchronized patterns in the network. Through the application of these methods to various integrated networks, we have gained a deeper understanding of the structure and functioning of dynamic patterns in these integrated systems. Our research showcases that in some cases, synchronized patterns emerge due to the unique properties of specific groups of coupled neurons, while in other situations, the connectivity of the network itself gives rise to these patterns. Furthermore, we have a method to identify the impact of specific groups of coupled neurons on the emergence of synchronized patterns in the network. Our methods are also capable of handling a wide range of types of coupled networks. We have discovered that a specific type of synchronized pattern, known as a rotating spiral, can arise from the integration of two separate parts of a network: one that is similar to a spiral wave and another that is composed of a spiral wave that is reversing direction. We have further found that in some cases, a rotating spiral wave can emerge due to the connection between two separate groups of coupled neurons located at different points in the network. Our research has also provided a method to detect the areas of a network that are contributing to the emergence of a traveling spiral wave. We have discovered that a specific type of synchronized multi-part pattern, known as a mirror spiral, can arise from the integration of two separate parts of a network: one that is similar to a spiral wave and another that is composed of a spiral wave that is reflecting. We have further found that in some cases, a mirror spiral wave can emerge due to the connection between two separate groups of coupled neurons located at different points in the network. Our research has also provided a method to detect the areas of a network that are contributing to the emergence of a traveling spiral wave. These discoveries have a broader implication on understanding the dynamics of complex networks as they demonstrate that highly interconnected networks can still exhibit precise patterns of activity due to the specific characteristics of their connected components. This insight enables us to formulate a more comprehensive solar photon flux function that can be used to explain long-lasting solar gamma-ray bursts. Furthermore, we discover that the spherical model's flux is consistently higher than observed values, likely due to the Earth's viewing angle or additional photon sources. This photon flux function can be applied to predict solar photon flux at any energy level, solar distance, and angle of observation. Additionally, we use this function to model typical solar photon flux at the Earth over a prolonged solar cycle period. This model demonstrates that the Earth experiences high-energy photons even when solar activity appears low. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling conflicts efficiently. Writing to the most recent version eliminates conflicts, but this approach is inefficient due to replication factors greater than two. Our Eliminate-Win design framework focuses on non-blocking, tuple-based data storage with low latency conflicts resolved by writing to the most recent version, allowing for replication factors greater than two. The framework involves three core components: Version Management, Value Management, and Elimination Logic. Version Management tracks version histories for each data item, using a version tree with nodes representing versions and their corresponding values. Value Management selects the version to write based on version relationships and the replication factor. Elimination Logic prevents conflicts by checking version relationships, triggering a new version merge when necessary. We applied the Eliminate-Win framework to design a Conflicts-Avoiding Distributed Map data structure, demonstrating its effectiveness with a peer-to-peer implementation. Our evaluation shows that, compared to a conflict-free base implementation using vector clocks, our design exhibits up to 17x performance improvement, 27% lower memory usage, and 1.5x more transactions per second with a replication factor of 8. Additionally, we open-source our implementation to facilitate further research and system development. With wide applicability, our design framework can be adapted to create various conflict-free replicated data structures. We discover that fast waves can generate long-lived shocks at the star's boundary, potentially leading to mass loss rates comparable to observed values, while slow waves cause heating in the envelope and eventually induce a broader shockwave that can break free from the star and continue into the surrounding interstellar medium. We also find evidence that these wave-shocks can result in multiple distinct phenomena, such as fast-moving "nascent" blastwaves, interacting shocks, and temporary increases in mass loss rates. The outcomes of our study have important implications for the development of deep learning algorithms capable of handling big data streams. Recent advancements in wide professional context use cases, such as autonomous vehicles and large language models, demand substantial computing power and have sparked significant interest in system design that maintains high performance while reducing energy consumption and heat generation. To achieve this, we propose a new design approach, HyperDegrade, which degrades the instruction stream through a combination of unnecessary instruction suppression and data re-arrangement to utilize existing out-of-order execution capabilities. To facilitate efficient electrochemical memory access, we introduce a new memory access pattern called gradient access. The proposed system design, encompassing both CPU and memory components, is showcased using a specific memory technology. Our results indicate that HyperDegrade can attain a 5-10x decrease in energy consumption, from GHz to MHz ranges, for various applications demonstrating substantial performance improvements over conventional system designs. The source code of our evaluation is openly available online. To maintain scalability, future research should concentrate on increasing system tolerance to program overhead. To this end, we outline initial evaluation results on various applications with varying levels of program overhead. Our preliminary findings suggest that future research directions focusing on program overhead should aim for a 10-20x decrease in energy consumption. To facilitate further research on program overhead, we define a criterion for acceptable system overhead known as the hybrid threshold, which balances the system's overhead against performance degradation. Our investigation on various applications with different levels of program overhead contributes to defining this criterion. To utilize this criterion in future studies, we introduce a method for predicting program overhead before actual execution. Our results on various applications with unknown program overhead, using our prediction method, show data points below the hybrid threshold, indicating they could benefit from further research on program overhead. To facilitate such research, we highlight potential research directions on program overhead by categorizing existing applications into four zones based on their overhead along with the hybrid threshold. To explore future system design possibilities with programs having unknown overhead, we outline a protocol for evaluating such applications. Our evaluation protocol utilizes a combination of actual system evaluations and program analysis. To utilize this protocol for any new application with unknown overhead, we outline a set of criteria along with a method for program analysis. To facilitate fair comparison of future research on program overhead, we introduce a standard system design configuration along with a method for program analysis. To utilize this standard configuration along with program analysis for any new application, we outline a protocol for actual system evaluations. To explore future system design possibilities with programs having unknown overhead, we introduce a method for program analysis along with a combination of actual system evaluations and program analysis.

A recent study suggesting the Higgs boson's mass could be over 1 TeV to avoid violating experimental limits from the LHC has rekindled interest in resolving the anomaly within the Standard Model's (SM) magnetic moment of the muon. To investigate this, we examine existing one-Standard-Model-Extension (1SME) models that address the SM muon g-2 anomaly and evaluate which of these models can still successfully explain the Higgs mass. Out of the 50 1SME models considered, 17 can still fit the Higgs mass data accurately, whereas models that fail to do so often require a significantly large new energy scale, thus potentially contradicting existing limits from the tau g-2 and Higgs diphoton decay width. Moreover, we find that within the viable range, the average new energy scale for the 1SME models that can explain the Higgs mass is still below 10 TeV, indicating that future high-precision measurements of the Higgs mass could provide further clues about these models. To support theoretical model builders, we also introduce an open-data repository that incorporates a publicly accessible Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) engine, enabling the derivation of confidence intervals or specific values for the new parameters of these 1SME models based on existing data from the LHC, muon g-2, and tau g-2. This repository can be accessed through an online interface at https://github.com/1SME-Anomaly/analysis/tree/data-release-2022, where we have incorporated the statistical analysis for the 50 1SME models considered in this study. This work serves as an expansion of our earlier study in arXiv:2005.03140, where we explored 16 out of these 50 models, and it presents a more comprehensive analysis of the 1SME frameworks that could potentially resolve the SM's internal anomalies while still fitting the Higgs mass data accurately. The ratio of the width to the mass of the Higgs boson, $\gamma$, is a critical parameter that determines the fate of the Higgs sector and has profound implications for the mixing between the Higgs boson and other scalar fields.  As a two-body decay process from a parent that is neither a meson nor a baryon, the $\gamma$ parameter's influence is evident in a range of processes however, its value cannot be directly determined from tree-level deaths alone.  In order to obtain an estimate for $\gamma$, a parameter $\kappa$ is introduced which represents the deviation of the Higgs boson's interaction strength with a particular parent particle type from the predicted standard model value.  As a result of these deviations in the Higgs boson's interactions, changes in the rates of the associated decay processes are generated which, in turn, enable the determination of $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ by utilizing data from multiple processes.  Given that a broader range of processes contribute to the decay of the heavy parent particles, such as top quarks and heavy non-Abelian gauge bosons, which all share similar $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ parameters, it is clear that future global fits will likely provide more precise estimates of these parameters.  In fact, studies have already demonstrated that a future 100 TeV pp collider will be capable of accurately determining the value of $\gamma$ in 1 standard deviation or less.  In order to further investigate the feasibility of achieving such a precise determination at a 100 TeV pp collider at the LHC's expected energy and luminosity, a series of studies has been conducted by combining results from the CHAMPION-WT and HiggsFeynMan working groups and the outcomes will be presented in this paper.  In particular, attention will be paid to controlling the systematics in a global fit, the impact of higher-order corrections, and the role of experimental constraints in determining the value of $\gamma$.  In addition, the outcomes of these studies will be presented in the context of the current understanding of the behavior of $\gamma$ in various processes as a function of the mass of the parent particles.  In order to determine $\gamma$ with the highest level of precision possible, it will be necessary to accurately model the underlying physics in a manner that is consistent across all processes and to incorporate all available experimental constraints in a global fit. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of tropical curves can be expressed as a finite extension of the tropical semifield. This involves breaking down tropical weights into a set of independent weights, achieving a rational function semifield that is isomorphic to the product of fields associated with these weights. Furthermore, we prove that the rational function semifields of tropical curves are finitely generated by examining the fields within these products. Specifically, for a tropical curve defined by inequalities given by $g_i(x_j)\geq 0$, its rational function semifield can be represented as the product of fields based on independent weights derived from the inequalities. This representation provides a foundation for further studying the algebraic properties of tropical curves through the lens of model theory. We extend this understanding to tropical schemes by demonstrating that their rational function semifields can be obtained as the product of rational function semifields of their irreducible components. Additionally, we explore the relationship between tropical schemes and their geometric interpretations. We establish that the rational function semifield of a tropical scheme can be expressed as a finite extension of its generic point's rational function semifield. This connection between geometric points and rational function semifields enables us to utilize geometric techniques to analyze the latter. We also prove that the rational function semifield of a tropical scheme is a prime semifield if and only if its geometric realization is a non-singular variety. Building on this, we show that the rational function semifield of a tropical projective space is a finite extension of the rational function semifield of its geometric counterpart. Finally, we investigate the Descent Property for tropical schemes. We define a stronger descent property, which we term'strong descent', and demonstrate that it is equivalent to having a geometric realization consisting of disjoint components. We then prove that a tropical scheme exhibits strong descent if and only if its rational function semifield can be expressed as the product of fields, providing a more nuanced understanding of this property. We explore how strong descent relates to other algebraic properties such as being a discrete valuation ring (DVR) or a principal ideal domain (PID). We demonstrate that a tropical scheme with a strong descent property is always a DVR, and conversely that a tropical DVR always possesses strong descent. However, we also identify a counterexample showing that not all tropical schemes with strong descent are DVRs, and another counterexample demonstrating that not all DVRs exhibit strong descent. Lastly, we examine how strong descent relates to the algebraic-geometric duality of tropical curves, showing that it holds for all tropical curves.

To accelerate fixed-speed point light source localization in planar environments, this research introduces a novel method that involves multiple agents collaborating. By treating each agent's location as a virtual light source and applying a minimum sum technique, the method splits the search space into regions defined by bisecting lines. These regions are then prioritized for detection based on their distance from the origin, with the closest one being identified through a voting system. To efficiently manage data exchange between agents, the protocol limits notifications to only those regions that could potentially contain the source or have already been ruled out. This collaboration-centric approach is comparable to traditional source-finding methods in terms of complexity and can be implemented using basic robotics tools. A demonstration of the algorithm in an office environment utilizing a 2D lidar sensor and multiple robots is also presented. By assuming each agent has a separate source and applying a method called ordinal multi-agent search, the protocol can be extended to find the closest source in a scenario where the light sources are not distinct. This extension is then tested with a dataset generated by a 3D simulator. In addition, the paper explores a method called K-ordinal multi-agent search for finding the k closest sources and demonstrates its performance with a dataset created by a 3D simulator. This approach has potential applications in a wide range of source-finding scenarios beyond point light source localization. Finally, the paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00431. Additionally, an associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/5Q5s1jL5s5Q. This research was funded by the AFOSR under award number FA9550-20-1-0394 and included a demonstration of the algorithm at the 2022 ICRA conference in the form of a poster. In 2023, the protocol was nominated for the Best Application Paper Award at the 2023 IROS conference. This research involved a collaboration with the University of Colorado Boulder and took place at the University of Colorado Boulder. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ku2497/ordinal-mas. The 3D simulation environment used in this research is based on Vizard from WorldViz and can be set up with a default configuration provided in the code repository. As Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) precision tools mature, their applications will soon require more accurate calculations that go beyond leading-order approximations. To achieve this level of accuracy, researchers need to develop effective ways to combine perturbative predictions with non-perturbative effects at small distances. To address this challenge, the amplitude-based resummation approach has shown promise, but its current limitations mainly stem from the absence of a proper matching framework. Without a common language to describe both perturbative properties and non-perturbative effects, it's difficult to trust their combination. To break this barrier, we've established a clear set of criteria that potential models of non-perturbative QCD must satisfy in order to be compatible with the amplitude-based resummation framework. We also demonstrate the feasibility of this framework in correctly describing static QCD quantities and improving the accuracy of dynamic processes at intermediate energies. However, we also identify static quantities as particularly sensitive to how non-perturbative effects are modeled, underscoring the need for further exploration of amplitude-based resummation in its own right, independent of its potential for precision predictions. Ultimately, we emphasize that the development of a proper matching framework remains a critical open issue in the field. To move forward, we need to consider a broader framework that accounts for both perturbative properties and non-perturbative effects, and we must push the boundaries of current research beyond static quantities if we hope to make precision progress in QCD. To that end, we conclude by highlighting several promising directions for further investigation. We also examine the issue of IR enhancement in amplitude-based resummation more closely, including a more detailed analysis of static vs. dynamic processes, as well as a more in-depth exploration of the role of soft functions and their relationships to the Borel-Laplace sum. We also raise the question of whether impact factors can be effectively used in place of amplitude-based resummation in certain cases, and we provide a more detailed explanation of the requirements for non-perturbative models in the context of amplitude-based resummation, including a more close examination of the problem of potential IR divergence in amplitude-based resummation, as well as a more detailed explanation of the proposed resolution. Finally, we also provide a more detailed explanation of the results for static and dynamic processes in the context of amplitude-based resummation, and we provide a more close examination of the issue of whether amplitude-based resummation can be effectively used in place of impact factors in certain cases.

This paper uncovers an array of cunning attacks on models being trained vertically using federated learning. These attacks deliberately circumvent the security measures in place by exploiting the behavior of users in a manner that is common to all and, therefore, goes undetected. We demonstrate that threats of this kind significantly compromise the efficacy of model training and may force researchers to sacrifice both model accuracy and privacy for protection. Moreover, we show that even seemingly minor assaults can achieve undesirable outcomes and, therefore, urge the community to acknowledge the existence and gravity of these issues so that more robust security protocols can be devised. We also introduce an innovative method called 'Private Assailant Model Learning' that identifies and counters these attacks by training a second model that is used for prediction purposes and includes both user behavior and data in its classification features. We evaluate this approach using a range of assaults and find it to be an effective solution in safeguarding both training and inference through the use of encrypted models. We believe this work will serve as a foundation for creating more secure and robust protocols in the field of vertical federated learning. We have made our code and data set publicly available at https://github.com/PranavSurya/PAMLE. For further information, please do not hesitate to contact us at pranav.surya@utdallas.edu or zhewang@utdallas.edu. We are open to any form of collaboration or discussion. We have included a Chinese version of this abstract at the end of this document. It has been pointed out to us that research into the realm of vertical federated learning through publicly available data sets is in its nascent stages. We are currently expanding the scope of our work to include horizontal federated learning and look forward to receiving valuable feedback from our peers. It is our intention to present this research as a part of Federated Learning 2023 Workshop but we might consider submitting it to a premier conference such as NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR instead, should the community deem it worthy. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various tasks including classification, regression, and clustering. Despite their widespread use, kernel functions require substantial memory to store, especially for methods like kernel principal component analysis (KPCA). To circumvent this issue, researchers have explored low-rank approximations and implicit kernel methods which can achieve similar results without storing the full kernel matrix. Another approach is kernel estimation, which can be either a fixed or data-dependent method. This paper focuses on the latter, where the kernel function is determined based on input data and aims to enhance the accuracy of subsequent kernel-based applications. We introduce an innovative method called pseudo random Fourier traits (PRFTs) that utilizes a random Fourier feature map to implicitly represent the kernel function. By leveraging the characteristics of Fourier transforms, we propose an efficient and data-dependent kernel estimation formula which can be computed in O(n d^2) time, significantly outperforming existing alternatives. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a simplified noise model and extensive experimentation on real-world datasets for both classification and clustering. Our results show that our PRFTs-based kernel estimation surpasses existing methods and often achieves comparable or better performance than fixed kernel functions. The implementation and data used in this paper are now publicly available online. This research provides a thorough theoretical framework for implicit kernel feature maps and sets a new high standard for future research in this area. It also offers a practical solution that can be applied to numerous kernel-based methods, potentially leading to improved results in those applications. This work is a direct outcome of our earlier research on low-rank kernel learning and the associated challenges it poses. We hope this paper will contribute meaningfully to the development of next-generation implicit kernel learning algorithms. Additionally, we anticipate our results to serve as a performance benchmark for future research in this domain. This paper represents a culmination of our research over the course of two years. It has already been presented at ECML PKAW 2017 and our results are derived from the extended version of that research. We first introduced our approach in a paper presented at the 2015 ICDM workshop on "Advanced Techniques for Related Tasks" and has since become a well-established research outcome from our research team. We are now exploring potential connections between our work and the recent breakthroughs in implicit kernel learning. It is our intention to formalize our approach as a kernel implementation in an open-source repository that can be used for various kernel-based methods.
