In this study, we illustrate how to represent groups using wreath products by breaking down natural numbers into non-empty subsets (cartesian factors), which yields a product whose components align with the groups acting transitively on these subsets. We also establish rules for a suitable action on the union of these subsets, enabling us to derive the structure of the resulting group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every group with a specific permutation representation can be expressed as a wreath product over its subgroups acting on individual elements of a given set. This technique is applicable to both finite and infinite groups. We further expand on this by generalizing group representations using cartesian factors, which allows for the expression of a given group as a product whose components act on individual elements of a given set. We also provide a more versatile version of this general case, which includes group extensions and the infinite version of group representations using cartesian factors. We apply these general cases to group extensions with abelian subgroups and the infinite version of Baer-Kurosh theorem. Additionally, we explore group actions on natural numbers using a specific ordering, which leads to the conclusion that every group with a specific permutation representation can be expressed as a Gaussian or regular wreath product over its subgroups acting on individual elements of a given set. We also provide a more general version of this conclusion for groups with a specific permutation representation on natural numbers using a specific ordering, which includes group extensions and the infinite version of this conclusion. We also provide a more general version of this conclusion for groups with a specific permutation representation on natural numbers using a specific ordering, which leads to the conclusion that every such group can be expressed as a Gaussian or regular wreath product over its subgroups acting on individual elements of a given set. This study investigates the capability of U-Net-based cardiac segmentation networks to accurately output reliable results on individuals with rare congenital heart defects, using data from adult cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Given the limited nature of available medical imaging data, particularly in the field of congenital heart disease, we hypothesize that models trained on more common conditions will struggle with segments that are uncommon or hard to differentiate. To test this hypothesis, a diverse range of rare heart defect cases were selected and their segmented MR images assessed for both intra-rater reproducibility and inter-rater accuracy. Two models were trained and their performance was compared to automated segmentation results. Our data shows that while U-Net-based models can generate clinically acceptable results for certain rare defects, others yielded significantly inferior outcomes. These findings highlight the difficulties of modeling uncommon cardiac structures and suggest that more advanced models or data sets will be required to produce high-fidelity results across the full spectrum of congenital heart disease. Given the growing need for precision medical tools in the treatment of congenital heart disease, this study provides a starting point for further research into these issues. To facilitate further inquiry, the results and models presented here have been made publicly available through an online repository. To overcome the limitations encountered in this study, potential solutions such as incorporating unlabeled data sets or using models that learn from raw imaging data are also discussed. Finally, the high variability inherent in manual cardiac measurements and assessments, coupled with the potential for both human error and bias, underscores the need for the automated analysis of cardiac structures that can provide both reproducible and unbiased results. In the context of cardiac care, this implies using machine learning models with a focus on diversity-sensitivity training, data set diversity, and measures to mitigate any potential bias. In the long term, incorporating such models into clinical practice will be essential for producing accurate and unbiased assessments that can guide surgical planning and other medical interventions. In the case of cardiac surgery, models like deep learning-based models should be trained on diverse data sets that include a wide range of heart structures found across the full spectrum of congenital heart disease, as well as on validation data sets that have been vetted by multiple experts to ensure accuracy and reliability. Furthermore, the development of more sophisticated models that can handle not only segmentation but also other key aspects of cardiac imaging analysis will also be a crucial area of research. The primary aim of Word Meaning Clarification (WMC) involves comprehending a target word through the analysis of its definitions, typically found on online lexical resources such as Wikipedia. This project focuses on leveraging context-specific information found in Wikipedia definitions to enhance the understanding of a target word. Initially, we develop a strong baseline model, named GlossBERT, which incorporates BERT-based representations of a word's definitions to predict its relatedness to various context sentences. This model is trained on a vast dataset created from Wikipedia definitions and is evaluated through a Word Meaning Clarification Task. To further improve performance, we introduce an innovative strategy called Contrastive Definition Augmentation, which enriches the representations of definitions by matching a target word's definitions to its own contextual appearances. Compared to conventional approaches, this method proves particularly effective for less common words. As a result, GlossBERT has shown substantial enhancements in predicting a target word's semantic similarities, lexical substitutes, and classification on Google's WordSense. Moreover, it demonstrates superiority over other strong BERT-based competitors. Additionally, we discover that GlossBERT accurately captures the grammatical aspects of a target word from its definitions, outperforming state-of-the-art neural models in tasks such as Part-of-Speech Tagging and Morphological Analysis. This work has the potential to contribute to the development of strong neural-based models for Word Sense Disambiguation and Semantic Role Labeling. The code and models developed in this project are now publicly available for further research advancements. Moreover, it paves the way for exploring other contextual inference tasks that rely on definition-specific information. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on individual node removal. In contrast, our analysis investigates the effects of removing entire edges from a random Erdos-Renyi graph, providing insights into the standard of living of the remaining nodes. We measure this through the average degree of the nodes in the network. Our findings show that, as the number of removed edges increases, the distribution of node degrees in the remaining network follows a skewed, almost normal pattern, until it converges to a Poisson distribution. To facilitate this understanding, we develop a theoretical model for the degree distribution of subgraphs extracted from an Erdos-Renyi graph. This model demonstrates that, for a large enough subgraph, the degree distribution approximates a Poisson distribution, given that each edge is independently included in the subgraph with a specific probability. This inclusion is based on the specific conditions of our reference scenario, namely removing edges from a large Erdos-Renyi graph with n nodes. In this scenario, the probability of including each edge is approximately 1 - (log n)/n. This understanding enables us to analyze the standard of living of the nodes in the subgraph by utilizing the properties of a specific random variable that represents the degree of a node in the subgraph, now known as the "Cayley variable." To further demonstrate the effects of removing edges, we derive the distribution of this variable for a large enough subgraph and show that it follows an exponential distribution with a specific mean. This distribution provides a clear standard for measuring the living conditions of the nodes in the subgraph, allowing us to identify the specific subgraph sizes where the standard of living of the nodes begins to converge to this exponential distribution. This convergence occurs around a subgraph size of 10^16 for a graph with 10^6 nodes. To place this in context, modern online social networks typically have fewer than 10 million nodes. A subsequent analysis of two distinct power-law networks, constructed using the configuration model, reveals that removing edges in these networks induces a more gradual shift in the standard of living of the nodes, when compared to the exponential distribution observed in the Erdos-Renyi graph. The concept of "Big Apple" strength, representing a critical opulence of nucleon pairs across the entire nuclear spectrum, is redefined in this study through the use of chiral unitary theory. We demonstrate that a pronounced signal, characterized by a significant gap in spectral density, is necessary to assess the degree of convergence in a system's density of states. By applying this concept to finite nuclei, we find that only systems with a significant spectral gap exhibit "Big Apple" strength. Conversely, systems without such a gap fail to achieve the critical opulence of nucleon pairs. These findings are further illustrated by analyzing the $K^+$ meson production process in finite nuclei and the properties of neutron stars. The latter reveals that only dense matter models featuring a spectral gap can support two phases of dense matter existence, thereby providing an added "Big Apple" strength indicator alongside the onset of density. Additionally, we explore the relationship between "Big Apple" strength and the magnitude of meson condensation in dense matter. The proposed "Big Apple" strength criterion can be utilized to distinguish between fundamental models of finite nuclei and those of quark matter models. The associated implications are displayed through the study of absolute $B$ values in finite nuclei and the equations of state of dense matter. The "Big Apple" strength also exerts a significant impact on the dynamics of rotating neutron stars, with potential consequences observable through radio velocity measurements. The associated effects on rotating neutron stars include changes in their velocity profiles, angular velocities, and the formation of spiral density patterns, all of which are all closely linked to the unique spectral structures of quark models. The interplay between "Big Apple" strength and various physical properties of neutron stars under rotation will be the subject of our forthcoming research. We anticipate the existence of non-synchronized neutron star rotation, accompanied by oscillatory modes of dense matter, to be detectable through future radio velocity measurements. The associated wave patterns in the equatorial plane will provide valuable insights into the intricate internal structures of neutron stars. In recent years, significant progress in modeling dynamic processes has been made by combining temporal linear models with sophisticated loss functions and optimization methods. Despite achieving high performance on various tasks, a notable characteristic of these combinations is their tendency to exhibit excessive complexity, often surpassing the number of observed data points. In this research, which focuses on the temporal linear model with an invertible covariance structure, we explore how working with an over-parameterized model leads to benign overfitting. This is accomplished by establishing a theoretical framework that leverages a modified information criterion and a theoretical risk bound. This framework enables the derivation of a computationally efficient estimation method that balances model complexity and fitting accuracy. In addition to its theoretical advantages, this method also outperforms existing estimation methods in simulations and real-world experiments. In particular, it shows improved performance in high-noise settings. The source code for our experiments is available online. By addressing overfitting in temporal linear models with an invertible covariance structure, our results provide insights that may be applicable to other dynamic process models. The study also highlights the potential benefits of over-parameterization in dynamic time series modeling. The use of linear models for dynamic processes is a well-established approach with multiple applications, including forecasting, signal processing, and control system design. The recent resurgence of interest in temporal linear models, fueled by the availability of large-scale datasets and advancements in computational methods, has led to impressive performance on various tasks. However, the estimation of such models often faces challenges due to their sensitivity to noise, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. In recent years, the field of machine learning has experienced a significant surge in research driven by the availability of vast amounts of high-quality data and the development of cutting-edge computational methods. This increase in data quality has enabled researchers to explore high-dimensional parameter spaces, estimate model parameters with greater accuracy, and develop more sophisticated models. As a result, models with complex structures, such as nonlinear models and models with infinite dimensions, have become popular choices for modeling dynamic processes. These models have consistently outperformed traditional approaches in various performance metrics. One such model is the temporal linear model with an invertible covariance structure, known for its interpretability, efficiency, and effectiveness in modeling dynamic processes. However, working with an over-parameterized version of this model has raised concerns about overfitting, a well-documented issue in machine learning where the model becomes too complex to generalize from the data. In such cases, the model performs exceptionally well on the training data but fails to accurately predict outcomes on new, unseen data.

A simplified global circulation model is analyzed to understand various atmospheric circulation patterns in a simplified version of a planetary atmosphere. This analysis focuses on medium-to-high altitude circulation patterns and verifies that a specific model produces natural cyclostrophic rotation in its upper atmosphere. It then examines how other atmospheric circulation patterns are created using a simplified model that incorporates geostrophic turbulence. Some versions of the model produce geostrophic turbulence at medium altitudes and a stable, barotropically driven circulation in the lower atmosphere. It also shows that a stable wave pattern in the lower atmosphere can cause turbulence in the medium altitudes, leading to a stable, barotropically driven circulation there. Additionally, it identifies the existence of a critical altitude in these atmospheric systems, below which wave patterns dominate and above which turbulence prevails. It then explores how increasing temperature differences between the poles and the equator affect these atmospheric circulation patterns. It finds that this increase enhances turbulence in the medium altitudes and reduces the stability of the circulation in the lower atmosphere, potentially leading to wave breakdown and the formation of tropical cyclones. It also examines how this temperature difference affects the level of turbulence in the medium altitudes, finding that it shifts the critical altitude for turbulence but does not change the fundamental relationship between this turbulence and stable wave patterns in the lower atmosphere. It then analyzes how this temperature difference influences the location of maximum wind speed in the upper atmosphere. It finds that it moves it poleward due to an increase in the angular momentum of the atmospheric system, but remains unaware of previous works on this topic. It also discusses the simplifications used in these models and potential sources of geostrophic turbulence. It then sets the stage for the second part of this study, which will examine low-altitude circulation patterns in these atmospheric systems. It uses a model that includes the effects of a rotating planet on atmospheric circulation and assumes that atmospheric rotation is weak compared to the planet's rotation. It also discusses the implications of these models for other gas giants and super-rotation in general. It concludes that these models can be applicable to various gas giants despite their simplifications and that they provide a foundation for investigating the atmospheric circulation of these planets in greater detail. It also highlights the importance of further research into the atmospheric circulation of these planets using high-resolution numerical models that can capture the formation of turbulent eddies and unstable wave breakdown in these systems. It finally suggests that such models can be used to study the atmospheric circulation of these planets more accurately and provide a greater understanding of the formation of turbulent winds in these systems.

Further analysis highlights the significance of dynamic learning for large-scale 
learning via increased model reliability and improved performance.

Researchers suggest that the fourth-order cumulants of the energy-magnetization correlations in the Ising model can distinguish between different universality classes. To confirm this, we calculate the scaling dimensions of these cumulants in three-dimensional Ising, cubic discrete Ising, and classical Ising models. Using conformal field theory, we find that the scaling dimensions of the fourth-order cumulants in the Ising model are $y_{EEHH} = 4.80011(4),$ $y_{MMHH} = 1.80011(4),$ and $y_{EMH^3} = 7.79994(5),$ which are all unique and distinct from those in the cubic discrete Ising universality class. Additionally, we determine the central charges of the Ising model using the Bavrh-McGovern and cardy formulas, obtaining $c_{BM} = 0.7937(2)$ and $c_C = 0.7935(2)$. Our findings support the theory that the Ising model belongs to a distinct universality class than the cubic discrete Ising model. Furthermore, we observe that the scaling dimensions of the fourth-order cumulants in the classical Ising model are $y_{EEHH} = 4.80011(4),$ $y_{MMHH} = 1.80011(4),$ and $y_{EMH^3} = 7.79994(5)$. This means that the classical Ising model also belongs to the same universality class as the Ising model. Our results also provide evidence that the four-dimensional discrete Ising model, using the cardy formula, has a zero central charge. Long music playlists often struggle with clear summaries, making it difficult for users to understand their content. This problem is a key challenge in summarizing extensive music collections found in online platforms. This research focuses on automating playlist summaries by selecting and annotating a limited number of tracks, incorporating a special symbol to indicate exclusion. We combine text-based data augmentation with a novel annotation formula to achieve this task. Our results show that our method produces high-quality summaries for both individual tracks and entire playlists, compared to existing models and human-generated summaries. This technique demonstrates potential for summarizing large music datasets by reducing the emphasis on explicit negative feedback. In addition, it allows for flexible summary formats, including the inclusion of implicit important tracks. This is the first study on music playlist summarization through annotation. Some future work areas include exploring other annotation rules, such as multi-step instructions and conditions, as well as comparing different text-based data augmentation strategies. These potential extensions may provide valuable insights that can advance the field as a whole. Finally, we believe that developing efficient and effective algorithms for music summarization will inevitably lead to further breakthroughs in this area. In particular, we anticipate gaining valuable experience from solving these sequential annotation problems, which may eventually enable us to tackle other challenging tasks in the music domain. This, in turn, will allow us to make significant contributions to the broader field of natural language processing. With regards to the annotation task at hand, we propose the use of a special symbol, denoted as \#, to indicate the exclusion of a track from the playlist. We then introduce a data-driven approach to specify the conditions under which a track should be included in the summary, which we term the annotation formula. This approach is unique in that it leverages a combination of explicit and implicit criteria, which are used to select the most representative tracks for the summary. We represent the annotation formula as a linear combination of features derived from the network, which is learned through a process involving both supervised and unsupervised components. Continual learning aims to allow a model to consistently perform well on new data sets after being trained on multiple independent data sets. Several methods have been proposed to achieve this by preventing the model from overfitting to new data, reducing the impact of previous learning, or exploiting the structure of sequences. Surprisingly, many of these methods assume that the model should be retrained from scratch on each new data set, without exploring the benefits of pre-trained models. This study challenges this assumption by comparing the performance of pre-trained models against a straightforward baseline that freezes the model's weights and only updates the head layers on each new data set. The evaluation is conducted across four tasks and reveals that the baseline consistently outperforms the methods that aim to prevent the model from overfitting to new data sets. The study suggests that the reason for this superiority lies in the improved capacity of the model to process new data without being hindered by the constraints of previous learning. The findings imply that the model's ability to process new data is more critical than its ability to extract features from previous data sets. This insight has significant implications for the field of continual learning, emphasizing the need to address the challenge as an efficient use of computational resources rather than a problem of overfitting. To this end, the study contributes a new evaluation protocol that assesses the performance of models on new data sets while also considering the additional computational costs incurred during training. This protocol enables a more comprehensive comparison of methods that aim to achieve continual learning without sacrificing too much performance on new data sets. This study further explores the benefits of pre-trained models in continual learning through the lens of information theory. The analysis indicates that the model's initial training facilitates an increase in the entropy of its internal representation, enabling it to effectively capture the mutual information between data points from different categories. This, in turn, allows the model to efficiently learn from new data sets with reduced entropy. The study also delves into the benefits of pre-trained models in continual learning from an information-theoretic perspective. The analysis reveals that the model's initial training results in an increase in the entropy of its internal representation, making it well-suited to capture the mutual information between data points from different categories. We define a new concept of relative $1$-homotopy type for surfaces in a metric space and use it to categorize surfaces that minimize energy, showing that this category is both local and compact. This leads to the existence of a discrete, finite set of surfaces that are relative 1-homotopically distinct and have the lowest energy among all surfaces with the same boundary in a compact metric space. Additionally, we find that these surfaces are all minimizing when the ambient space has a curvature greater than or equal to a certain positive value. Furthermore, we establish that in a manifold with a non-positive curvature, the set of relative 1-homotopically distinct surfaces with the lowest energy is infinite. Building on this, we investigate how these surfaces evolve over time in a dynamic setting and use our results to provide evidence for the Variton Form of the Harnack's Conjecture. Specifically, we demonstrate that in a homogeneous space with a positive curvature, any surface that minimizes energy while preserving its structure, will do so for all time. Moreover, we show that in a manifold with a non-positive curvature, the set of surfaces that minimize energy while preserving their structure, form a discrete, finite subset of the space of relative 1-homotopy types. Additionally, we explore how these results can be applied to a broader class of surfaces, known as varifolds, and discuss several open questions in the field.

By putting forward a dimensional analysis that takes into account surface forces, density, and friction, as well as conducting a thorough examination of prior experiments, scientists have derived a universal stress scaling that holds true across numerous types of shear-thickening materials, including polymers, composites, and granular materials. According to their stress scaling, the point at which the transition occurs is directly proportional to the square of the ratio of surface forces to shear rates and the inverse of friction. This stress scaling has been mathematically verified through a dimensionless analysis and holds true across a wide range of conditions, demonstrating that the transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity can be captured through a global scaling that is independent of variables such as particle size, shear rate, and surface force. Furthermore, this stress scaling enables the prediction of stress at which shear-thickening materials will become rigid for any given mixture, providing a fundamental understanding of the physics underlying shear thickening. Additionally, scientists have derived a new equation for scaling that takes into account the effects of surface forces and friction on shear thickening, presenting a pathway for the design of materials that can withstand high stresses without becoming rigid. In particular, by increasing the ratio of surface forces to shear rates beyond a critical point, scientists have observed a sudden decrease in the stress at which shear-thickening materials will become rigid, revealing a stress gap in materials that can remain fluid-like even at high stresses. Moreover, by scaling this stress gap in relation to surface forces, density, and friction, researchers have discovered a universal stress gap that is a nonlinear function of the dimensionless surface force-friction ratio. While shear-thickening materials will always exhibit a stress gap in some form, scientists have found that dense suspensions with low cohesivity or high compressive strength may not demonstrate a stress gap at all, whereas granular materials will always exhibit a stress gap due to their low compressive strength. Furthermore, by exploring the underlying physics of shear thickening, scientists have discovered that dense mixtures will inevitably become rigid due to the formation of temporary clusters that persist over time, providing a new perspective on the microscale behavior of these materials. Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving superfluid and supersolid phases,
especially when the two layers are interconnected. To understand the magnetic
properties, we utilized a spin-boson model and a legarithmic renormalization flow
technique, suitable for large systems. Our findings indicate that spatially
nonuniform triplon motion can be utilized to create curved superfluid phases,
supersolid phases with triangular lattice structures, and vortex lattices of various
symmetries. These exotic states arise due to competing interactions within the
two-layer system, especially when the interlayer connections are moderate in strength.
Our research also indicates that curved superfluid phases can be stabilized more
easily than supersolid phases, particularly when the interlayer interactions are
stronger. These results can be potentially validated through experimental
observation of magnetic triangulization in materials such as NiCl$_2$ and Herbertsmithite.

To efficiently achieve extremely high energies in particle accelerators, a novel new concept called a muon-ion synchrotron has been developed. This design involves accelerating low-energy ions to nearly the speed of light and then using highly energetic muons, produced through cosmic-ray interactions or created in deep-learning-controlled neutrino detectors, in a reverse process known as "inverse Compton scattering." This design can efficiently achieve energies as high as 100 TeV. For example, combining 1 TeV electrons with 100 GeV muons results in 1 TeV of energy through inverse Compton scattering, whereas using 1 TeV protons in a traditional collider would require a 100 GeV beam, which would be more technically difficult to achieve. Furthermore, a muon-ion synchrotron can operate in two modes: in "front-end" mode, it produces neutrinos by accelerating protons to near the speed of light and then using a neutral current interaction to transfer the energy to muons, and in "back-end" mode, it produces antineutrinos by first producing antimuons through a similar process involving a muon-ion conversion process. This design can also be modified to include a detector system that detects events simultaneously with the acceleration process, providing real-time feedback to the accelerator controls through a deep-learning algorithm. Examples of this design include the CLICkey and CEPC-SPPC-MI proposals, which leverage existing infrastructure such as Higgs factories and cosmic-ray detectors. These designs can potentially achieve energies as high as 100 TeV using existing detectors and infrastructure, making them highly feasible and attractive options for future high-energy particle accelerators. Additionally, a muon-ion synchrotron can also be used for photon-photon and muon-nucleus interactions, in addition to neutrino and antineutrino production, providing numerous research opportunities in physics, such as the study of hadron spectrum, quark-gluon plasma, and neutrino mass. Furthermore, a muon-ion synchrotron can also be used for space missions such as producing energy through a synchrotron in orbit or producing antimatter through a muon-ion ring in orbit. With its numerous benefits and research opportunities, a muon-ion synchrotron is an extremely promising new concept in particle acceleration that can efficiently achieve extremely high energies in a feasible and attractive design. A novel approach for obtaining respiratory motion compensation in 4D MRI is presented, where image acquisition is decoupled from motion detection. A three-point scoring system based on image quality assesses respiratory phase sorting methods, comparing the effectiveness of central k-space sampling, peripheral k-space sampling, and fetal heart rate analysis. Results show that central k-space sampling yields high scoring averages, outperforming the other methods. A body scan protocol utilizing this approach is also described, producing high-quality 4D images without the need for breath-hold poses. Data from 10 healthy adults demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in producing high-quality 4D images without significant respiratory phase errors. Additionally, a comparison with breath-hold turbo spin-echo MRI reveals comparable image quality, while data from a patient with liver metastases demonstrates the method's applicability in clinical cancer surveillance. Further optimization and testing are needed to fully evaluate the approach's cancer detection capabilities. The open-source code for this method is publicly available online. Due to its straightforward implementation, this method can be easily integrated into existing MRI systems. Despite some residual motion artifacts, the high-quality images produced make this technique suitable for body scanning. This study defines a novel topological space called the fabric space, serving as a topological framework for ordered collections of simplices from a triangulation of a manifold. It demonstrates that the fabric space incites a natural equivalence class of triangulations, which is utilized to rephrase the Homotopy Partitioning Problem in terms of analyzing the topological properties of fabric spaces. To facilitate this computation, a direct approach is outlined to explicitly determine the topological features of a given fabric space. This approach is coupled with an implicit computational strategy for examining an extensive subset of triangulations. Additionally, this study introduces the Refined Homotopy Partitioning Problem, which involves assigning a non-negative integer value to each simplex in a triangulation, before developing a computationally efficient algorithm to solve this problem for a broad class of instances. This algorithm's efficacy is illustrated through a real-world application spanning a high-dimensional manifold. That is, in total dimensions 4 and above, this problem can be efficiently solved for any locally consistent integer data set. This provides a practical solution to a previously insolvable case for a renowned problem in scientific visualization. Furthermore, this study lays the groundwork for a broader research direction centered on combinatorial topology. It is also shown that the fabric space framework is compatible with the Pyramid Decomposition Strategy, an established approach for optimizing the complexity of triangulations. This study's algorithms and concepts are implemented in an open-source software package called Hompix, which is available for download. It is a powerful tool for visually exploring high-dimensional data by rendering its underlying topology. With Hompix, data analysts can efficiently identify topological patterns within their data by simply interacting with 2D projections of the data. It supports data sets with up to 10 million points in 10-dimensional space and has already been used to analyze several large real-world data sets. This study also introduces the Hompix Challenge, an open research initiative aimed at further advancing the state-of-the-art in combinatorial topology and its applications. However, GNNs often struggle with sparsely connected graphs, generating poor performance on various benchmark datasets as a result. To overcome this limitation, our approach acquired sparsification (AS) is designed to be an efficient and flexible method that gleans a sparse subgraph from the original graph, thereby extracting a reduced GNN model while maintaining the original's classification accuracy. AS's unique mechanism, based on a tailored K-centers approach, is an intra-layer only operation, ensuring full GNN flexibility. We demonstrate AS's effectiveness through comprehensive experiments on six diverse datasets, showcasing enhanced performance over other reduction methods and even outperforming standard GNNs on several metrics. Notably, AS achieved a 92% image classification accuracy on the VGGFace dataset, a 4% improvement over the original precision. AS's reduced models also exhibited real-world applicability in graph data visualization, revealing a 20% further improvement in visualization evaluation. These models also facilitate effective visualization of the underlying structure, addressing another critical issue in GNNs. Now, AS has been incorporated into the PyTorch GNN framework. Due to its computational expense, the K-centers step is now executed using a distributed approach, with a proposed evolutionary algorithm alternative also presented. These simulations typically focus on mimicking individual characters' movements rather than the entire scene. We introduce SceneGen, an innovative system that uses neural networks to model not just individual vehicles but the entire traffic scene. Our results show that SceneGen produces scenes with movement patterns indistinguishable from actual traffic scenes, as verified through both direct comparisons and the ratings of multiple human assessors. Furthermore, SceneGen can generate vehicle paths that are practically executable in real-world scenarios. A critical aspect in developing numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of creating and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including preserving a equation's invariance, stability, or specific solution characteristics. Although such methods are highly effective at maintaining these properties, they can be computationally expensive due to their inherently high complexity. To address this limitation, a new approach has been proposed, involving the application of a lower-cost, structure-preserving discretization as a first step, followed by a more efficient implicit method for solution approximation. However, this approach introduces an implicit system of equations that needs resolution, which can be achieved via an iterative method such as Newton's method. To accelerate this process, researchers have employed Newton's method in a limited number of iterations, resulting in a highly efficient implicit code. However, the authors of this study investigate whether a simpler, non-Newton multigrid method can be an equally effective alternative for solving the large, nonlinear systems of equations arising from such time-integration methods. By constructing a specific example solution that preserves both L2 and H1 norms, the authors demonstrate that such a multigrid method can indeed successfully preserve these properties on a global level, regardless of the specific time step size. Furthermore, the authors also examine under which conditions local preservation can be achieved, providing a detailed analysis of the underlying requirements and considerations, including mesh independence, superconvergence, and smoothness. The study concludes by exploring further potential applications and considerations for such non-Newton multigrid methods, including how they can be employed in conjunction with other time-integration methods, such as the semi-implicit method, as well as potential extensions to multilevel and multiderivative methods. The authors' reference examples, spanning both one-dimensional and two-dimensional scenarios, serve as a testament to the method's practical effectiveness, resulting in highly optimized and efficient implicit codes that outperform their explicit counterparts by a factor of up to a hundred, while also up to a 30% improvement in computational time compared to their Newton multigrid counterpart. The study's findings are complemented by an open-source software library providing fully documented examples and benchmark tests that can be replicated across multiple platforms. The study's results are verifiable through the inclusion of detailed numerical experiments, accompanied by their corresponding visualizations, alongside a comprehensive reference list that highlights significant contributions from numerous researchers over the course of nearly two decades. The study's findings have a potential impact on a broad range of applications spanning fluid dynamics

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances is a crucial yet demanding task in 3D object detection. Distant objects pose a problem because their sizes are often minimal, making them easily masked by false positives. Additionally, the limited point clouds from LiDAR sensors in such ranges can result in shape ambiguity. Not only do the scores of distant objects drop more rapidly than closer ones, but the current top-performing 3D detection methods also prioritize intermediate distances over far ones. To address this, we present Far3Det, a new evaluation protocol that distinguishes intermediate and distant detection into two separate categories, with separate masks for evaluation. By applying this protocol to the Argoverse dataset, our results show that intermediate and distant detection scores drop by half when evaluated in isolation. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel range-ambiguity metric and incorporate it into an existing LiDAR-based dataset's quality assessment. Based on this analysis, we introduce a new evaluation metric that accounts for shape completeness and size, supplementing the conventional IoU metric. To tackle the sparse point clouds issue at far ranges, we present a new method for collecting supplementary LiDAR data with increased density. By incorporating boundary points and utilizing a custom filter, we enhance the density of point clouds while preserving object shapes. Our experiments demonstrate that Far3Det outperforms the baseline method by a significant margin on the Argoverse dataset, achieving a mean average precision (MAP) of 0.303 on the evaluation protocol. Our improved model's expertise was also successfully transferred to real-world applications. The code for Far3Det is publicly available at https://github.com/kuangdang/Far3Det. Our research provides a solution to the 3D detection at far ranges and offers a more comprehensive understanding of objects in this range. It paves the way for further study on middle-range objects and may be applied to other middle-range detection tasks. Additionally, our method can be a more general 3D detection benchmark. Furthermore, our results suggest that middle-range detection could serve as a pre-training task to boost performance on far ranges. This research explores the relationship between certain blocks of arrangements consisting of hyperplanes and the distribution of prime values among polynomials. A significant discovery is found in the section on "Systems of Polynomials over F_2" where we establish that for any set of linear polynomials in F_2[x], with the exception of the trivial case, the coefficients of the product of these polynomials will always include a prime value. Additionally, for a specific set of polynomials defined by arrangements of hyperplanes, we demonstrate that the number of prime values obtained from evaluating these polynomials at various points will be exactly equal to the number of hyperplanes. The research further delves into examining arrangements of hyperplanes within the context of prime values among polynomials through the use of combinatorial methods and finite fields. A key contribution involves describing a wider class of block arrangements that maintain the desired property, thereby providing a more general framework. This new framework applies not only to polynomials over F_2 but also to polynomials within finite fields of any size, except for the case where the field size equals two. In such cases, exceptions may arise, as illustrated by a specific set of polynomials in F_4[x]. A crucial aspect of this research involves identifying both upper and lower limits for the number of prime values that may result from evaluating a set of polynomials, depending on the configuration of their arrangements. This discovery has significant implications, given its connection to a more broadly defined problem concerning the number of possible configurations within a given range. As a result, this research provides a solution for a specific instance of this problem, namely when the target value is any number within the range of (1/4)n to (1/2)n, for any number n. During its brightest phase, spectra were collected by the AstroSat in detail, resulting in the detection of a specific type of spectral feature known as a cyclotron line and a quasi-periodic oscillation with a frequency of 0.52 Hz, both of which were in line with past observations of this source. Our study delves into the physics of this event with a focus on the interaction between the accretion disk and the electromagnetic radiation it produces, as observed by the AstroSat's optical and ultraviolet detectors. Modeling this interaction helped constrain the angle at which the accretion disk is oriented and the characteristics of the hot interstellar medium along our line of sight. Notably, the frequency of the QPO was found to be directly proportional to the inverse of the angular momentum of the accretion disk, in line with the laws of disk dynamics. This relationship also enabled us to determine the black hole-like spin parameter of the neutron star, which, however, requires further confirmation due to the marginally significant confidence level. This finding is significant as it identifies a natural limit to the accretion process's impact on the star's spin, which could have implications for understanding the evolution of compact binaries. Additionally, the detected QPO and the presence of the cyclotron line line during this flare provide valuable insights that could be utilized in studying future outbursts of this source. Furthermore, the absence of any high-frequency oscillations in this particular flare, which are often associated with the disruption of the accretion disk due to the star's strong magnetic field, may indicate that they are linked to the star's internal dynamics rather than its external environment. Hence, their presence or absence could serve as an indicator of the system's internal workings, providing a means to study the star's magnetic field through its effects on the surrounding disk. Ultimately, the detection of these phenomena in IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 flare offers a new path for exploring the physics of its accretion process, its neutron star, and its binary dynamics. We find that the heat capacity can be obtained from the second derivative of the energy with respect to electron doping. To achieve this, we first compute the electron correlation energy for various doping levels. Subsequent analysis of the data using a quadratic fit yields the heat capacity and yields a result that is an order of magnitude higher than that of doped graphene at zero temperature. Additionally, we observe that the peak intensity of the heat capacity is inversely proportional to the distance between the doping level and the Dirac point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the shielding of the long-range electric field by doping can be estimated from the heat capacity and that it varies linearly with the square of the doping level. Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball phenomenon, where a secondary symmetry acts as a 'core' within the Q-ball, and we provide a generic condition for its occurrence. This discovery is further supported by a numerical example using a SU(5) Grand Unified Theory, where we calculate the stability and mass of Q-balls comprising a single, large 'core' formed from the $SU(5)$ symmetry. This approach also facilitates a discussion on (possibly) unstable Q-balls and offers this: in scenarios where a secondary symmetry's potential curve is entirely nested within that of the primary symmetry, the charge of a Q-ball formed through a true vacuum transition will always be an integer multiple of that of a Q-ball formed through a false vacuum transition; this relationship, however, may not hold for unstable, over-sized Q-balls. This rule allows for the identification of potentially unstable, large Q-balls by analyzing their charge in relation to that of their smaller, stable counterparts. This provides a means to address the intriguing observation made in ref.[1] where the authors found a discrepancy between their results for a false and a true vacuum, suggesting a more complex Q-ball structure, without a specific theoretical framework to explain it. This framework now offers a plausible, underlying cause for such discrepancies, pin-pointing them as indicators of a Q-ball with a core. Nonetheless, this paper also highlights that, in the vast landscape of supersymmetric models, it is not uncommon for a true vacuum to feature multiple local minima, making it possible for a false vacuum to become a local minimum as well, thus allowing the formation of charged objects like Q-balls in a landscape previously thought as false. This implies that such Q-balls could, in fact, be more common than initially assumed. Furthermore, this study also suggests that even if such a true vacuum with multiple local minima does not correspond to the global minimum, still, in the vast landscape of supersymmetric models, it is not uncommon for it to feature a local minimum with a smaller symmetry, making it possible for a Q-ball to form in a symmetry that, from a field theory point of view, appears 'useless'. As a result, this phenomenon causes the rotation velocity to gradually increase, potentially culminating in a state of stable chaotic behavior characterized by abrupt directional shifts. By modeling and analyzing data from three asteroids, (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, we were able to use their observed light curve patterns to determine their rotation velocities. The resulting values showed that (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro have rotation velocities induced by the YORP effect in excess of the critical threshold, predicting they will experience sudden directional shifts in 1.37 million and 4.33 million years, respectively. On the other hand, (1620) Geographos' rotation velocity falls short of this threshold, indicating it will not exhibit sudden directional shifts in the next 300 million years. The rise of governmental interference in electoral processes worldwide has underscored the need to safeguard voting decisions through critical thinking and media literacy. Young adults, in particular, rely heavily on social media platforms like Instagram for information, often without recognizing the underlying mechanisms that shape their online experiences. Political conversations on Instagram exhibit dynamic characteristics, with users interacting with each other in ever-changing groups. To gain insight into these interactions, our research applied an epidemiological approach to study the temporary associations, or "clusters," formed around shared topics. By analyzing cluster size, influence, and lifespan, our findings revealed crucial aspects of online political discussions. Specifically, we discovered that communities based on topic similarities exhibit diverse sizes, with a average of 122 users, and a maximum of over 17 million. Notably, certain topics, or "influential nodes," tend to attract a significantly larger audience. A significant proportion of online interactions, about 55%, are short-lived, with only 6% of clusters lasting more than 30 days. Our analysis also uncovered patterns indicating a rapid shift in user attention between different topics. To maintain the integrity of online discussions, our results suggest that platforms like Instagram should implement adaptive methods to filter out deceptive information effectively, as their efficacy can decline over time. Furthermore, we propose the concept of "temporary credibility," where sources are viewed suspiciously if they post the same information to multiple clusters, as this approach considers the underlying mechanics of online discussions and the potential influence of deceptive information on users' opinions. By exploring data from Instagram conversations, our research provides a unique perspective on online discussions that can be applied to other social media platforms as well. Ultimately, our study highlights the value of analyzing online discussions through a dynamic perspective, where temporary associations play a crucial role in shaping users' experiences. By understanding and addressing these temporary aspects, we may be able to develop more effective methods to protect young adults from deceptive information in their online interactions. In the long run, this could contribute to creating a more informed citizenry. In the current digital information landscape, online discussions are constantly evolving, and our research demonstrates that studying them through a static approach can lead to an incomplete understanding. These models eliminate the need for artificial sign flipping methods by naturally producing well-balanced wave functions. We examine a specific complex-valued neural network called the complex-valued graph neural network and apply it to solve the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Our results, compared to a renowned neural network implementation, show comparable accuracy without the need for sign flipping. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of this approach by discussing potential solutions to fundamental issues facing neural network-based quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our work highlights the potential of complex-valued neural networks to resolve long-standing challenges in quantum simulation. We also contribute a publicly accessible code for training complex-valued neural networks, taking inspiration from open-source quantum simulation tools. This code is written in PyTorch and is easily modifiable to accommodate custom Hamiltonian projections. We demonstrate the efficiency of this code by providing high-resolution data for the half-filled two-dimensional Hubbard model. This data shows exceptional agreement with existing data and marks a significant advancement in complex-valued neural network-based simulation. We make this code available on the NeuralNetworkHubbard GitHub repository. It builds upon previous work by incorporating an updated neural network architecture that addresses the sign issue and showcases the benefits of complex-valued learning. This architecture has the added benefit of eliminating the need for artificial sign flipping methods, a problem that neural network-based QMC faces. Our results also highlight the accuracy of complex-valued neural networks, demonstrating a maxima energy error of 0.048 for the 38-site lattice and further highlights the potential of these models to model ground states in QMC simulations. We leave for future work the investigation of anti-ferromagnetic states using this model due to the inherent imbalance of the wave function. Despite only eliminating the sign issue, our results show that neural network-based QMC faces an even greater challenge in achieving the correct phase of the ground state. This is further compounded by the fact that neural network-based QMC is only capable of modeling un-improved versions of the Hamiltonian due to the inherent over-counting that occurs with improved methods. This presents an even greater sign issue that needs to be addressed, making anti-ferromagnetic state simulations an even more difficult task. Nonetheless, we believe that complex-valued neural networks offer a promising path forward for addressing this challenge and potentially other complex issues in quantum simulation. We also highlight another potential solution to this problem, namely the use of quaternion-valued neural networks

This study seeks to offer a thorough classification of requirements engineering approaches tailored to the gaming sector, building on prior research. Over the past decade, the global gaming market has experienced significant growth, with various types of games being developed across multiple platforms. Despite this success, the gaming industry still faces challenges in creating complete, functioning products within the allotted time and budget. To gain insight into this issue, our research examined 48 relevant studies on requirements engineering in the gaming industry, categorizing them according to standard frameworks such as Kaspersky, Garcia, and Dube. Our analysis reveals a pronounced gap in available data and highlights the benefits of combining principles from multiple approaches, such as volatility-based methods and goal-oriented techniques, to effectively address the dynamic and ever-changing requirements of game development. However, our findings also indicate a notable absence of studies focusing on real-world applications and practical solutions, with an overreliance on theoretical approaches. To fill this knowledge gap, our team is calling on researchers and industry professionals to contribute their expertise, with potential follow-up studies aiming to explore specific aspects of requirements engineering in the gaming industry and identify key areas of improvement. By building on this foundation, we hope to create a more comprehensive understanding of how to develop high-quality games by accurately capturing and satisfying the evolving needs of users. To achieve this, we will need to bridge the existing gap between theoretical approaches and actual development practices, with potential solutions including the development of more effective requirements engineering methods tailored to the gaming industry, with better tools and techniques that address the unique dynamics of game development, and with strategies to further leverage the knowledge gained from completed game projects. A trail map for potential follow-up studies is also presented in this study. With the gaming industry's growing dependence on digital distribution platforms and the increasing popularity of cloud gaming, there is a pressing need to adapt existing approaches to address the evolving requirements of game development, with potential studies on topics such as the evolution of requirements over time, the role of artificial intelligence in game design, and the lo-fi development of games also warranting exploration. By doing so, we aim to provide a more cohesive and industry-relevant understanding of how to apply requirements engineering principles to create engaging, technically sound games that meet both the needs of users and the capabilities of developers. With this enhanced understanding, we hope to facilitate the design of more effective, user-centered games by accurately capturing and satisfying the evolving needs of players, with potential benefits including increased customer satisfaction, improved retention rates, and a positive industry reputation. This study investigates the challenges of hyperparameter optimization for differentially private deep learning models. Due to data privacy restrictions, it is difficult to conduct grid searches for the best hyperparameters. A further complication arises because the private learning process is inherently stochastic, making it essential to account for this uncertainty in hyperparameter optimization. To address these issues, we propose a non-linear adaptive genetic algorithm for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The new approach avoids the need for sensitive private data when calculating fitness scores during the search process. A specific modification of the adaptive genetic algorithm is also introduced to account for the variability inherent in private model performance. Our research demonstrates that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to alternative hyperparameter optimization techniques in private deep learning settings. Furthermore, the results show that the non-linear adaptive genetic algorithm outperforms the linear version, highlighting the importance of selecting a suitable hyperparameter for success in private deep learning. The proposed method has been thoroughly evaluated across multiple differentially private settings, including fully private training, private federated learning with a single user, and private federated learning with multiple users. The code for the proposed non-linear adaptive genetic algorithm has been openly repurposed and is now available on the GITHUB repository https://github.com/ParasSing7/NGA-HPT-PrivateDL. The research has also been extensively illustrated using visualizations of its performance on confusion matrices. The results show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to non-private models, with a notable improvement in cases involving private federated learning. The success of the proposed method is attributed to its ability to adapt to the unique performance characteristics of private models. The results with confusion matrices provide valuable visual insights into the trade-offs involved in hyperparameter optimization in private deep learning. The research has been conducted using multiple differentially private settings, highlighting the potential of the proposed method to be applied across various private deep learning scenarios. The study has also highlighted several potential research directions, including the integration of knowledge from multiple datasets in private federated learning and the development of efficient hyperparameter optimization methods for large-scale private deep learning models. The study has provided extensive empirical validation of the proposed method, along with a comprehensive comparison with alternative hyperparameter optimization techniques in private deep learning settings. The results have been thoroughly analyzed using performance metrics, along with confusion matrices that provide visual insights into the performance of the proposed method. The study has a practical relevance to the development of private deep learning models, along with several real-world applications such as private speech analysis, private text analysis, and private biomedical research.

This method bypasses the limitations of parametric models and accurately captures the multi-dimensional structure of the disk's stellar population. We applied this technique to the APOGEE data, dividing the disk into distinct regions based on their chemical characteristics. Our results showed a notable two-process model in the formation of the disk, with stars differing in metallicity and abundance of specific elements like carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. These findings also revealed previously unseen patterns and uncovered a significant population of 2 Gyr-old stars in the disk's outer region. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in January 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, where social distancing measures and lockdowns were implemented to contain the virus's transmission. To examine the impact of these measures on the dissemination and effects of online rumors, we developed an epidemiological model for rumor spread. The model accounts for pre-intervention spread, impact assessment, and a disinfection mechanism resulting from interventions such as fact-checking. Our analysis of Chinese microblogging platform data suggests that government-issued announcements can significantly reduce the spread of rumors. Additionally, we found that prior exposure does not affect subsequent spread, and a more transmissible version of a rumor may have a more significant impact. Our study provides insights into the complex dynamics of online rumors and highlights the importance of continuous disinfection through social media platforms' internal measures and public critical thinking. A novel method for determining the distance to galaxies using planetary nebulae as standard candles has been developed and applied to a comprehensive dataset of 2496 extragalactic objects within the Fornax cluster's central region, extracted from the VST/Omega2d Fornax Atlas. By accurately measuring the expansion velocity of low-z type Ia supernovae and standardizing the maximum brightness of planetary nebulae, a new approach has been taken. Specifically, a second-order polynomial has been fitted to a large sample of local planetary nebulae based on their helio-centric distances, velocity dispersions, and 5000Å luminosities. This has enabled a standardized maximum brightness to be established for each planetary nebula in the Fornax cluster, and ultimately a distance of 17.03 ± 0.29 Mpc to the center of the Fornax cluster, which is consistent with previous estimates. By considering various effects and applying a quality control process, a sample of 1340 planetary nebulae with reliable standardized maximum brightness measurements has been refined. These findings provide a comprehensive dataset that other researchers can draw upon to study the stellar population, structure, and dynamics of early-type galaxies within the Fornax cluster. Additionally, a comparison with a similar study conducted in 2019 has been conducted. That study conducted by the same research team used a similar approach but was based on a less comprehensive dataset; it reported a distance of 16.42 ± 0.29 Mpc. That study's results were subject to correction terms that were derived from a smaller sample of 546 planetary nebulae, whereas the current study's results are based on a more comprehensive analysis of 7494 spectral fractions spanning 10.5 billion years of cosmic evolution. That study's correction terms have been re-evaluated using the comprehensive dataset available today. By re-examining the relationship between velocity dispersion and standard planetary nebula brightness within low-redshift type Ia supernovae host galaxies, a cubic term has been discovered, which significantly improves the accuracy of the distance measurements to a distance of 16.94 ± 0.26 Mpc. This enhanced understanding of the standardization process has the potential to further enhance the method's accuracy when applied to other galaxies. A comprehensive database of planetary nebulae in the Fornax cluster has been established and is available for download, along with a user-friendly interface for exploring and analyzing these data. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which arises from the interaction of this component with the superconducting Hall current. A notable result of this interaction is the appearance of a paramagnetic response in the direction perpendicular to the applied magnetic field, potentially overshadowing the normal diamagnetic response exhibited by normal metals. The magnitude of this paramagnetic effect is shown to be sensitive to temperature and can be assessed through magnetic specific heat, which may be measured via experiment. Notably, the paramagnetic response is found to be more pronounced in the chiral phase than in the nematic phase. A qualitative analysis indicates that this distinction arises due to differences in the pairing function's symmetry in these phases. A numerical computation of magnetic energy in the ground state is also carried out to provide a more intuitive understanding of this phenomenon. An alternative perspective on this effect is provided by considering it as a consequence of the superconducting Hall current induced by an external magnetic field. A previously developed framework for the quantum capacity and compressibility of spacetime is adapted to a thermal region with varying temperature properties. The thermal region is divided into three areas: a high-temperature part that does not differ significantly from the Hawking temperature, an intermediate area where temperature variations become more pronounced, and a low-temperature section that exhibits temperature oscillations. The quantum capacity and compressibility of each thermal subregion are calculated, revealing that they proportionally correlate with the respective temperature properties. Notably, in the intermediate and low-temperature areas, quantum capacity and compressibility exhibit non-linear relationships with temperature. The compressibility of the intermediate thermal area is negative, indicating a non-expansive nature, while the low-temperature area displays periodic fluctuations in both quantum capacity and compressibility. The implications of these findings are explored within the context of the holographic principle and the thermodynamic properties of spacetime. The adopted model is then expanded to consider a rotating thermal area in spacetime, yielding a Harmond-type potential and a resulting, non-integral number of black holes. The analysis of this modified model highlights the presence of gravitational field gradients, which give rise to oscillatory temperatures and corresponding, intricate quantum capacity and compressibility patterns. The inherent relationships between quantum capacity, compressibility, and temperature/pressure within these thermal regions are shown to adhere to the principles of both the holographic code and the holographic energy density, respectively. The ultimate outcome of these interactions is the formation of intricate, fractal-like patterns within the spacetime continuum. The integration of quantum capacity into the holographic energy density theorem is also presented, resulting in the theorem's extension to encompass quantum compressibility. This revised theorem is then applied to derive the compressibility of both the AdS and Minkowski spacetimes. The compressibility of the AdS spacetime is found to be negative, indicating a non-expansive nature, while the compressibility of the Minkowski spacetime is zero, reflecting its stable, uncompressible Nkowlersian state. The study concludes by exploring the relationships between quantum capacity, compressibility, and the spacetime continuum's thermal properties, underscoring the necessity of considering both capacity and compressibility in a unified quantum framework. Furthermore, the incorporation of quantum compressibility into the holographic energy density theorem paves the way for further research into the compressibility of spacetime, ultimately enabling a deeper understanding of the quantum properties inherent within the spacetime continuum. However, labeling rewards for individual states is a time-consuming and impractical step in real-world applications. To circumvent this issue, we propose a framework that combines machine learning and human expertise to accelerate reward learning. Specifically, we suggest a visually aided cluster ranking method, where human evaluators group similar states together based on visual features and then provide relative reward preferences for these clusters. We demonstrate that this method significantly reduces labeling costs by comparing it to a traditional approach. We also showcase the efficacy of our accelerated reward learning method on complex tasks, including control scenarios and goal-based navigation tasks, with costs that are up to 13x more cost-effective. We also conduct a comprehensive study on the time-effective goal-based navigation task, with results indicating that our method can provide high-quality goals in as little as 5 minutes of human time. We believe that our work paves the way for accelerated experience-based reinforcement learning methods that leverage human input more efficiently. Model partnerships, as seen in model-parallel neural networks, mitigate memory constraints by dividing the network among multiple processors. This technique, however, leads to a memory duplication effect, as each processor must have its own copy of the weights. In a paper titled 'Mitigating Memory Requirements in Deep Neural Networks through Model Parallelism and Low-Rank Approximation', the authors explore strategies to minimize memory requirements by combining model parallelism with techniques like low-rank approximation, sparse connections, and batch normalization. Their findings show that even without reducing the rank of the weights, employing model parallelism alone is sufficient to achieve a significant decrease in memory consumption. To further investigate this'memory duplication' issue, the authors introduce a theoretical continuum model, which uses a combination of model parallelism and low-rk approximation to optimize memory usage. This continuum model helps identify strategies for determining ideal model partitioning and rank parameters, thereby providing a framework for tackling the memory duplication problem inherent in model parallelism. This approach is then applied to multiple network architectures, resulting in a practical guide for designing memory-efficient neural networks using model parallelism. This approach is then applied to a real-world image classification application using a mobile device, showcasing the effectiveness of this approach in developing deployable neural network models. Our extensive database, called ATOMIC, is an advanced knowledge base that comprises over 750,000 verified two-part connections (A causes or is caused by B) among nearly 200 diverse areas of knowledge.  This resource is exceptional due to its unique composition, as most common knowledge databases are extracted from web content and thus prone to containing inaccuracies.  In contrast, ATOMIC is assembled from trusted sources, including Wikipedia, YAGO, and UMBEL, eliminating any potential stochasticity that might exist in such databases.  These relationships in ATOMIC form the foundation for numerous possible additional connections, which can be learned through machine learning techniques.  Our evaluation of this database across 12 diverse tasks demonstrated that models trained on ATOMIC-based data significantly outperform models trained on other public datasets.  Furthermore, our analysis shows that while YAGO does share some overlap with ATOMIC, the two hold distinct differences, primarily due to YAGO's more limited scope and accuracy issues in certain areas.  Despite these limitations, we discovered that models trained on YAGO still achieve impressive results across multiple tasks.  In an effort to advance the study of common machine knowledge through if-then reasoning, we publicly release both ATOMIC and the associated models used in our evaluation, which can be accessed via https://github.com/nyu-dl4fashion/atomic and https://github.com/nyu-dl4fashion/atomic-models, respectively.  We strongly advise other researchers to utilize these models in their own work.  We also invite the broader research community to collaborate with us in exploring common machine knowledge through if-then reasoning and to consider contributing to the ATOMIC database.  We are particularly interested in receiving suggestions on how to incorporate more diversity across all domains of knowledge and to explore potential statistical biases present within this area.  Additionally, we are seeking input on suitable evaluation metrics and methods that can be employed to assess the performance of models trained on common machine knowledge.  We believe that answering these questions will not only shed more light on common machine knowledge but also contribute to the development of more reliable machine learning models.  We are confident that models trained on this type of knowledge will ultimately prove more dependable in comparison to models trained on other data.  We anticipate this to hold true not only for our ATOMIC-based models but for models trained on common machine knowledge across all domains and to facilitate this, we are more than happy to provide this opportunity for the research community to collaborate with us. Large-scale scientific computations involving complex linear systems can be solved efficiently with the HHL algorithm, albeit with a significant computational cost for large matrices. Despite advancements in quantum computing, current hardware constraints limit the practical application of HHL on near-term devices. This study introduces NISQ-HHL, an iterative method that uses a portfolio of multiple partial circulations to enhance the performance of HHL on noisy and fault-prone quantum circuits. Experimental results with circuit simulations of 48-qubit Gaussian unitary circuits demonstrate the effectiveness of NISQ-HHL, showing that when applying HHL to a matrix with $n$ independent blocks, using a portfolio of size $p$ can lead to $p^{n-1}$ times improvement in execution probability, $p^{n-1}$ times better output amplitude, and $p^{n-2}$ times better final state fidelity. Notably, this approach can facilitate HHL implementation on noisy near-term quantum devices by overcoming the challenge of sufficiently long quantum registration windows and offers potential solutions for solving other high-dimensional linear system problems in the near-term quantum era. The source code of NISQ-HHL has been made available open-source on GitHub at https://github.com/QuantumPhysicsGroup/NISQ-HHL. The study also presents its theoretical foundations in the accompanying technical report available at arXiv:2206.07808.
