This paper investigates the distribution of starting points for a specific class of sequences called uniform parking functions, as their length increases without limit. We first demonstrate that the limiting distribution of the initial points is a unique mixture of uniform distributions, tailored to the specific parameter 'p'. This limiting distribution is derived analyatically for p equal to zero or one; however, for other values of p, we employ a probabilistic approach to obtain a non-uniform asymptotic distribution. Through extensive computer simulations, we verify that the asymptotic probability measures for initial points correlate with the structure of Kashiwaga lattices. This connection holds for all integers p greater than zero. We also establish a link between the uniform parking function sequences and a specific multidimensional lattice, referred to as the Kashiwaga lattice, and explore how this relationship evolves as additional dimensions are added. This connection enables us to identify specific subsets within the lattice and derive formulas for the number of uniform parking functions for particular parameter values. This further enables us to demonstrate that the limiting distribution of initial points for uniform parking functions is unique and cannot be expressed through an additive approach. This conclusion is supported by a general proof applicable to any dimension. We also provide a more general framework that connects sequences of uniform parking functions with respect to a specific parameter 'p' to a particular multidimensional lattice, referred to as the Bojanov-Macigegi-Simeonov lattice, and derive formulas for the number of uniform parking functions for particular parameter values. This further enables us to investigate the distribution of starting points for uniform parking functions. This investigation yields a unique corollary that the binary representation of any element within this specific dimensioned lattice is unique. This in turn raises an interesting open question that could be of broader interest in the field of discrete mathematics. This question pertains to the distribution of starting points for a particular class of sequences called 'gray codes', which generate all possible binary combinations in a specific order. This open question could provide valuable insights into both the uniform parking functions and the Kashiwaga lattices. It also offers a concrete approach for further research in the field of discrete mathematics. This approach combines elements from both combinatorial and probabilistic disciplines. It is therefore relevant to a broad range of academic and research communities. It could provide a valuable research opportunity for graduate students or postdoctoral researchers. It is also highly relevant to a broad range of practical applications that deal with sequences of actions. It is therefore important to contribute to the body of knowledge in this field.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate a significant reduction in DC conductivity when an adjacent gate electrode is used to apply voltage. The critical thickness of this reduced conductivity region varies depending on the measurement methodology but can be quite large, potentially exceeding the de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron charge. Theoretical models suggesting the presence of coherent quantum phase slips fail to accurately predict the observed data, especially when considering the relatively long times required for such events. An alternative explanation proposes that these conductivity reductions are instead caused by Coulomb blockage within the nanowires. This argument is supported by the presence of a threshold voltage, which is necessary to overcome the nanowire's capacitance and enable phase slips. Additionally, the required time for these events is consistent with measurements of the nanowire's capacitance and the resistance of the normal state. A key aspect of this model is the assumption that the nanowire operates in a high-displacement-current regime, resulting from the large electric field induced by the nearby gate electrode. The serial dictatorship method ranks voters in a specific order and assigns the item to the first available voter. This research explores why this method is effective by considering the preferences of an "outside observer" who is not part of the ranking. It is demonstrated that if the observer's preferences mirror a particular version of the voters' collective interests, assigning the item using a serial dictatorship method is equivalent to doing so with complete knowledge of individual preferences. The research also identifies situations in which a modified version of social welfare-based methods can produce the same outcome as more complex procedures like the Gibbard-Sattherthwaite theorem suggests, provided the voters' rankings are consistent with their own individual preferences. It is therefore proposed that these modified methods should be referred to as "efficient" methods. It is further shown that, unlike their irreversible counterparts, both the Gibbard-Sattherthwaite theorem's requirements can be met by a social welfare-based method when the voters' rankings are part of an "expansion path". The implications of these findings for the design of electoral systems are discussed. It is suggested that, in the absence of strategic voting, the standard definition of "efficiency" in economics is a suitable goal for election methods. It is also proposed that this definition could be applied to methods that generate the same outcome as social welfare-based methods on all possible sets of voters' rankings, provided such methods are part of an "expansion path". It is argued that this definition is more appropriate for inclusion in a theorem about election methods than the original version of the Gibbard-Sattherthwaite theorem. It is demonstrated that one of the earlier known exceptions to the Gibbard-Sattherthwaite theorem can be explained by applying the new definition and that no other exceptions exist when there are three or more voters. It is also shown that for two voters, there are instances in which any method that assigns one item to one voter and the other item to the second voter will not generate the same outcome as social welfare-based methods on at least half of all possible sets of voters' rankings. It is proposed that this phenomenon could be avoided by modifying the standard social welfare-based method so that it always selects the most preferred alternative to the least preferred one. It is further shown that this modified method generates the same outcome as social welfare-based methods on all possible sets of voters' rankings when there are three or more voters, but there are instances in which it fails to do so for two voters on at least 10% of all possible sets of voters' rankings

We designed an advanced detection method for identifying binary asteroids by utilizing their changing light pattern in images. Traditionally, discovering binary asteroids relied on light curve observations during a single event, which only provided a limited understanding of the asteroid's orbit. Our approach enhances the likelihood of detection by combining images showing different aspects of the asteroid's orbit. By utilizing the NOAO Source Explorer, we searched the Pan-STARRS1 image database covering the period from 2013 to 2019, focusing on 200 known binary asteroids to identify new instances. We developed a matching algorithm based on the asteroid's orbit, light curve, and orbital period to filter potential binary asteroids. This study is the first comprehensive search for binary asteroids utilizing a sophisticated detection method across a substantial database of images. Our results show that eight new binary asteroids were found among the previously known 192 instances. Additionally, we discovered potential second components for two asteroids and one suspected binary asteroid. Our study paves the way for future research approaches that incorporate images from multiple observations, which is likely to significantly improve the detection of binary asteroids. We are currently integrating our algorithm with the PS1 archive's updated database of images. We anticipate this to result in a comprehensive database of binary asteroids that will be valuable for further studies and space mission applications. Additionally, this study's approach can be adapted for detecting other multi-body asteroid configurations. All discovered binary asteroids are listed in Table 1. Their light curves were derived from combined images and are displayed in Figure 1. Orbital information for these binary asteroids is provided in Table 2 and their orbits are graphically represented in Figure 2. Comparisons between our observations and existing data on these asteroids are presented in Figure 3. All code and data used in this study are available at https://github.com/aresearcher/binasteros. We utilized the Pan-STARRS1 Image Database Interface developed by Chang et al. (2019) to execute our research. Our results show that searching wide-area images is an effective approach for identifying binary asteroids. RCSED is an open-source software currently providing graphical representations of spectral data and fake images generated from these spectra. This software is designed for visual analysis and verification of spectral data, as well as the generation of fake images to determine optimal observation parameters. It addresses limitations in software available for visualizing astronomical data, such as STAN, MATCALC, and DIFTOOL, by providing unique features including multi-dimensional data display, custom color palettes, and spatial Radon transform. With enhanced capabilities, this updated version, RCSEDv2, allows for additional analysis of data, including calculation of maximum intensity along a specific axis, and includes a user-friendly interface for adjusting settings via a configuration file. RCSEDv2 is an openly sourced software available for use and for contribution at https://github.com/astro-difftools/RCSED. It is developed to support the analysis of extended spectral data, specifically designed for the MAMBO2 and NIFA instruments but is also applicable to other 9.6 GHz sub-mm bolometer arrays. This software is part of the astro-difftools suite of open-source software. Studies using geophysical and geological data have mapped the King Brand and Rio Grande rifts, as well as other intracontinental extensional basins within South America. However, based on their geometry and age data, researchers have developed a kinematic model that describes how the rift system has changed over time. Then, as it broke apart, it evolved into two converging beta faults during the Cenozoic Era. These faults have caused the extension to shift to an NW-SE direction. A prominent approach in medical image segmentation is information-theoretic optimization, which motivates the development of a novel method for self-supervised segmentation. Leveraging cross-entropy loss and KL-divergence, medical experts can define a region of interest (ROI) to focus the optimization process, ensuring the model produces accurate predictions within this area. To facilitate efficient training, the proposed method splits the ROI into two regions with differing densities, utilizing over-sampling for high-density areas and under-sampling for low-density areas, based on probability density estimates. The method is tested on two types of medical image datasets, achieving superior or comparable performance to state-of-the-art self-supervised segmentation models and a baseline model with data augmentation, in terms of Dice similarity coefficient (DSC). Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrates practical applications in clinical workflows, producing consistent results on a dataset with limited training data and successfully integrating density-based clustering, resulting in enhanced segmentation accuracy. The implementation and evaluation of the method are also open-sourced for the broader medical imaging community. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms self-supervised baselines in real-world challenging medical image segmentation tasks. Additionally, the code is made available at https://github.com/strawdog/roisselfsup. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. Our proposed functions can be accessed via quasi-parton distribution functions (quasi-PDFs) that account for the dependencies on impact parameter, enabling their extraction from data containing $k_\perp$ information. Notably, our proposed functions lead to a more comprehensive understanding of quark spin alignment than the picture provided by Boer-Mulders function and functions related to the Sivers effect alone. Our research paves the way for investigating quark spin alignment in experiments that involve semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering at a future electron-ion collider or other DIS facilities. A comprehensive study on our proposed functions has been published in the article "Quark Spin Alignment in the Electron-Ion Collider" in the journal "Phys. Rev. X". Our results also highlight the importance of considering the impact of the wave function overlap when interpreting data from such experiments. Furthermore, our research indicates that even in the case of relativistic quark models, the wave function overlap plays a significant role in quark spin alignment. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional potential is the subject of this study. We examine how protein knots interact with each other and their surroundings under stress. To investigate this, we developed a new mathematical model that measures the entanglement of proteins based on their surface properties. This model shows that knotted proteins' native states are topologically distinct from each other. We then identified unique characteristics of these states that determine how they respond to external stress. Specifically, we distinguished between proteins that will unwind (loose), bend (slant), or become tangled (twist) under pressure. By analyzing these behaviors, we found that bending is the most common response to stress among knotted proteins. We further investigated the underlying factors that influence this stress response and discovered that it's largely determined by the geometry of the protein's core and its connection to the outside world. We based a predictor on these findings that can accurately forecast which proteins will bend under stress just by analyzing their sequences. This predictor's performance is impressive, even compared to other models that use a broader range of data. We also used this predictor to explore how different species' proteins interact with each other and their surroundings. Interestingly, we found that the instructions embedded in the DNA of different species can influence the shapes that their proteins are programmed to take, even if those shapes are unstable. This knowledge can be used to design new proteins with desired properties, such as the ability to withstand high temperatures or chemical stresses. Furthermore, it may also provide insights into how proteins become disordered in diseases like cancer, and could offer a basis for developing new medications that target the physical structure of proteins rather than their function. This approach is particularly appealing because many proteins have complex structures that are difficult to modify with traditional methods. By controlling a protein's shape, it's possible to regulate its function more effectively, which could be especially helpful in addressing multifunctional proteins involved in different diseases. This study demonstrates the value of integrating topological and geometric approaches in analyzing the intricate properties of proteins. It shows that by considering a protein's structure as a whole, rather than individual components, it's possible to uncover unique patterns and underlying mechanisms that would have gone undetected otherwise. This research highlights the potential of using geometric methods to study other complex systems that are interconnected and sensitive to changes, and it paves the way for further investigations into the relationships between structure, function, and the environment of various systems. A thorough examination of the underlying mathematics is instead shown to be necessary. A explicit, generalized development of the NG theorem is then presented, drawing upon a more fundamental symmetry breaking framework. This framework essentially combines both relativistic and nonrelativistic symmetry breaking approaches, thus providing the context within which the NG theorem can be proven. Recent studies indicate that current language models can generate factually inaccurate information, including statements contradicting established facts.  To address this shortcoming for potential practical applications such as generating realistic counterfactual data, a key issue needs to be resolved - the current method for creating counterfactual statements through modification of Sensitive Attribute and Counterfactual Task (SAFE) techniques is not effective when applied to a broader range of phrases.  To tackle this problem, a novel framework called Discourse-Centric Counterfactuals (DISCO) has been developed and evaluated on the CLINICAL-REALISTIC TASK (CRT) dataset, which is designed to generate counterfactual statements within medical discharge summaries.  DISCO utilizes a discourse-based approach, modifying both a task-oriented model and a universal language model to leverage both their strengths.  The results show that DISCO can generate more accurate and coherent counterfactual statements compared to existing methods.  To facilitate future research, DISCO along with the CRT dataset is made publicly available and can be accessed through a web interface that allows for counterfactual statement selection and ranking.  The effectiveness of DISCO is further verified by a user study that showed the generated counterfactual statements are not only linguistically fluent but also plausible in more than half of the cases.  One limitation of DISCO is the inability to generate counterfactual statements for phrases that are not easily identified using a Part-of-Speech tagger.  To address this issue, a technique called Phrase-based Role Indentification (PRI) has been proposed and evaluated on the CRT dataset, resulting in successful application to phrases that were previously unworkable.  PRI has been integrated into the DISCO framework, further enhancing its performance and efficiency.  The enhanced version of DISCO, PRI-DISCO, has been made available for public access through a web interface that can be accessed at http://www.disco.nlp.org.  This work has significant implications for generating realistic counterfactual data, a critical issue for multiple applications such as training machine learning models in an unfair-free manner and creating realistic hypothetical scenarios. Research into Heusler materials has been gaining momentum due to their exceptional electrical and magnetic properties. Achieving high quality Heusler films however poses a significant challenge, largely because the traditional method of growing them - through the remote epitaxy of Strontium or Calcium on Silicon - is not very reliable. A novel approach has been recently discovered, where remote epitaxy can be substituted with van der Waals epitaxy on Graphene substrates. Specifically, it was found that growing Co2MnAl films by depositing atoms on Graphene is highly effective. A study was conducted to explore the mechanisms behind this success and it was discovered that a pinhole in the Graphene substrate plays a crucial role in starting the growth process. Notably, the study found that there are three distinct modes of Heusler film growth: remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. The conditions required for each mode were examined and it was found that the quality of the film is highly dependent on the mode used. For example, films grown through van der Waals epitaxy have a lower density of defects and are therefore of higher quality. The studies also provided valuable insights into the technology required to control Heusler film growth on Graphene and it is believed that this research will be a significant step towards the successful production of Heusler materials. The studies consisted of analyzing Heusler film growth through a range of techniques such as Auger electron spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, low energy electron diffraction, atomic force microscopy, scanning transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy. A theoretical model of Heusler film growth has also been proposed and it is believed this will be valuable for further research into this topic. Given their widespread use, it's not surprising that most languages incorporate them into their vocabulary. While they are initially unfamiliar to newcomers, they become integral parts of the language over time. Unfortunately, identifying these abbreviations can be challenging, especially when their original form is no longer apparent. To address this difficulty, a technique called acronym disambiguation has been developed, aiming to provide the expanded form contextually. In this research, our primary objective is to introduce a web-based platform called MadDog that enables users to submit acronyms along with the surrounding text, allowing the system to generate accurate expanded forms. To achieve this, we propose a mixed approach that combines both machine learning and rule-based methods to tackle this challenge. Specifically, we leverage a deep learning model to classify the acronym's part of speech and a set of predefined patterns to trigger the expansion. To facilitate user interaction, an interface is also introduced along with a utility to evaluate the system's performance. Finally, we showcase the versatility of our system by applying it to detect and resolve ambiguities within a large corpus of technical documents. Overall, MadDog represents a significant advancement in the field of acronym disambiguation, addressing both classification and resolution issues by providing the expanded form in the text's context. Additionally, we explore the application of MadDog in resolving ambiguities within a large corpus of technical documents. This paper presents an original method able to accurately analyze shadows in a differentiable way, making existing optimization techniques usable. We experimentally demonstrate that this method allows for high-quality scene reconstruction, even in the presence of artifical shadows, and compares favorably to state-of-the-art shadow removal methods. Furthermore, this method proves particularly useful for reconstructing when shadows fall across multiple boundary lines. This method is also shown to be part of a full 3D reconstruction pipeline. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghliu/diff-shadow. This differentiable shadow evaluation approach represents a significant advancement over prior methods and provides a means to incorporate optical flow and other differentiable features in 3D reconstruction tasks. A trio of linear system solvers -- ULF, ULV, and ULV+ -- has been extensively evaluated in terms of memory usage, factorization time, and solve time for multiple versions of a finite element method model representing cardiac mechanics. These solvers, which utilize different memory compression techniques, have been tested against increasingly large problems comprising up to 43 million dofs on a range of memory configurations. Our study reveals that the ULV+ solver, featuring the least expensive and most effective compression approach, consistently yields the best results across all measures and should be the default choice. Furthermore, this study highlights the urgency and potential impact of further research in developing efficient memory management for emerging high-performance computing architectures. Our ULF and ULV code are made publicly available for use in conjunction with the Bardy 2018 model. (LBNL-0970499)

The wave equation has played a pivotal role in advancing various fields of science and engineering, where its numerous applications serve as evidence of the equation's universal significance. Within the context of quantum theory, the wave equation assumes a distinct form known as the Schrödinger equation, and it is through solving this equation that we can comprehend the intricate dynamics of quantum phenomena. This paper seeks to present the Schrödinger equation in a comprehensive light, highlighting both the successes that have stemmed from it as well as the controversies that surround it. Additionally, we explore how it has given rise to wave equations in non-Lorentzian geometries proposed by variable speed of light theories, such as the modified Klein-Gordon equation and the non-Lorentzian Klein-Gordon equation. These discussions reveal the intimate connection between the wave equation, geometry, and the Schrödinger equation, underscoring the implicit assumptions that underpin our current understanding of physics. Furthermore, investigations of the modified Klein-Gordon equation have yielded intriguing findings, including scalar field theories that might provide a glimpse into the fundamental nature of quantum gravity. These ideas also raise important philosophical questions about the perception of physical reality, underscoring the need for a coherent, consistent approach that integrates geometry and wave equations. Ultimately, this paper makes a strong case for the wave equation to remain a central focus of research in quantum science. Its successes serve as a beacon, encouraging us to push beyond the controversies and push the boundaries of our current understanding. In the process, we may uncover novel perspectives on quantum physics, its underlying principles, and the geometry that gives rise to it. This, in turn, may pave the way for novel interpretations of physical reality, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of quantum phenomena and the development of innovative approaches to addressing its computational challenges. With this paper, we aim to spark a lively debate that will propel the study of wave equations in quantum science forward, breaking new ground in this field and sparking a renewed interest in the celebrated wave equation. This debate will not only shed light on the intricacies of quantum phenomena but also provide a rigorous examination of the underlying mathematical frameworks, making it an invaluable contribution to the field. As we embark on this research, we are also driven by a fundamental question that has plagued physicists for centuries: what are the inherent properties of physical reality that give rise to the distinctive behaviors of quantum phenomena? This study offers a unique opportunity to address this question, to explore novel concepts, and to push the boundaries of our current understanding of quantum physics.

These results imply that the actual limit on spatial resolution in such systems could be much lower than previously estimated, potentially enabling the measurement of spaces less wide than the wavelength of light. We also present a method for quantifying the resolution in these systems and demonstrate that a state of high entanglement between the two photons is not necessary to achieve the best results. These advances have significant implications for the development of future photonic instruments that can measure space spacings down to a fraction of the wavelength. Recent studies have investigated the correlation between star formation rates and stellar masses, particularly focusing on a parameterized form known as M*-SFR. While it's established that this relationship turns over at high stellar masses, the underlying cause remains the subject of ongoing research. To further explore this phenomenon, researchers have analyzed extensive data sets from SDSS and WISE, incorporating bulge-to-total light ratio information. By modeling the intrinsic properties of galaxies, they established a probability distribution that fits observed data based on morphological characteristics. This model reveals the correlation's break at approximately 10^10.2 M$_\odot$ in solar masses, and indicates that starburst galaxies dominate the union of galaxies above this mass threshold, contributing around 30-50% to the observed SFR. However, even after controlling for SFR, the M*-SFR relationship continues to rise at these high masses, suggesting other non-STAR-forming processes also occur. Furthermore, when considering only quiescent galaxies, the relationship becomes even steeper, at a power law of 0.35. Additionally, a separate but similar slope is seen for bulge-dominated galaxies alone. Through comparisons of massive star-forming and quiescent galaxies, based on their rest-frame UV-visual color, researchers found the latter exhibit more massive bulges, and that bulge mass alone fails to capture the behavior of quiescent galaxies. These findings provide new insights, suggesting the M*-SFR break is a result of a shift from disk to bulge-dominated galaxy morphology, and that non-STAR-forming processes contribute to the relationship's steepening in quiescent galaxies. These results also imply that when considering the relationship in its entirety, a combination of both star-forming and non-STAR-forming processes must be taken into account. Lastly, based on their model, researchers estimate that when comparing massive star-forming and quiescent galaxies, the latter have bulge masses approximately 1.5 to 2 times greater. This, along with additional model parameters and distributions of light ratio and SFR, are all available in the supplementary material.

Parallel programs can be slowed down due to cache conflicts, reducing performance. A new technique called self-invalidation and self-devaluation is proposed to minimize delays caused by cache conflicts. This approach uses a reliability metric that evaluates the trustworthiness of data based on its location. When a thread accesses data from an untrusted cache line, it is delayed until the data is flushed and reloaded from memory. Meanwhile, the cache line is marked as untrusted by other threads to prevent similar delays. When a thread accesses untrusted data, it is delayed again. Additionally, the cache line is removed from the L1 cache and its entry in the L2 cache is set to untrusted. This technique is challenging to implement efficiently due to the need to check the reliability of data at every memory access. To overcome this, the proposed system architecture integrates a new pointer format that indicates whether a memory access is for data or for other purposes such as address calculation. This feature, combined with a new load instruction that can handle both data and non-data loads, allows the system to reduce overhead by only checking the reliability of data loads. As a result, the proposed technique can significantly reduce average slow-down factors and improve program completion times. In particular, it can complete 18 out of 24 programs 10 times faster and can complete all programs with a less than 2 times increase in average time. Furthermore, it can provide full performance for 8 out of 24 programs and can provide over 80% performance for all programs with only a small increase in energy consumption. The proposed technique can also be more energy-efficient than other approaches with only a limited performance improvement. Finally, its potential applications and areas for further optimization are also identified. Additionally, it can be combined with other techniques such as speculative execution to further improve performance. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with quantitative information that can be an effective means of evaluating a patient's condition, including their suitability for ICU admission. By combining medical experts' insights with image analysis, we can develop a scoring system that integrates visual assessments with algorithmic findings, providing an objective, data-driven approach to evaluate patients' condition for ICU admission. In partnership with multiple hospitals, we assembled a diverse dataset of COVID-19 X-ray images along with scores from multiple medical professionals regarding the images' quality and whether the patients should be admitted to the ICU. Our initial findings, based on a comprehensive analysis of both score-based and direct assessments, reveal that high-scoring images are more likely to be consistent in indicating the patient should be admitted to the ICU. Conversely, images with lower scores show no clear pattern, potentially indicating noise in the ratings. To further enhance our scoring system, we propose additional features that can be integrated with existing expertise-based guidelines. Our approach paves the way for a collaborative model that leverages both medical professionals' insights and advanced image analysis algorithms to evaluate patients' conditions through the scoring system. In this context, we explore multiple architectures for a combined model that can provide a more objective evaluation of COVID-19 patient conditions based on X-ray images, looking ahead to our future work in this area. In particular, we plan to engage more medical professionals in the study, gather more clinical data, and fine-tune our proposed combined model. To address this, we present a novel balanced negative proposal selection approach, drawing from a diverse range of challenging negative examples. This study offers a supervised activity recognition solution suitable for limited and low-light video data. Notably, activity recognition performance is commonly impeded by insufficient or poorly illuminated video by incorporating only a brief delta duration of video data. Our approach, known as delta sampling R-BERT, overcomes these challenges by enhancing recognition accuracy through robust feature extraction. This method involves three key steps: first, a limited amount of training data is used to derive initial R-BERT features for classification; second, only a short period of testing video data is analyzed to obtain refined features: third, these features are combined with R-BERT features for final classification. Experimental results confirm our hypothesis that delta sampling R-BERT outperforms conventional methods when working with restricted and low-light video data. Notably, our delta sampling R-BERT method achieves notable performance improvements on the i3D-based benchmark, specifically +3.3% on the wild dataset and +5.2% on the low-light dataset of ActivityNet-1.3. Moreover, our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the YouTube Activity (YTA) dataset, gaining +5.6% on the unrestricted dataset and +7.6% on the low-light dataset. YTA evaluation using an i3D-based benchmark reveals a +4.5% improvement on the unrestricted dataset and a +6.4% improvement on the low-light dataset. Our method also successfully applies to binary classification on the PASCAL VOC dataset, achieving a +2.4% improvement on the VOC dataset. A key method parameter, defined as temporal crop size, is empirically determined through comprehensive experiments using activity recognition datasets, including ActivityNet-1.3 and the YouTube Activity (YTA) dataset. Our study paves the way for further research into optimal temporal features for activity recognition. We've performed an in-depth analysis of nine galaxies at $2.37 < z < 2.55$ within a massive galaxy cluster, and studied how their bulges and star formation patterns evolved over time. These galaxies have compact, ultrabright cores and were actively star-forming in the early universe; however, their host galaxies are now quiescent, with only moderate activity in their centers. We explored the development of these bulges by identifying continuous star formation patterns and analyzing the movement of gas, morphological changes, and bulge growth. Notably, all galaxies exhibited lopsided exteriors and tidal tails resulting from past interactions with nearby galaxies, and our analysis indicated that these interactions triggered continuous star formation on their outer disks. These galaxies also showed evidence of gas accretion, likely fueled by their interactions. The growth of their bulges was primarily driven by the collapse of gas, with some evidence of gas recycling from tidal tails. We found similar behavior in multiple lines of evidence and confirmed that these galaxies' bulges developed due to the collapse of gas, and that their star formation patterns were shaped by their interactions with nearby galaxies. Additionally, we found that their disks were using accreted gas to fuel their star formation, and that we can apply this understanding to similar galaxies at these redshifts. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for studying the development of bulges and star formation in these galaxies. It also offers a new approach to recognizing and analyzing similar galaxies at these redshifts, and can be used to explore how galaxy interactions affect their development. This is particularly relevant because these galaxies are similar to those that gave rise to all galaxy bulges in the universe. Therefore, understanding how their bulges developed is critical to comprehending the collapse of matter in the early universe. This research is now being extended to study these galaxies in greater detail and with even more sensitive data. Additionally, it has paved the way for a related study that is investigating whether these galaxies will continue to form stars at these rates, or if they will eventually become similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, which is primarily composed of an old, quiescent disk. This new study aims to explore when galaxy interactions cease to fuel their star formation, and when their bulges will be completed. Furthermore, it is also considering whether these galaxies will ever exhibit any central black hole activity similar to that of AGN. Therefore, monitoring these galaxies and their host galaxy cluster at these redshifts will provide valuable insights into the life cycle of galaxy mergers

The Global Structure Zero (GSZ) flavour model maintains that neighbourhoods of all quark and lepton masses are randomly generated, averaging out to zero. However, we employ a Monte Carlo method to instead model neighbourhoods within the flavour group, thereby obtaining a comprehensive understanding of the model's structure. Utilizing this approach, we derive a flavour oscillator expression for the average up-quark mass across neighbourhoods, displaying the effects of symmetry and predicting the existence of rare phenomena. Additionally, we establish oscillation frequencies for both charged and neutral flavours within the model. A more comprehensive flavour oscillator formula is also proposed, demonstrating the influence of higher-frequency oscillations on average mass values. We then leverage this framework to analyze existing GSZ models, identifying trends between up- and down-quark masses, as well as predicting the existence of down-quark oscillations at specific frequencies. Moreover, we identify a primary flavour oscillator peak at approximately 10 GeV, which may be detectable via high-energy particle collisions. A Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis confirms the naturalness of quark mass values within this framework. Models of this type may provide a compelling explanation for the standing anomalies in baryon asymmetry distribution, as well as the observed neutrino oscillation lengths. Nonetheless, distinct models of this type may also result in models that are inconsistent with established experimental data. Further investigation through particle collider experiments and flavour anomaly studies is highly recommended. In addition, a derivative model is proposed, where the average up-quark mass is set at a positive value, offering an even more intricate flavour oscillation landscape. This new flavour landscape may lead to the detection of additional, lighter flavour particles, alongside long-lived neutral flavour mesons and baryons. This model also provides a more comprehensive explanation for the existence of rare, short-distance processes. Nonetheless, it also increases the number of unobservable flavour particles by at least five. A critical examination of the flavour particle spectrum derived from this model is essential. Recent breakthroughs in neural program synthesis have yielded models that excel at generating short, simple codes from natural language descriptions. Nonetheless, current models often struggle when confronted with more intricate tasks. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel approach that leverages the efficacy of static program analysis to enhance neural code generation. Our method enables a neural network to suggest a preliminary code, which is then evaluated statically for errors. If found, the network refines its suggestion to rectify the issues. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the task of generating Python function definitions from natural language descriptions. Our results show that this approach outperforms the standard neural network methodology and surpasses the previous state-of-the-art in accuracy. Furthermore, we discover that this approach is highly effective at producing diverse codes that other methods may not achieve. We have made this project an open-source initiative that other researchers can build upon. Additionally, a user interface based on this model is available for direct use at https://codegen.iit.edu. We have also explored the applicability of this approach to the generation of Python classes and sequences. Our code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/arjunprakash/NeuralCodeGenEval. We have further analyzed the statistical findings of this project, including the distribution of evaluation errors, the comparison between static and dynamic code evaluation, and the assessment of program quality through structural features. These discoveries provide valuable insights into the performance of this approach and potential avenues for improvement. We have also examined the underlying neural code generation patterns and uncovered distinct modes of operation such as straightforward reproduction, partial guidance, and complete start-from-scratch generation. These patterns hold implications for the systematic development of program synthesis models. We have also explored several enhanced variants of this method including the integration of additional static evaluation tools, the incorporation of natural language processing techniques, and the inclusion of additional program synthesis approaches. While these variants show promise, further research is needed to fully assess their benefits and limitations. We have outlined a more comprehensive research framework that builds upon this project, along with identifying key challenges and potential future directions for both program synthesis and static program analysis. On November 4, 2004, a significant X2.0 solar flare occurred, followed by a massive coronal mass ejection (CME) that interacted with a partial CME on November 7, producing another substantial X1.0 solar flare and CME. As a result, extremely hard and dense protons appeared suddenly in solar flux spectra on November 7, 2004, likely resulting from the neutron-induced production of protons in the solar atmosphere due to the interaction between high-energy electrons and atomic nuclei on November 6, 2004. We develop a decompression model explaining the origin of these hard protons and present its solution for proton energy spectra, obtaining the neutron decomposition time as 17.5 hours, consistent with CME arrival times at various solar distances, and estimate the decompression energy as 535 MeV, above the binding energy of 517 MeV, which supports the model's validity. Additionally, we analyze observed solar flux spectra and identify their harmony with the model, also providing hourly solar flux predictions for November 6, 2004, and validating them with actual data, showing a close match. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of precise neutron decomposition modeling in distinguishing genuine hard proton origins from false explanations. We propose the term "decompression protons" to describe this phenomenon and suggest the name "Solar Neutron Decomposition Protons Event Type" (SND-ET). Lastly, we stress the value of monitoring and analyzing such events, as they may forecast hazardous deep space proton flux increases. Nonetheless, more research is needed to fully comprehend the effects of these events on both astronauts and electronic systems in deep space. We also outline key aspects for future study in this field.

This study takes a detailed examination of the linearized versions of the conservation equations in relativistic hydrodynamics, specifically in a system with multiple fluid types and in a single-fluid model. We present the general dispersion equation for relativistic hydrodynamics and apply it to both adiabatic and dissipative cases, also considering both single-fluid and multi-fluid scenarios. In the case of a single fluid with non-zero viscosity and anisotropic pressure, our analysis yields a dissipative dispersion equation, whereas in the case of a multi-fluid system with no energy exchange between fluids, our analysis yields adiabatic modes and dissipative modes at the interface between fluids. We validate these findings against existing literature and employ the dissipative dispersion equation to model relativistic viscous signal propagation in a multi-fluid scenario. This work provides a foundation for further linear stability analyses in relativistic hydrodynamics. Additionally, a numerical method for solution integration is introduced, demonstrating the potential for numerical solutions of linearized conservation equations to be obtained. This work is relevant to large-scale simulations of relativistic fluid dynamics involving multiple fluids. 

In the context of first-principle simulations, this work is an important step for an ongoing project described in [1] and involves further development of relativistic hydrodynamic simulations for use in modeling real fluids such as electron--photon plasmas. This work is also an extension of previous research on non-relativistic hydrodynamics presented in [2]. 

The current work extends previous research to a multi-fluid model and includes a new section on relativistic hydrodynamic simulations for systems with viscous fluids.

This study introduces InQMAD, a framework aimed at detecting exotic, non-standard scalar field theories through anomaly detection in vacuum data. InQMAD utilizes a machine learning algorithm to identify patterns in data obtained from quantum field theory, specifically focusing on the QMAD operator. This operator measures the difference between a system's anomalous and expected energy spectra. InQMAD employs a neural network to train on simulated data featuring standard and non-standard scalar field theories. It then identifies targets representing exotic, non-standard theories by pinpointing areas with significant energy anomalies. In our analysis, InQMAD effectively pinpoints targets at various scalar field theory parameter settings and under different quantum field theory conditions. Furthermore, InQMAD excels when compared to a simpler machine learning approach, demonstrating its potential as a powerful tool for identifying energy anomalies in scalar field theories. This study also explores integrating InQMAD with existing lattice QCD data extraction methods, with implications for discovering exotic, non-standard theories in lattice QCD. This approach is highly versatile, with potential applications in distinguishing standard and anomalous processes in particle physics. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical approach based on the Lagrange-Galerkin method for solving the linear transport equation with the collisional term specified in integral form. Specifically, it considers the equation $\partial_t f + v\cdot\nabla_x f = \beta f + \beta(1-f)$, where $f$ represents the probability density function and $\beta$ is a non-negative scalar representing the rate of collision. It is demonstrated that when $\beta$ is nonzero, a unique solution $f$ exists across the space $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and is bounded by $1$. When $\beta$ equals zero, the equation reduces to the pure transport equation. The paper also derives a conservation-based discretization for this equation, ensuring that the cumulative density function is precisely conserved. This approach is applicable to solving systems of equations and can be employed to solve time-dependent equations. Notably, it provides an innovative way to solve systems of equations where different components have distinct rates of collision. One example involves an average cost problem with a continuous distribution over initial conditions, while another example is a time-dependent game. The paper also explores the limitation of its numerical solution in cases where the rate of collision is zero and provides an alternative method that achieves second-order accuracy in such situations. Overall, this study provides an advanced numerical approach for solving a broad class of Fokker-Planck equations and highlights its numerous applications in solving systems of equations, including those arising from the formulation of mean field games. This paper analyzes the average updating time of a discrete time status refreshing system that utilizes a single server with a Ber/G/1/1 queue. To derive the result, we employ probability generating functions and establish key properties, including the existence and bounds of the average updating time, as well as a closed-form expression for its moment of any order. Specifically, we find that in the steady-state, the square of the updating time has a finite moment when the arrival rate is less than one half the service time's reciprocal. We also demonstrate that in this efficient regime, the square of the updating time is approximately equal to twice the square of the system's utilization. To validate this finding, a simulation model is developed. Additionally, we explore similar systems with multiple servers and find that, counterintively, increasing the number of servers may actually decrease the updating time in certain cases. To deal with the complexity of calculating the updating time directly, we establish an alternative approach based on the system's phase process. This method provides an efficient way to evaluate the updating time's moment, but comes at a higher computational cost. It is worth noting that the discrete time status refreshing system can be seen as a special case of the Ber/PH/1/1 queue's renewal process. However, due to the requirements of a continuous service time distribution in the latter, it cannot be applied to the former directly. Therefore, a new approach is devised to analyze its performance. This study's results are particularly useful in providing average updating time values for systems that utilize a single server with a discrete time status refreshing system. This type of system is commonly employed in wireless sensor networks, where the updating time can significantly impact the performance of cross-layer applications. Finally, future research could be directed towards analyzing more complex systems, such as those with multiple servers or networks, as well as developing approximation methods that are applicable to a broader range of queueing systems. In the context of wireless sensor networks, future studies could explore strategies for optimizing the updating time, such as dynamic sampling techniques, as well as evaluating the performance of cross-layer applications using realistic traffic models. Additionally, considering new technologies such as time-synchronized wireless sensor networks that provide precise time for system's status refreshing, is also worthy of investigation. In this regard, a study on the update time of such systems is also needed. On the other hand, studies on complex systems, such as those with multi-server or network configurations, as well as on developing approximation methods for a broader range of queueing systems, are also highly recommended.

Specifically, we demonstrate that set-theoretic genre solutions lead to semi-hopfian quasi-bialgebras, and conversely, we show that these quasi-bialgebras give rise to set-theoretic genre solutions. This link between set-theoretic genre solutions and quasi-bialgebras is utility-driven, as it enables us to derive counter-examples. For instance, we use this relationship to create a counter-example to the question of whether finite quasi-bialgebras are equivalent to finite set-theoretic Yang-Baxter algebras. Additionally, this link allows us to construct more general counter-examples regarding the specificity of set-theoretic Yang-Baxter algebras and quasi-bialgebras. These counter-examples showcase the diversity of finite set-theoretic genre solutions and highlight the variability of finite quasi-bialgebras. Lastly, we utilize this link to provide a counter-example to a statement made in a previous paper. This counter-example demonstrates that neither the Yang-Baxter operator nor the R-matrix of a set-theoretic genre solution is necessarily an algebra morphism. This discovery also leads to the identification of a more general property for set-theoretic genre solutions, specifically that they can be characterized by first-order equations. This characterization contributes to our understanding of set-theoretic genre solutions in comparison to other types of Yang-Baxter algebras. The ultimate speed of computer memory systems is constrained by the time it takes to switch individual atoms within a solid. To overcome this limitation, researchers need to understand and manipulate atomic-scale interactions in solids. This study leverages highly developed surface science techniques and advanced computational modeling to investigate silicon, which is widely used in electronic manufacturing. By examining silicon's atomic-scale electrical properties, the team employed highly precise measurement methods to identify three fundamental barriers to fast electronic switching: opposing valleys that compete for electron occupation, electron spin polarization, and atomic displacements that affect electron transmission. These findings provide a foundation for investigating these limitations in other solids and exploring new paths to overcome them, thus holding promise for significantly accelerating electronic data transfer.

Recent studies in medical imaging have seen the emergence of generative neural network models generating realistic cerebral lesion images. However, these models are developed in isolation without consideration for the underlying probability distributions that govern image generation. This research introduces a novel approach that combines a progressive variational auto-encoder with a adversarial component to capture complex data distributions and produce high-quality images of cerebral lesions. To improve training stability and efficiency, we split the training process into separate stages for code learning and adversarial optimization. By leveraging a convex relaxation technique called log-normal relaxation, we transform a non-linear problem into a linear one, facilitating efficient code learning. Our proposed method, termed PVALE, outperforms existing generative models and meets realistic cerebral lesion generation standards, as evidenced by results from multiple evaluation metrics and visual inspection. To support model selection and evaluation, we also develop a novel lesion detection evaluation method that assesses models' ability to generate diverse lesions. This approach not only prioritizes statistical modeling over simple neural network-based approaches but also over conventional auto-encoders that can result in biased code representations. To facilitate code learning, we employ a progressive approach that utilizes multiple intermediate code vectors to capture complex data distributions. To further enhance training stability, we incorporated a adversarial component that leverages a generator and discriminator model to optimize code quality. To overcome the limitations of latent variable models, we introduced an efficient training strategy that facilitates fast and stable training. This approach is also highly adaptable to various medical imaging applications that involve complex data distributions and diverse sample generation. In terms of computational resources, our model requires a relatively small embedding size of 64 dimensions, which can be easily deployed on multiple platforms. To validate the model's performance, we conducted extensive experiments using multiple evaluation metrics and visual inspection. We examine the nonlocality of multipartite states used in unextendible product bases (UPBs) in a scenario where entanglement detection is compromised by strong environmental influences, essentially asking how much nonlocality these states possess when they can't be clearly extended. Building on previous research, we develop a new approach to analyze the robust quantum nonlocality of UPBs in a variety of systems by considering the largest number of nonlocality units, known as nonlocality number, that can be embedded within a given UPB. By calculating this value for UPBs in multiple systems, we find that it directly correlates with the cardinality of UPBs in many cases and displays unique growth patterns as the number of systems increases. Notably, we identify a specific combination of UPBs in six systems where the robust quantum nonlocality of one of the UPBs outperforms that of all others, demonstrating that this phenomenon isn't limited to small-scale systems. Our findings also provide evidence that robust quantum nonlocality of UPBs can exhibit reversible transformations, or "gates", when two systems are merged or split apart. These outcomes further our understanding of quantum nonlocality in heterogeneous systems and the relationships between UPBs in different dimensions. Moreover, the robust quantum nonlocality of UPBs has implications for improving broad-spectrum quantum nonlocality tests in systems where contamination is present. Ultimately, our research paves the way for exploring real-world applications of quantum nonlocality in systems prone to environmental influences. Additionally, we propose this robust quantum nonlocality of UPBs may enable novel strategies for scalable quantum computation, in particular in systems where the influence of environmental contamination can't be fully mitigated. Lastly, our findings also support the idea that quantum nonlocality in the physical world often exhibits a more resilient form than can be detected through conventional means. In essence, this robust nature of quantum nonlocality might be a hallmark of the unique properties of quantum physics that govern our universe. This is accomplished by observing the motion of these masses in the gravitational field of the Earth via laser interferometry. The experiment's ability to validate the WEP depends on specific frequency components of the signal and is susceptible to interference from glitches, mechanical failures, and unusual events that can occur in the satellite's hardware. In this study, the statistical analysis of these incidents in the Microscope data is presented, along with an assessment of their impact on WEP validation. A threshold of 1 m/s^2 was used to identify significant events and their associated acceleration readings. Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, while maintaining the necessary functionality and maintaining the unique magnetic properties. This study demonstrates a breakthrough by integrating minute amounts of ferrimagnetic alloys within a gold nanoarray to create a highly complex structure that reacts strongly to light and controlled magnetic fields. This interaction with light results in a deep and narrow range of light that can be manipulated, combined with a rapid response to change and strong impact from either light or magnetic fields. This means that just a small amount of the material, approximately one million times smaller than the width of a hair, is enough to split light into two separate parts. This discovery provides a foundation for developing rapid and highly sensitive devices that can manipulate light with external controls. Furthermore, this discovery can lead to a better understanding of how light interacts with small scales of rare earth and transition metal alloys, potentially enabling the development of new technology that combines light and magnetic control. This study demonstrates a unique model of light interacting with these alloys and it suggests that, in some cases, light might not be effectively utilized due to a lack of control over the alignment of the alloys' atomic structure. This study was conducted by researchers from the National University of Science and Technology, the Russian Academy of Sciences, and the University of the Basque Country. It introduces a novel photonic device that operates rapidly in the visible light range of the spectrum and demonstrates complex light-matter interactions that could lead to the development of new technology in fields such as communication, medicine, and metrology. This study provides a foundation for further research into rare earth and transition metal alloys that could enable the creation of rapid, highly sensitive devices that can manipulate light with external controls. This study demonstrates a new light-matter interaction phenomenon known as orientation-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattice effects and proposes a design for a rapid, high-sensitivity device that can manipulate light with external controls. It is believed that incorporating minute amounts of rare earth and transition metal alloys within a gold nanoarray provides high control over the alloys' atomic structure and enables rapid, high-sensitivity devices that can effectively utilize light. In the context of machine learning and specifically model-agnostic post-processing, we are addressing a critical issue: obtaining knowledge from a trusted, but inaccessible model. Our solution is a novel knowledge acquisition method that enables us to import a variety of knowledge types, including classifications, regressions, and anomaly detection, from a black-box model via a decision interface. We successfully demonstrated this approach by successfully replicating the performance of a restricted access model on the test set, using a simple replacement model that only provides classification decisions. Furthermore, our method requires minimal information about the target model and no information about the data used to train the trusted model. We have also shown that our method is robust, flexible, and able to import a wide range of knowledge types with minimal adjustments. Additionally, we found that even a small amount of target data is sufficient for successful knowledge transfer. We have made our implementation publicly available on GitHub, under the name KnowledgeTransfer. KnowledgeTransfer is a Python package that includes a command-line interface and examples for classification, regression, and anomaly detection. It can be used with scikit-learn models and includes support for LightGBM and CatBoost. KnowledgeTransfer is an open-source implementation of our zero-shot knowledge transfer method and can be used as a starting point for other knowledge transfer projects. We have also published a paper that presents our research in detail and includes additional experiments and results. The paper is available on arXiv preprint server under the title Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer from a Decision-Based Black-Box Framework. KnowledgeTransfer is an original contribution that represents a significant advancement in zero-shot knowledge transfer. It overcomes several significant hurdles that other approaches face, such as the need for access to the model's internal workings, the type of data used to train the model, or the specific model architecture. KnowledgeTransfer can import a wide range of knowledge types from a black-box model via a decision interface. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct the lattice of submodules of a module using its character table, this approach remains largely unexplored for modules based on their character tables, mainly due to the complexity of computing these tables. However, Lass, Jow, and Lutsyak have recently made progress on this front by constructing the lattice of submodules of modules based on their multiplicity-free character tables. Building on their work, we provide a step-by-step guide on how to extend this construction to modules that are multiplicity free with a certain global character. Additionally, we verify that the constructed lattice corresponds to the actual lattice of submodules of the module. To support this proof, we also introduce a new order relation for modules and show that it is a partial order, and further, that it is a lattice order for modules that are multiplicity free with a certain global character. This concept can be applied to modules that are multiplicity free with a certain global character over a finite field using the computer software Sylven. To facilitate this application, we make the constructed lattice of submodules of a module available online through the Sylven software, by allowing users to input the character tables of the module and its submodules. This, in turn, enables us to explore some interesting properties of the constructed lattice. For instance, we discovered that the constructed lattice of submodules of a module includes all of its minimal submodules, and that the number of submodules of a module is less than or equal to the number of intervals in its lattice. Moreover, we found that the constructed lattice of submodules of a module is a poset lattice, and that this property is inherited from the same property shared by its submodules. Machine learning models typically learn from their own data, training independently on multiple tasks. We investigate a unique approach where a model can learn from the observations of its peers, leveraging the predictions of others for improved performance. To overcome the challenge of obtaining expert predictions, we develop a novel co-observation learning framework that enables models to learn from each other without requiring manual labeling of comparison data. This framework introduces a novel distillation method called comparison distillation, which automatically extracts comparative knowledge from interactions between models. By incorporating comparison distillation in addition to traditional distillation, we show that models can achieve better results than those trained using a single distillation method. Our method also significantly reduces labeling costs, eliminating the need for expert comparisons and improving efficiency. Through experiments on both classification and generation tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving performance with limited peer observation data. Our method also exhibits robust performance by incorporating comparison distillation methods that are not optimized for the task at hand. Our method is particularly useful in large-scale multi-task learning settings where many models need to be trained on multiple classification and regression tasks. Notably, we applied our method to a large action recognition dataset, obtaining results that are on par with those achieved using comparison data labeled by human experts. Our method is also suitable for real-world applications involving machine learning models in areas such as customer service, where models need to be trained to recognize their peers' behavior and adapt to that knowledge. Through successful application of our method to action recognition tasks, we show that it is possible to train models to recognize the observations of others, even when those observations are derived from different modalities. Our method facilitates the exploration of novel comparison distillation methods by automatically generating comparison data from model interactions. Through this exploration, we discovered that a comparison distillation method designed for action recognition was surprisingly effective on a regression task. Our method enables the exploration of many other comparison distillation methods that could be discovered from its output. This is particularly useful in large-scale machine learning projects involving multiple models and tasks, where time is a critical consideration. Our method outperforms previous work on action recognition tasks by obtaining higher accuracy with the same amount of peer observation data. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations for a specific class of codes and can be applied to the efficient parallelization of decoding, enabling the practical use of high-throughput turbo and LDPC codes. The proposed function is based on the well-known density function of the Gaussian distribution and can be calculated using a simple lookup table method, making it particularly suitable for hardware implementations. We demonstrate the excellent performance of this metric function, which is comparable to that of sophisticated density-evolution-based bounds, in the successful decoding of various turbo and LDPC codes. The proposed method calculates the entire code density in a single step, outperforming the conventional breadth-first search (BFS) traversal approach by approximately 10 times in terms of computation complexity and can be parallelized using a parallel BFS algorithm, achieving a further 5-6 times improvement. We also provide a hardware implementation example of this metric function, which successfully demonstrated the correct decoding of a 4K/16 spatial diversity turbo code and had a throughput of approximately 2.5Gbps. The proposed method reduces the computational load to a level where it can be efficiently combined with any turbo/ldpc decoder, making it a versatile and useful decoding method. We anticipate that this metric function will find wide application in future high-throughput turbo and LDPC code designs. The source code of our study has been made publicly available on GitHub. Due to the high success rate of this metric function in decoding, we are confident that it can also be effective in other modulation schemes and code designs and therefore welcome any further research or contributions in this area. Based on the marginal contribution to default risk and expected loss, the qfs-area calculates the area under the marginal default distribution curve. It leverages the Marginal Contribution to Default (MCD) approach, considering multiple rating transitions from default. The characteristics of the qfs-area are examined through stylized facts, and its relationship with other metrics is analyzed through correlation. Studying a periodically driven and isolated two-qubit system, consisting of resonant lasers and a hybrid solid-state qubits, we find a consistent empirical framework that maps periodic driving parameters to a critical disorder point, describing the transition from a stable, periodic state to a mixed, periodic state. Our empirical model specifically predicts the critical disorder point, steady-state entropy, and periodic state coherence for a specific, periodic driving regime. Notably, this empirical framework can be applied even when periodic driving induces rapid, rotational movements within the system's energy levels, a scenario that undermines traditional, adiabatic descriptions of the steady state. Our theoretical model also provides a fundamental understanding of this non-equilibrium behavior, using a rotating-reference-frame approach that accounts for rapid, periodic fluctuations in the system's energy levels. This approach identifies a quasi-stationary Hamiltonian that describes the system's periodic state, and demonstrates that periodic driving induces an irreversible transformation of the system's energy levels, a phenomenon that holds broader implications for describing and controlling periodic states in quantum systems. A rational fraction p/q is considered identifiable within a set A if knowing p mod q helps in determining whether the point (x, y) belongs to A, even when x and y are restricted to lie within the interval [0, 1]. The term "identifiable" is used here for brevity. We aim to examine which rational fractions are identifiable over specific sets and offer a more general identification criterion applicable to any set defined by a formula. This criterion enables us to identify identifiable rational fractions for various commonly used functions, such as polynomials, piecewise linear functions, and continuous functions on a closed interval. Furthermore, we discuss the variations of our basic identifiable sets, particularly focusing on even or odd identifiable fractions, and provide an algorithm to convert equivalent identifiable fractions. These conversions are further demonstrated through identifiable exponential and logarithmic functions. Additionally, we explore the relationship between 1/q-identifiable sets and other well-known classes of sets, such as those with a rational slope or a rational zero. We also show that for any irrational identifier p mod q, there are sets where p mod q identification provides a more efficient classification than q mod 1, indicating a more complex decision boundary in the p/q dimension. We also introduce the concept of almost-identifiable sets and propose a more efficient algorithm for identifying certain types of fractions, such as 2^d identifying 1/2^nd. We explore various 1/2^nd identifiable sets and present several 1/3^nd identifiable sets. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings within the context of binary search and its modifications, particularly highlighting the differences caused by using an identifying fraction other than 1/2. We provide several examples of such modified binary search, along with their corresponding names, and discuss their overall performance in relation to other well-known search algorithms. We also touch on the topic of choosing an identifying fraction and propose a simple yet effective method, which we apply to several examples. This method enables us to generate many new identifying fractions, such as all identifying fractions with a denominator of 3 up to 2^9. However, we note that this method has a significant drawback, which leads to a much less efficient performance compared to binary search for large datasets. We believe this inefficiency arises from the fact that many of the newly identified identifiable fractions mod 1/3 appear to have a much more complex decision boundary than those for 1/2. We conclude by outlining several open problems and potential areas for further research within this topic.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed deep, limited-field observations for four $K$2 plates, covering an area of roughly $1.25$ square degrees in the sky. Furthermore, our approach enables us to evaluate the MongoDB snapshotting restoration process. We validate the effectiveness of our method by employing it to assess the transactional features of MongoDB. The technical details of our approach, along with the results of our evaluation of MongoDB 5.0, are presented in this paper. The implementation of our protocol emulator and test utilities has been made open-source and is now available on GitHub. Despite being designed to facilitate the verification of MongoDB's transactional behavior, this approach can be adapted to evaluate other distributed database systems. The development of computational models for simulating hard-drive failure has evolved over time, driven by increasing data storage needs and the growing criticality of reliable information, particularly since the turn of the century. In this work, we examine the underlying mathematical structures of these models, identifying a distinct division between categorically based and probabilistically derived methods. We provide an in-depth analysis of prominent computational models, such as the mean-time-between-failures (MTBF), Arrhenius law, Markov chains, and Monte Carlo simulations, offering a comprehensive overview from a computer science perspective. Specific examples of implementation in the hard-drive industry are used to illustrate the applicability of these methods, highlighting their ability to calculate key performance indicators like MTBF and failure rates in various environments. We also explore the generalization of these methods to adapt them for use in the evaluation of reliable technology in general, rather than hard drives in particular. Finally, potential research directions for this area are presented. Specifically, we propose the development of a reliability model referencing structural compression, the creation of an open data set for hard-drive failure, and an exploration of machine learning applications in this domain. Additionally, we suggest investigating temporal models, multi-dimensional environmental effects, and the integration of bayesian methods. This work is intended to contribute to the hard-drive failure research community by providing a thorough review of computational models from a computer science perspective, setting the stage for future advancements in this area. Furthermore, it is our hope that this work will serve as a primer on computational modeling for reliability in general, making it accessible to a broader audience beyond the hard-drive failure community. This way, other areas that deal with reliable computation and failure can benefit from the knowledge gained in this domain. In the context of computer science, this includes areas like algorithms, data structures, database systems, networking, parallel processing, software engineering, theory, and virtual machines. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now.
