Our study reveals the internal structure of this scheme, including its extensive network of defrauded participants and the top-tier scammers who profit greatly. By utilizing time-series pricing data and model-based estimators, we demonstrate the illusory nature of Forsage's pretend cryptocurrency investment opportunities and the excessive returns promised to participants. Our findings show that participation in Forsage results in an expected loss of 85% of a user's initial investment, with a significant majority of participants (approximately 84%) losing their entire initial investment. Furthermore, our data highlights the extreme returns achieved by the top-tier scammers and the unfavorable conditions offered to later participants. To achieve these excessive returns, Forsage forces participants to recruit more new users through a complex system of bonuses that discourage skillful investing. Our study also examines the scheme's impact on users, including the premature freezing of user funds due to lack of knowledge about blockchain transaction fees, as well as the emotional distress caused by Forsage's deceptive advertising and the loss of investment. By highlighting the adverse effects of pyramid schemes on participants, our study aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion between regulatory approaches to decentralized applications. We define the state of situational awareness for a single UAS and expand this to achieve independent situational awareness across multiple UAS. This enables each UAS in the swarm to make independent decisions based on its unique perspective. Unitary matrices whose entries are independently and identically distributed according to a standard real Gaussian distribution, denoted as $U_N$, exhibit unique properties. They maintain three key features: asymptotic stability under matrix multiplication, a freeness structure relative to Type $B$, and the satisfaction of various conditional independence conditions. These features hold regardless of the matrix dimension $N$. It has been proven that in order for a square matrix to possess these features, it must be unitarily equivalent to $U_N$. However, this equivalence does not extend to non-square matrices. A counterexample exists in the form of the standard real Gaussian matrix, demonstrating that such matrices can still exhibit freeness or various conditional independence properties while not being unitarily equivalent to $U_N$. Moreover, in the case of independent entries with a specific correlation structure, a condition has been derived under which a square matrix exhibits freeness or various conditional independence properties. This condition is shown to be both necessary and sufficient. It has been further proven that in the case of independent entries with a specific correlation structure, a matrix exhibiting freeness or various conditional independence properties must be unitarily equivalent to $U_N$. This proof employs non-commutative polynomial dimension extension, a recently introduced dimension estimation tool. This technique allows pseudo-probability measures, including matrices with independent entries under certain conditions, to be treated as genuine probability measures. As a result, many established results concerning independence in the context of classical probability theory can be successfully applied to matrices with independent entries. In addition to freeness and conditional independence, this technique is also shown to be effective for other forms of independence such as free log-normal, free gamma, and several variants of semi-free matrices. It should be noted that the proposed condition for a matrix exhibiting freeness or various conditional independence properties is more comprehensive than previous results in the literature. In particular, in the case of square matrices, this study provides the first explicit description of the set of matrices with independently distributed entries that exhibit freeness or various conditional independence properties. This description is shown to be a rotation of the unitary group, demonstrating that the proposed condition is optimal. In the case of non-square matrices, this study fills a long-standing gap in the literature by providing a general framework that accurately describes the set of matrices with independently distributed entries that exhibit freeness or various conditional independence properties. Once the equations are solved, the generated spacetime map can predict geodesics, thus allowing the calculation of particle trajectories. A key challenge in using numerical solutions to the Einstein field equations lies in creating a suitable initial conditions setup that complies with the constraints of the equations. We developed the conformal transverse traceless decomposition technique to tackle this issue. Our approach involves decomposing the extrinsic curvature into three components, then imposing constraints on two of these components to derive the gravitational wave generation equations. This strategy enables us to generate initial conditions without the need for a coordinate system modification, thus allowing us to maintain physical accuracy throughout the process. To expedite model training, student models can benefit from being trained on data labeled by multiple pre-trained models (multi-teacher labeling). Nonetheless, the current methods for multi-teacher labeling are hampered by insufficient consideration of the differences in labeling behaviors among teachers and lack of an effective method for aggregating student outputs. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Aggregation (PILE) to address these shortfalls. The success of cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) research heavily relies on vast amounts of data being made available by the general public, necessitating the creation of user-centered platforms that make contributing easy and rewarding. To tackle the challenge of scaling these platforms, we introduce the concept of "crowds-SI," which unifies the principles of crowd sourcing, human-computer interaction, and computer science to design efficient and engaging systems for mass user participation. We have developed a platform for crowds-SI at the Microsoft MakeCode platform, which has gathered over 4 million registered users and features a user-friendly online environment where people can easily contribute to various open-source projects by writing simple code. Through an exhaustive examination of 50+ projects on the platform, we have identified key characteristics of high-performing projects that engage users through code-based activities, exceeding 13,000 daily submissions and totaling over 2 million contributions. Our study also reveals the effectiveness of these projects in recruiting diverse groups of contributors and providing them with a meaningful sense of accomplishment, as reflected in the satisfaction ratings of over 120,000 users. Furthermore, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the human factors that influence contribution rates, uncovering insights that can guide the design of more effective crowds-SI systems. To facilitate the replication of our studies and the development of optimized human-computer interfaces for these systems, we have created an interactive visualization tool that enables the exploration of a vast dataset comprising over 120,000 user evaluations of over 40 open-source projects. This research contributes significant advancements to both the fields of human-computer interaction and computer science, with potential applications in multiple domains such as artificial intelligence, computer networks, and software engineering. These domains often require large-scale, collaborative software development efforts that involve large groups of users, making the development of effective crowds-SI systems critically important for their success. Overall, our work provides a foundation for further research into the design of high-performance human-computer interfaces for these systems, along with practical solutions that can be applied to real-world projects at large-scale user centers. These solutions leverage machine intelligence to monitor system performance, identify areas for improvement, and inform the design of more engaging interfaces that can handle a high volume of submissions from mass user participation. These advancements have already been incorporated into the MakeCode platform, with over 2 million contributions from users worldwide. A particular failure mechanism of quantum annealing, specifically involving non-stoquastic Hamiltonians, was recently identified and categorized as 'catastrophic collapse.' This failure mechanism arises from the interaction of two opposing processes within a quantum system undergoing transformation via quantum annealing. To rectify this issue, the role of environmental interference, or decoherence, on quantum annealing was investigated. It was found that, under certain conditions of decoherence strength, quantum annealing can still successfully converge to the ground state of a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian, even in the absence of stoquastic approximations. This insight may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the efficacy of quantum annealing, especially in addressing difficult computational problems. A proposed protocol for mitigating catastrophic collapse through decoherence control may also facilitate the successful application of quantum annealing to various problems of science and technology. A theoretical model including environmental interference is derived, which facilitates the analysis of quantum annealing via a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian. This derivation involves a combination of both theoretical modeling and experimental simulation using a superconducting quantum annealing unit. The findings mentioned earlier were validated through actual experiments conducted with superconducting quantum bits. A further extension of this concept may also provide a path for resolving another critical issue in quantum computing, namely the problem of weak quantum control. This solution strategy involves optimizing the parameters of a specific temporal-spectral transformation protocol, which is itself derived from a combined quantum annealing and adiabatic evolution algorithm. This protocol was successfully tested on a variety of Hamiltonians, including both stoquastic and non-stoquastic types, and demonstrated a significant improvement in the convergence to the ground state, compared to standard quantum annealing. The use of this protocol allows for the successful solution of a binary Ising model in the case of a randomly generated Hamiltonian, which exhibits a driven-dyning instability in the absence of environmental interference. This achievement may provide a breakthrough in overcoming one of the fundamental obstacles in implementing a scalable quantum annealing algorithm. The critically optimized parameters of this protocol also demonstrate a surprising correspondence with the catastrophic collapse phenomenon, as well as its rectification through environmental interference. Furthermore, this solution strategy may also offer a path for resolving the binary Ising model in cases where quantum annealing itself fails due to a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian. This protocol can be viewed as a prototype for a broader class of time-spectral transformations, which may provide a new approach for addressing various computational issues in physics, chemistry, and materials science

This approach is referred to as RNECE. By conducting extensive simulations under controlled and realistic conditions, we demonstrate that our method outperforms comparative methods by producing more accurate results and a more natural and intuitive temporal connection structure. Furthermore, RNECE is applied to analyze real-world EEG data, yielding results that align with prior research and reveal temporally varying connection patterns. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. Given a given set of species trees and their associated alignments, various methods can be employed to construct phylogenetic networks, utilizing maximum-likelihood principles to create the most plausible networks. Notably, different methods may generate distinct topological features in the resulting networks, with potential implications for the fields of computational biology, applied mathematics, and computer science. This study aims to offer a theoretical framework for analyzing and comparing the topological properties of phylogenetic network construction algorithms. Specifically, we develop a specific metric called the network reconstruction ratio to evaluate the ability of a method to accurately identify reticulate evolutionary events. Additionally, our study provides a comprehensive comparison of the topological properties of several phylogenetic network construction algorithms. The chosen algorithms represent a broad cross-section of available methods, spanning both maximum-likelihood approaches and others, with applications in biology, computer science, and machine learning. Our analysis highlights the intrinsic differences and similarities between these algorithms, with implications for the development of future methods and potential use of existing ones. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of a network reconstruction threshold to distinguish between algorithms that can handle reticulate evolutionary events and those that cannot. With the growing use of phylogenetic networks in evolutionary studies, understanding the algorithms used to construct them takes on increasing importance. Our study provides a starting point for further research into the development of more efficient and effective phylogenetic network construction algorithms. The extensive online database of benchmarked networks, along with the proposed theoretical framework, is open-source and available for further exploration and improvement. Our study initiates a deeper examination of these algorithms and their capabilities, potentially spurring further innovation in this area. The extensive online database of benchmarked networks is available for further exploration and is an open-source project that can be improved upon. With this in mind, we invite researchers to engage with this study and contribute to the development of future phylogenetic network construction algorithms. This study confirms the recently discovered property of energy eigenchannels in scattering systems, specifically that the sum of certain eigenchannels equals the total amount of energy transmitted.  To demonstrate this, a general method for calculating eigenchannels has been established.  Furthermore, the paper shows that the scattering matrix can be decomposed into a product of two unitary matrices, one of which dictates the energy distribution among eigenchannels.  A key finding is that the absorption eigenchannels, which contribute to energy loss, form a complete set of vectors similar to transmission eigenchannels.  Specifically, the inner product of transmission and absorption eigenchannels is shown to be zero, meaning they are orthogonal to each other.  A practical application of this research involves optimizing light transmission through disordered materials by controlling their structural properties.  A numerical example, which models solar cell efficiency, is also provided.  The research centers on the general concept that eigenchannels are a valuable tool for understanding energy transport in scattering systems.  A new direction for investigation is also identified – the use of eigenchannels in studying polarization properties of scattering systems.  To facilitate further research, a note is made on the potential variation of polarization eigenchannels with respect to the polarization state of an incident light source.  A new term, "polarization eigenchannels," is also proposed and it is suggested that they could be obtained through a similar decomposition process applied to a polarization-transmitting matrix.  However, the theory of polarized light transmission is not as well-developed as intensity transmission and further research is needed in this area.  Finally, the paper concludes by highlighting several potential areas for further study inspired by the recent breakthroughs in understanding energy eigenchannels and the proposed concept of polarization eigenchannels.  A numerical example which could be explored involves the application of eigenchannels to understanding luminescence patterns, specifically in studying and optimizing the light distribution in photon upconversion materials. We investigate topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary, position-dependent disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that, depending on the correlation of the disorders, the system exhibits either short-range or long-range correlations in its spectral fluctuations. Based on the disorders' strength and correlation, the system may transition between various topological phases, effectively merging them and generating a non-trivial Anderson localizing phase with intertwined winding numbers. This phase is characterized by random fluctuations of both the bulk Chern number and spectral winding, separating it from other areas on the phase diagram. Notably, this phase can be identified by measuring transport properties through a diverse range of parameter spaces without the need for high-resolution spectral analysis. Additionally, we demonstrate that a gapped surface state can be induced within the Anderson localizing phase by shattering a topological insulating phase with uncorrelated disorders. This research provides valuable insights into understanding and controlling topological properties in realistic systems with spatially correlated disorders. It also paves the way for exploring new types of topological phenomena in one-dimensional systems on random networks. Finally, we propose an experimental realization of this model using cold atomic gases on optical lattices, which can offer a versatile platform for observing and studying topological phenomena in complex, spatially correlated systems. Nonetheless, numerical simulations indicate that binary disorders are less efficient at creating a topological non-trivial state compared to their independent counterparts. This finding is particularly evident in models without surface states, such as the one-dimensional Hofstadter model, where topological states require spatially correlated disorders that are strongly correlated over large distances. In contrast, quasi-one-dimensional materials with naturally occurring surface states may provide a more feasible path to topological non-trivial states in 2D parent materials. This knowledge can be utilized to develop strategies for identifying topological states in experimental measurements of transport properties. In the case of cold atomic gases, this knowledge may lead to the creation of topological states using optical lattices and a range of other quantum simulation tools. This research provides a theoretical framework for analyzing and numerical simulations of one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated disorders, which can be applied to a broader class of systems utilizing mean-free path approximations. Our analysis evaluates the linearity requirement for continuous-time network autoregressive models, assessing their performance in forecasting time series data. Specifically, we investigate whether relaxing this constraint enhances prediction accuracy across various network architectures. Our research indicates that non-linear NAR models outperform lineal NAR and GRAN models, confirming the linearity requirement relaxation's positive impact on forecasting in network autoregressive frameworks. However, this benefit is limited to specific NAR dimensions, as further analysis reveals a dimensionality issue affecting NAR estimators. Consequently, we introduce an alternative estimation method addressing this limitation, enabling more effective use of available data and boosting the performance of lineal NAR models. Notably, this new approach surpasses the performance of both lineal and non-lineal NAR models, demonstrating that removing the linearity requirement is necessary but not sufficient for optimal results. Additionally, we explore parameter selection for NAR models, identifying a suitable approach that prioritizes forecasting accuracy over parameter smoothness. This research provides lineal NAR's foundation for future studies on network autoregressive models and highlights the significance of linear models in low-dimensional data sets. Finally, given the widespread adoption of NAR models in economics and finance, our results also emphasize the necessity of linear models in these domains due to the inherent non-linearity of economic systems. Due to potential generalizability, we encourage researchers from other domains to reconsider linear models' value. Overall, our analysis offers linear and non-linear NAR models' comparative performance, providing a platform for further research on network autoregressive models across multiple domains. This research is conducted in collaboration with the N4M 2021 challenge organizers and participants. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a substantial number of error-correction codes, necessitating efficient classical software to handle the associated measurement process, known as decoding. Encouraging progress in this area has been made through the development of quantum error-correction codes and decoding algorithms, but this research often assumes a seamless flow of data and ignores code's faulty original state. In reality, the need to periodically switch between different types of codes and collect their outcomes poses additional challenges. To tackle this problem, we've introduced a new framework that incorporates a specific type of codes called quantum extension codes, capable of handling faulty data streams and reducing the required classical communications. To tackle the decoding problem, we propose a variety of coder strategies, drawing from reinforcement learning, that can efficiently process code measurements, navigate the code switching scenario, and minimize the necessary measurements. Our code corders also exhibit a desirable property of being composable, allowing for seamless integration with other quantum computing systems. When applied to realistic scenarios involving multiple codes and frequent switching, our approach outperforms a previously established benchmark by at least an order of magnitude. This quantum coding problem provides a challenging test for both machine learning and quantum computing, providing a unique opportunity for researchers from these disparate fields to collaborate. To facilitate this collaboration, we've introduce the Quantum Coding Competition, an open competition aimed at developing the most resilient and efficient coding corders. The competition's focus on both theoretical progress and the development of a practical tool for fault-tolerant quantum computing makes it an engaging challenge for researchers from both the machine learning and quantum computing communities. To participate in the competition or for more information on the quantum coding problem, we've established a dedicated website that provides access to available code corders, as well as details on competition rules and evaluation metrics. This opportunity for interdisciplinary collaboration is crucial for advancing the development of efficient code corders, a critical component for the successful implementation of large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing. Furthermore, this problem also highlights the potential applications of coding corders in other complex systems subject to errors, such as distributed storage and communication systems. To demonstrate the value of this problem for machine learning researchers, we've show that solving this problem can lead to a data set that allows the training of highly effective machine learning models for addressing other complex coding problems. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult. An alternative approach, known as "quantum leap" metrology, suggests using continuous observations to collect information, with this study demonstrating the feasibility of this method in a dual-cavity setup that utilizes optical entanglement. Using a three-level atom system, quantum leaps in two separate cavities can be correlated with each other, producing a massive entanglement of around 10^7 photons. Evaluating the performance of this system shows that quantum leap metrology can achieve similar levels of precision with significantly less complexity than other quantum states, making it a more practical solution for implementing advanced precision measurements. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that quantum leap metrology can be applied to determine unknown variables, such as the frequency of light, with an accuracy of around 1/100 of a Hz in a dual-cavity setup that is about 10 cm long. This has significant implications for the measurement of physical constants, such as the speed of light, which could be determined with an accuracy of around 1/1000. This could potentially be achieved with a setup that is around 1 meter long, further showcasing the vast potential of quantum leap metrology. This study also shows that quantum leaps in optical systems can be highly reliable, with an accuracy of around 0.1 radian in a dual-cavity setup that is about 10 cm long. This has implications for the development of highly accurate rotational spectroscopy, which could be used to study the internal structure of molecules and the external electromagnetic field that they are exposed to. This study demonstrates the potential of quantum leap metrology to be applied to study a range of phenomena, including the frequency splitting of light, the absorption and emission of light, and the rotation of molecules. This could provide highly accurate data, with potential applications in the development of rotational spectroscopy, chemical analysis, and the study of complex quantum systems. The PHENIX Collaboration has released initial findings on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011 data. These results provide early evidence for jet-medium interactions and offer insights into jet production and medium response. A significant excess in same-side near-side yields in Au$+$Au collisions distinguishes them from $d$$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions, indicating extra particles emitted at the same azimuthal angle as the jet. This excess is more pronounced at higher transverse momenta and lower $p_T$ counterparts, and its magnitude is proportional to the binary collision count in A$+$A collisions. This feature vanishes in $d$$+$Au collisions at the same $p_T$ range, and Au$+$Au results exhibit an increase in same-side near-side yields with rising $p_T$, ultimately exceeding $d$$+$Au results by five-fold at 39 GeV/C $p_T$. These findings are compared to the JETRY model, which relates jet production to medium response and incorporates jet quenching, also being interpreted to indicate jet energy being extracted from the medium at a rate of 5 GeV/c per unit length. Furthermore, this excess in same-side near-side yields is largely independent of centralities and isolated photon $p_T$. Additionally, the results show no significant dependence on the photon's $p_T$, and a notable deviation in Au$+$Au results is observed for back-to-back and opposite-side cases. These findings offer valuable insights into jet production and the medium's response, and it is suggested that a more comprehensive understanding can be attained through the combination of direct photon-hadron correlations and semi-inclusive hadron production. Moreover, the results in this analysis provide a foundation for further investigation into jet-medium interactions and the properties of quark-gluon plasma at various collision energies.

Cloud-based HPC applications can experience significant delays due to network factors, which can be further affected by the variability of network performance. To better understand these factors, a new approach is presented that utilizes real-network testing with a variable network setup mimicking the behavior of cloud environments. The approach is applied to investigate the performance of HPC applications running in the cloud and located geographically dispersed, considering three types of network performance variability: application-to-application variation, individual test variations, and variation between simultaneous applications. It was also found that there can be significant variation in network performance between applications, with some achieving nearly double the transfer rates of others. To mitigate these effects, a dynamic system is proposed that adapts to changing network conditions and is shown to reduce average increases in data transfer rates by more than half and standard deviation by a quarter. We investigate a collaborative learning setting where multiple agents, acting as contextual linear gambits, learn from feedback in a collaborative learning environment without sharing context information. They receive individualized feedback after making joint decisions. We establish a key insight that effective learning can be achieved when the Bregman divergence between the agents' loss functions is bounded, a condition that holds for standard choices of surrogates. This boundary's influence diminishes over time as the agents' parameters converge. We develop algorithms that take the bounded divergence into account and prove the required condition holds for standard choices of surrogates such as squared Euclidean distance. These proofs hold without explicit context information transfer. The study's findings are experimentally verified using auctions and negotiations scenarios. This study investigates how telecommuting influences Scrum project success, a topic that has gained significance due to the global pandemic and the growing popularity of remote working. Despite the widespread adoption of Scrum, its effectiveness is often hindered by poor implementation, and project members working from home face unique challenges that can impact success. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of existing research combined with a quantitative survey of 264 respondents from the software industry. The results of the survey revealed a significant relationship between telecommuting and Scrum project success, and identified four key factors that mediate this connection: team collaboration, trust, product backlogs, and roll-up rate. Interestingly, our findings indicate that these mediators can have a variable impact on success, depending on the project member. A further investigation of these complexities through in-depth interviews with 10 software developers provided valuable qualitative insights, that can serve as a foundation for future studies in this area. Ultimately, this research offers concrete recommendations for project managers aiming to implement Scrum in remote working settings, and highlights the necessity for a flexible Scrum approach that accommodates the challenges posed by telecommuting. To achieve this, a new formulation is developed for obtaining maximum generalised degrees of freedom in networks with binary power control, enabling a more efficient calculation than previously known methods. Furthermore, this finding is shown to be a fundamental limit by demonstrating that the ratio of the highest achievable generalised degrees of freedom in optimal versus binary power control networks converges to a constant as the number of users increases. With this analysis, new insights are gained into the performance benefits of optimal power control in networks with multiple users. A key innovation is the derivation of a general mathematical expression for predicting a particle's new state following a series of N successful collisions over a given time period. This expression can be applied to create an iteration formula for updating a particle's state in each time step. This paper focuses on developing a simplified dynamic model for a one-legged hopping robot in a environment that deforms yieldingly, with the aim of achieving improved performance by optimizing its movements. By modeling both the robot and environment dynamics and incorporating ground reaction forces, control strategies can be effectively developed. The model and its implications are also explored through two control-related case studies. We present a comprehensive analysis of the elastic form factor for a meson in a unified quantum field theory. Our calculation of the charge and magnetization distributions comprehensively covers all types of mesons, from goldstone bosons to quarkonia, and incorporates a universal Poisson's-type integral formula for the charge distribution. This approach enables a thorough investigation of the magnetic properties of mesons and allows for a detailed comparison of the magnetic and charge distributions. We examine the elasticity of mesons using a contact interaction regulator and discuss the implications of our findings in the context of recent J/ψ elastic form factor measurements. Our results demonstrate that the charge and magnetic distributions of J/ψ mesons exhibit distinct differences, with the former displaying a more compact structure than the latter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the charge distribution of ρ mesons comprises two components: a central part resembling a goldstone boson and an external component analogous to that of a spin-1 φ meson. Our analysis also reveals that the magnetic distribution of ρ mesons is similar to that of a spin-1 φ meson. We discuss the applicability of our approach to other meson systems. Our research sets the stage for a deeper exploration of meson elastic form factors and potential-confining operators of quark and gluon fields. We outline a strategy for studying light mesons like π and K using lattice QCD in the future. Our study provides a framework for analyzing the elastic form factors of composite systems in general, and we anticipate that it will contribute to a greater understanding of the internal structures of mesons. This understanding will further be enhanced by a further investigation of the elastic form factors of mesons in the future. Our results for J/ψ and ρ mesons constitute a significant step in this direction. We hope that this study will motivate other researchers to explore the internal structures of these mesons via the study of their elastic form factors. Our research demonstrates that the charge and magnetic distributions of mesons are distinct entities that provide independent insights into the internal structures of these systems. We are confident that a deeper understanding of the elastic form factors of mesons will enable a more precise interpretation of their properties and a better comprehension of the underlying physics of these systems. This, in turn, will facilitate a more accurate prediction of their behavior in other processes. Effective text-based reasoning over multiple sentences necessitates a deep understanding of all available information, including explicit and implicit negations.  Despite the immense importance of negation in everyday life, negation-based text comprehension has been consistently overlooked in comprehension datasets.  To bridge this gap, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English dataset comprising 14,000 questions that call for a thorough analysis of three-Sentence passages with integrated negations.  Our investigation reveals that current leading models, although exceptionally good at answering general comprehension questions, struggle with negation-based reasoning.  We anticipate CONDAQA to contribute significantly to the development of cutting-edge negation-comprehension models that can robustly reason about multiple Sentence passages.  Our findings are backed by thorough evaluations involving human-generated reasoning assessments and direct comparisons with widely-adopted comprehension datasets.  Interestingly, we discover that models' negation-based performance lags behind their ability to answer non-negation-based comprehension questions by a significant 11% gap.  To further enhance the scope of CONDAQA, we append a new sub-catalog named CONDAQA-Few-Shot that introduces 1,500 expert-crafted questions using the conventional four-Sentence structure, mirroring real-world scenarios where reasoners typically draw inferences from shorter text passages.  These question-answer pairs are uniquely characterized by their frequent co-reference to implicit entities mentioned in earlier Sentences, making them even more challenging to address.  We boldly predict that successful models trained on CONDAQA-Few-Shot will successfully generalize to a variety of complex co-reference settings not previously considered.  To facilitate seamless model evaluation, we introduce an innovative Negation-Aware Reasoning Score that not only gauges the accuracy of explicit negation but also assesses the level of reasoning required to tackle implicit negations.  Our study serves as a wake-up call to the broader comprehension community to give serious consideration to the long-overlooked aspect of text comprehension - negation.  We firmly believe that CONDAQA will provide a crucial impetus for the development of cutting-edge negation-comprehension models capable of robustly reasoning about multiple Sentence passages with integrated negations.  As a result, we anticipate these models to significantly outperform their current incarnations and propel the field of comprehension models forward. Test case selection is an important component of software testing, specifically when using boundary value analysis and decision table testing methods. Determining the uniqueness of test cases is crucial in reducing costs by eliminating redundant tests. However, the algorithms used to assess uniqueness often slow down when dealing with large datasets, making parallel processing an attractive solution. We present a novel algorithm that leverages unique value decomposition to improve test case uniqueness determination, and Levene's test for variance homogeneity. This algorithm is efficient, accurate, and capable of taking advantage of multiple processors to accelerate calculations. Our results show significant speed gains when using up to eight processors, making it an excellent candidate for large-scale test case uniqueness assessments. The source code of this research is freely available on GitHub under the MIT License. Additionally, a pre-compiled executable can be found on the research website. Xinhua News Agency and Sina Weibo released a dataset containing 8000 annotated posts from users in China, expressing emotions towards news about the COVID-19 pandemic. This dataset offers valuable insights into public sentiment during the crisis. However, an issue arises when applying machine learning models to analyze COVID-19-related sentiment in extended periods, as models are typically trained on static datasets and struggle to handle news-based data with varying sentiment labels. To overcome this challenge, our proposed framework integrates both text and source attributes into a multi-task model, simultaneously predicting sentiment and classification labels. This approach enables the model to accurately classify COVID-19-related sentiment in extended periods. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms alternative models by approximately 15% in accuracy when analyzing COVID-19-related sentiment in extended periods. Additionally, we explore models' performance with both basic and advanced configurations, as well as their scalability with increasing dataset sizes. Notably, our study shows that the zero-shot regime achieves comparable performance to fine-tuning models, reducing computational costs by approximately 50%. This includes 300 GDP savings in cloud costs for a dataset comprising 280,000 COVID-19-related tweets. Our work contributes a 15% boost to the current state-of-the-art model when applying zero-shot techniques and paves the way for further research on public sentiment analysis during the COVID-19 pandemic. This work has been presented at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2021. Moreover, our team won the Best Student Paper Award at the 2021 Conference on Artificial Intelligence for Applications (AI4Society). This award recognizes our work that excels in applying artificial intelligence effectively to address real-world issues. This paper is an extended version of that award-winning paper and provides additional context and guidelines for public sentiment analysis during the COVID-19 pandemic. This includes not only text-based data but also recommendations for incorporating data visualization and source credibility. Phylogenetic tree estimation often begins with a multiple sequence alignment that is used to generate the tree. However, recent studies have shown that alignments can be obtained from a single sequence while still capturing the phylogenetic information. Moreover, these single sequence estimators can be viewed as mapping adverse tai sequences to the most likely phylogenetic tree. Building upon this concept, we propose a new mapping objective that aims to recover the original tai sequence from an unordered labeled phylogeny. This objective serves as a non-parametric phylogenetic tree depth minimization problem subject to a novel uniqueness constraint. To effectively solve this problem, we developed a greedy tai construction algorithm along with a more efficient solution using a custom tai space traversal method. Our study demonstrates that both approaches yield high-quality tai sequences when compared to their current state-of-the-art counterparts. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric called the labeling width of a phylogenetic tree, along with a corresponding algorithm for its computation. This new metric facilitates a more in-depth analysis of the tai construction problem's hardness. Notably, we prove that when the labeling width of a binary phylogenetic tree is greater than one, the tai construction problem becomes NP-complete, in contrast to the proposed algorithm's pseudo-polynomial time solution for trees with a labeling width of zero. To further explore the relationship between tai sequences and phylogenetic trees, we developed an open-source software package called TaiExplorer, allowing for interactive exploration of the tai space. This software is designed to be highly customizable and efficient in handling large datasets. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive examination of the tai construction problem from both theoretical and practical perspectives. Additionally, TaiExplorer represents a significant advancement in the development of single sequence estimators for phylogenetic trees. To facilitate further research, we have made the source code of our study publicly available. Specifically, we have open-sourced the custom tai construction algorithm, TaiConstructor, which is now freely accessible to the scientific community. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents a major breakthrough in the development of single sequence estimators for phylogenetic trees. Our research has been thoroughly vetted by multiple experts in the field. in their block inputs, which can result in information overload and diminish the impact of earlier
feature extraction layers. To rectify this issue, this paper introduces a novel layer called Dynamic
Entrance, which selectively incorporates previous layer outputs based on global context.

By leveraging observations of the system's performance, we pinpoint a low-dimensional space that captures its dynamic patterns and generate an extremely simple model that accurately represents the system's behavior within that specific area. We then employ the collected data to systematically explore the system's behavior in the identified low-dimensional space, thereby recovering a simplified mathematical model that can predict the system's dynamics across its inherent boundaries and in unexplored regions. This hybrid model combines elements of nonlinear dimensionality reduction and Gaussian processes, allowing it to adapt to new data and retain its physical plausibility. We apply this approach to two significant complex systems: a multiscale aircraft combustion engine and a subsonic jet reaction that drives turbulence. By condensing these systems into two-dimensional spaces using their primary underlying features, we can accurately predict how they function across their inherent boundaries and in unexplored regions, showcasing the vast potential of this approach in revolutionizing the computational modeling of complex systems. It achieves this through a continuous balance with the surrounding medium, which is created by a specific reaction-counteraction mechanism between the soliton and its environment. However, this balance is disrupted when a new wave with the same frequency as the soliton is introduced, as a result of the interaction with the medium. Interestingly, we've discovered that the new wave can take on a soliton's characteristics, establishing a new equilibrium with the medium. This new soliton form is remarkably robust, as it is not significantly affected by the presence of the original soliton or any remaining residual forces. Notably, this phenomenon occurs even when the original soliton is located far away, allowing for the creation of a self-sustaining soliton-through-soliton reaction-counteraction chain. This process is further analyzed in a three-dimensional setup, where the required initial conditions are identified and the resulting wave dynamics are studied over extended periods of time. The resulting film demonstrates high peak powers and a high average power, achieving a record 2 GW of average power. The specific conditions and variables of this phenomenon suggest that it may be observable in other areas, such as the study of sound waves in air or fluid dynamics. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and an untrusted server. The goal is to prevent the client from obtaining sensitive information other than the model's final output. To achieve this, a protocol is developed to securely execute an ML inference task, comprising the sharing of encrypted input data and model shares among the client and server. A critical component of this protocol is a shared library that encrypts the model's output in response to decrypted intermediate results from each party. To further enhance privacy, a modification is made to redirect the library's encrypted output to the server instead of the client. A performance assessment is conducted for the modified protocol, applying a publicly available dataset and various open-source ML models. To facilitate replication and further research, the study's source code is freely available for download. Moreover, a high-performance variant of the protocol, named SIMC 2.0, is also introduced. This new protocol reduces overhead by simplifying encryption operations within the shared library and transferring encrypted data blocks directly between the client and server. A comparative analysis is provided between the original and improved protocols. Additionally, SIMC 2.0 is integrated with an open-source framework for scalable ML training and inference, ensuring that both accuracy and performance requirements are met. The study's results demonstrate substantial improvements in overhead and runtime for both single-threaded and multi-threaded executions, with further optimization potential identified for large-scale ML models. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 is found to experience memory access patterns resulting in suboptimal cache performance, which presents an area for future research in cache-friendly model partitioning. The research concludes by highlighting potential applications and future directions for integrating SIMC 2.0 with encrypted data storage and leveraging it for encrypted ML training. The development of more efficient, scalable protocols is critical to enabling private ML inference across multiple clients and a trained global model. The protocol's code is made available on an open-source repository. In addition, a technical video detailing the study's work is available for viewing. The study has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW) 2023. The research was conducted by a single author at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). Typically, a master node relies on a user's dataset to train a machine learning model, but Random Stroll deviates from this standard method. To achieve this inference, the master node employs a random model that reflects the characteristics of a specific user. This random model is developed by utilizing ensemble methods, specifically ensemble neural networks, that combine the predictions of models trained on unrelated datasets. As a result, the master node can provide a model that accurately represents a particular user without needing access to that user's data. The current mental health crisis is exacerbated by inadequate healthcare services, resulting in poor mental wellness among both the general population and those within the criminal justice system. To assess the effectiveness of mandatory therapy for the mentally ill in the criminal justice system, a random sample of 300 convicted individuals was selected and surveyed. The results showed that those within the criminal justice system have significantly poorer mental wellness than the general population, but this didn't differ significantly from the population at large. Interestingly, those who completed therapy reported improved mental wellness, but this improvement was limited to those with a higher educational background. Those with lower educational attainments saw no improvement in mental wellness despite completing therapy. Notably, the effectiveness of therapy wasn't influenced by the type of mental health issue. Those who dropped out of therapy, on the other hand, experienced a decline in mental wellness. The findings suggest that therapy is only half the solution, with the other half being supportive healthcare services. The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is equipped with a sophisticated Level 1 trigger system designed to reduce event rates resulting from the abundant production of jets in the LHC. This jet trigger system relies on an array of custom-built digital circuits, known as Level 1 Digital Central Trigger Systems (CTSystems), which receive calorimeter data and compute jet quantities. A key component of these systems is the Level 1 Topological (TOP) FPGA module, responsible for calculating global variables, such as total energy and multiplicity within specific energy ranges. We present an innovative new design for the TOP module, built using an Actel SX5A UltraScale+ FPGA and capable of processing 40 Gb/s data streams from the ATLAS Level 1 calorimeter system. This design includes a custom 10 Gb/s Ethernet transmitter circuit and a 1.5 Tebyte/s data buffer. It executes jet trigger decisions at full 40 MHz system speed and effectively utilizes nearly all available resources within the UltraScale+ FPGA. This work also outlines the testing plan for the new design, which involves a combination of simulation, static testing, and dynamic testing with the full ATLAS Level 1 system. We have already completed the design and it is currently in the testing phase. It is expected that 24 of these modules will be required for the full ATLAS Level 1 system. We anticipate that the testing phase will be concluded by the end of 2017 and all systems will be fully integrated into the ATLAS Level 1 system by mid-2018. This new design offers a viable path for the further development of advanced Level 1 jet trigger algorithms that will be necessary to effectively identify jets at the upgraded LHC with pileup levels reaching up to 200. This work also highlights the capabilities of the Actel SX5A UltraScale+ FPGA in meeting the stringent requirements of high-speed digital trigger systems in particle physics experiments. It is expected that this new design will be of interest to other experiments that are upgrading or considering the use of FPGAs in their trigger systems. This new design is also expected to result in a higher velocity digital trigger system that can be more easily adapted to accommodate the upgrades necessary to maintain its performance in conjunction with the upgraded LHC. To address this threat, cryptographic constructions are adapted to resist quantum transformations, often employing non-commutative operations like matrix multiplication. In cryptographic proof design, SMT solvers are increasingly vital tools. However, existing SMT-based proof systems face challenges in efficiently handling complex theories like BMMT (based on matrix multiplication), which are fundamental to many homomorphic encryption schemes and other post-quantum secure constructions. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces Alethe, a novel proof structure language designed to be compatible with various mathematical theories, including but not limited to BMMT. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce performance. The proposed Unconstrained Gradients FedAvg method tackles this issue by allowing devices to send unoptimized model updates, enabling faster calculation. In the standard FedAvg framework, gradients are normalized by dividing by the batch size, but this normalization is omitted in Unconstrained Gradients FedAvg, and instead, a buffer is maintained to accumulate and process accumulated gradients more efficiently. The method is mathematically compared to the original FedAvg and a modified version without normalization, and experimental results show that Unconstrained Gradients FedAvg achieves a 2-7 times reduction in communication cost without a loss in accuracy. The method is also integrated with Mobilenet and ResNet50 for cross-device federated learning, yielding a 5-8 times reduction in communication cost. This paper introduces Arrangement Networks (ArNs), a novel neural network architecture that efficiently combines multiple linear combinations through a unique hyperbolic arrangement of points. It is shown that ArNs achieve exceptional performance on several challenging tasks, including TPC, MSL, and Inductive Reasoning, surpassing the performance of cutting-edge models like Neural Arithmetic Units and rotating Linear Units. Notably, ArNs exhibit remarkable performance on 50-TPC with a significant margin, establishing a new benchmark for comparison. The source code for our models has been made available online. Furthermore, we propose a simple method for systematically evaluating neural arithmetic units in an indirect way, by utilizing them as the base layer for ArNs. This technique enables us to thoroughly examine the effects of varying the number of points with just two 2-ARRs components. The study of ArNs provides valuable insights that can be applied to other linear-based networks, and our results strongly support the use of linear combinations as a fundamental operation in neural networks. Additionally, we explore the connection between hyperbolic arrangements and other linear units like Linear Units and rotating Linear Units, establishing that they are equivalent to the boundary cases of the arrangement of two points. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star in (1+3) dimensions, allowing for the presence of an anisotropic fluid and a nonvanishing Weyl tensor. By directly applying the Einstein field equations, we express the covariant four-acceleration vector in terms of the fluid's velocities and the Weyl tensor. Utilizing the vanishing of the four-acceleration in vacuum spacetimes, we derive an integral form of the gravitational field equations across an arbitrary boundary within the star. This derivation holds for both compact and noncompact regions. Additionally, we derive an integral form of the conservation equation of energy-momentum, expressed in a covariant form relative to an arbitrary observer in the exterior spacetime. Through these derivations, we lay the foundation for a relativistic stellar object's exterior geometry to be reconstructed through an integral form of the Einstein field equations. This reconstruction approach enables the determination of the star's mass and surface curvature in the presence of an anisotropic fluid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the conservation equation of energy-momentum forms the basis for the derivation of anisotropic Lense-Thiring perturbation equations. This perspective offers a new view on the relationship between the conservation equation of energy-momentum and the Einstein field equations. It distinguishes between the intrinsic properties of the star that are invariant under coordinate transformations from those that are not. It also highlights the crucial role that coordinate conditions play in reconstructing the star's intrinsic properties. This is accomplished by imposing a specific coordinate condition that is compatible with the conservation equation of energy-momentum. This condition facilitates the derivation of anisotropic perturbation equations in a covariant form, expressed in terms of the fluid's velocities and the Weyl tensor. This perspective provides a new framework for addressing relativistic stellar object dynamics. It offers a comprehensive approach that addresses both the physics of relativistic stars and the geometry of their surrounding environment. This framework admits a broader class of fluid velocities that are consistent with the constraints imposed by the conservation equation of energy-momentum. This, in turn, enables an investigation of relativistic stellar object dynamics through a study of velocity constraints. This investigation raises an important question regarding the possibility of relativistic stellar objects exhibiting oscillation modes that arise solely from the anisotropy of the fluid's velocities. This question is addressed by developing a new detector that can identify oscillation modes that arise from the anisotropy of the fluid's velocities

Most current research on grammatical error rectification (GER) focuses on a single domain, which is not representative of the diverse range of languages used in real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we're working on a new few-shot domain adaptation approach for GER, which aims to minimize the need for native data in target domains. By applying meta-learning techniques to aggregate information from multiple non-native domains, our model can effectively switch between new domains with only a few examples. In experiments using the L1 corpus and a recently introduced GER dataset, our results show a novel few-shot learning method and a simple data preprocessing technique both improve performance. Interestingly, we discovered that both native and non-native speakers can benefit from a few shots of target domain data, challenging the long-held assumption that non-native speakers only need native language guidance. With only 5 shots per domain, our model achieved a 62.8% improvement in F1 score in target domains compared to traditional fine-tuning. Notably, we observed significant room for enhancement in the few-shot setting for native speakers. By applying a mix of both native and non-native data, our model achieved a 12.3% higher F1 score in the few-shot setting than the current state-of-the-art method in the fully supervised setting. Our research also highlighted the challenge of adapting highly accurate models from other NLP tasks to the GER task. With only 10 shots per domain, the score dropped to a 23.6% F1 score. In contrast, models trained from scratch achieved a 5.4% higher F1 score in the few-shot setting. To facilitate further research, we're open-sourcing all preprocessed data, along with a novel few-shot learning method that can adapt models to rectify errors in new domains with only a few examples. This initiative aims to accelerate advancements in both GER and low-resource NLP tasks by providing accessible data and a scalable evaluation frameworks. In the future, we plan to explore both multi-domain and unsupervised adaptation settings, along with the integration of additional NLP components to enhance error rectification performance. This way, we can accelerate further research in both GER and low-resource NLP tasks, paving the way for more reliable and highly accurate models in the future. Researchers and survey takers often round their responses to the nearest integer when estimating total values or quantities. This study examines how survey respondents' rounding behavior influences the accuracy of their estimates when faced with uncertain information, particularly when that information is based on imprecise proportions or averages. The research finds that individuals employ an unusual strategy, averaging the two nearest category boundaries rather than the two nearest integers, which has significant implications for researchers working with categorical data and can result in an notable underestimation of totals, averaging 13.44% in this study. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy.

The task of allocating a set of items to agents in an efficient and fair manner is an important one, especially given the growing prevalence of online marketplaces. In these platforms, agents make decisions based on anticipated outcomes, which are determined by their individual preferences as defined by utility functions. The Fair Allocation framework, applicable to both private and public domain scenarios, seeks to find an allocation that minimizes the maximum utility loss across all agents, subject to their individual equilibrium requirements. Our study focuses on the examination of pure Nash equilibria in both domain types and reveals that, in the public domain, pure Nash equilibria can be found through a proposed method, whereas in the private domain, we demonstrate the existence of pure Nash equilibria for specific item and agent relationships, and provide evidence suggesting equilibria may not always be attainable in the private domain. Additionally, we investigate various equity criteria and discover that, in both domain types, the strongest such criterion is directly related to the minimum utility achieved by any individual in an equilibrium scenario. This research contributes a general fairness framework that can be applied across multiple specific fairness measures and provides a method for fairly allocating items through equilibrium calculations. The proposed framework and calculation method can also be applied to variants of the Fair Allocation problem. Re-identifying individuals across different video recordings, whether collected professionally or through crowd sourcing, can be a challenging task due to variations in camera viewpoints, lighting conditions and quality. This study investigates extensive unsupervised individual re-identification (UIR) which involves matching individuals across large data sets without any labeled data. To achieve this, a framework based on contrastive learning is proposed, featuring two main components: first, a view-wise pre-training method is employed to train UIR using individual video segments; second, a data-wise refinement protocol is used to refine the features for entire video recordings. The proposed framework is mathematically expressed and its efficiency validated using extensive unsupervised individual re-identification experiments on three widely used data sets. The results show that the proposed framework surpasses current state-of-the-art UIR approaches and matches the performance of supervised re-identification methods in three evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the framework's ability to handle large data sets is demonstrated. The source code of the proposed framework is made available online. A novel formulation for modeling tail hazards is developed, based on a specific type of Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model that incorporates an actual threshold measurement parameter. This model is the result of a collaboration between two research streams: GARCH models and actual threshold modeling. A specific type of GARCH model, known as the Exponential GARCH (EGARCH), is modified to include a specific type of time-varying conditional leverage parameter, leading to a formulation equivalent to the Power GARCH model. An alternative formulation is then proposed, based on a specific type of GARCH model known as the Asymmetric GARCH (AGARCH), which enables the estimation of a specific type of time-varying score function parameter. A new framework for forecasting extreme event probabilities is then proposed, based on the relationship between tail hazards and tail probabilities. By employing a Bayesian approach in combination with a precise timing model, we determined the posterior distribution of parameters, including their confidence intervals and how they interact with each other. Our research found that a specific parameter, characterizing the signal generated by primordial black holes, was accurately pinned down with a relatively narrow confidence interval, whereas another parameter, related to the formation of black holes through the collapse of matter and dust, was less precisely defined due to its impact on smaller irregular periodic variations in pulsar data. Evaluating how mass accretion rates fluctuate over time in the early stages of star formation is crucial for understanding how massive protostars and their outflows are regulated.  A long-term study was conducted on the intermediate-mass young object XX Cha using high-resolution spectroscopy over a 11.7 year period, and a key finding from this research was published recently by van Stadens et al. This previous work focused on the system's overall average behavior over time.  Utilizing the same dataset, our analysis reveals a much more dynamic aspect of XX Cha with significant short-term variations in the mass accretion rate that are likely caused by disk instabilities and/or changes in the object's internal properties.  These short-term variations in XX Cha are significantly more pronounced than those in the T Tauri star TW Hya and HR 4792's disk.  As such, if XX Cha's short-term and long-term behaviors are combined, its mass accretion rate display a factor of >10^2 times more variability than previously found for T Tauri stars.  This extremely high variability could be an indicator that XX Cha's disk is more unstable and features bridge dynamics.  Its temporary increase in mass accretion rate also could help explain the larger than expected dispersion in observed mass accretion rates in the T Tauri and Herbig Ae/Be populations.  More extensive studies of mass accretion rates across even longer time frames using higher resolution spectroscopy are necessary to fully confirm this findings' implications.  Additionally, future studies should also consider how other properties of these young objects vary over time as a function of mass.  This could provide a more comprehensive understanding of how massive protostars regulate their mass accretion and outflows. Social equality is often viewed as a matter of income equality, but research suggests that wealth inequality can persist even in scenarios with minimal income disparities. This study seeks to bridge the gap by linking these dynamics to the variance of random rewards in multi-armed bandit problems. We introduce a novel equitable learning algorithm that effectively minimizes the standard deviation of obtained rewards, thereby reducing wealth inequality and facilitating efficient income reallocation. Notably, this algorithm achieves comparable reward expectations compared to traditional approaches, while successfully addressing the challenges of stochastic transitions and multiple players. Through extensive simulations in both static and dynamic settings, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in mitigating wealth inequality and improving social welfare. These findings are further validated by applications to synthetic and real-world economic data, revealing that our approach can tackle complex problems with multiple features and large-scale datasets. These results imply that equitable learning can be an attractive solution for addressing wealth inequality in online learning settings. We also explore the theoretical properties of our algorithm and derive a regret bound that highlights its efficient learning capabilities. This study contributes a pioneering solution to the equitable multi-armed bandit problem and paves the way for further research in adaptive income allocation and social welfare optimization. The cause of this performance drop is commonly attributed to either model flaws or inadequate training data. However, pinpointing the exact issue is a significant challenge. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that combines the Shapley value algorithm with significant feature identification to address this problem by identifying crucial data points that significantly contribute to the model's poor performance. Traditionally, image registration is achieved through optimization techniques that maximize a correlation metric between images, but these methods can be challenging due to low-resolution Megavoltage images and the complex internal anatomy of patients. To overcome these difficulties, we employed a CNN-based approach that directly produces optimized transformation parameters for aligning the images. Our network consists of two parts: a segmentation branch that extracts contoured regions from both the CT and aligned MV images, and a dense regression branch that predicts transformation parameters from super-pixel features. We utilized a dataset of contoured organs at risk from 10 patients with cancer and performed leave-one-out cross-validation to evaluate our method. Furthermore, this work examines novel BlockFL frameworks that integrate Blockchain technology with IoVs, while also discussing challenges, future directions, and the inherent benefits of BlockFL frameworks through real-world application examples. Finally, this paper concludes with an outlook on future research paths for BlockFL frameworks in IoVs. V392 Persei was initially believed to be a classical nova from archival data indicating it had exploded in 2018 after a 41-year dormancy.  However, by examining all available historical data including the All Sky Automate Supernovae catalogue and the Gamma-Ray Burst Coordinate Network, we determined the system went into a 41-year low-brightness state not typical of novae and then entered a 17-day brightening period that included a super-soft X-ray burst and gamma-ray detection.  When comparing this behavior to other novae and cataclysmic variable systems, we found V392 Persei most similar to GW Of104, a compact binary system that went into a 7-month low brightness state before entering a brightening period that included a gamma-ray detection.  Like GW Of104 and other systems that exhibit both low and high brightness states, V392 Persei likely have a highly tilted orbit that prevents the accretion disk from forming during its low brightness state, and when it does form, it causes a massive explosion like a nova. These individuals typically rely on traditional metrics such as citation count and journal impact factor. Nevertheless, they may also consider alternative indicators including alternative impact factors, citation patterns, and networks analysis. Despite its widespread adoption, the citation count method has several limitations including its exclusivity to articles, reliance on outdated databases, and failure to distinguish between different types of citations. Consequently, researchers have investigated more comprehensive impact measures that take into account all types of scientific outputs, including books, data sets, software, and methodologies. Previous studies have analyzed specific fields or time frames; in contrast, our investigation seeks to explore the practical applicability of these measures across various research domains and time periods. Specifically, we examine six widely-used methods of calculation and evaluate the resulting metrics' variability, citing patterns, and practical implications for evaluating scientific progress. Our analysis indicates that different methods produce distinct outcomes with significant differences exceeding 50%. These discrepancies raise significant concerns regarding the uniformity of these indices and their potential inflationary effects when applied to evaluate individual research or institutional performance. Moreover, some of these methods prove unable to differentiate between high and low impact outputs. Notably, our analysis reveals that the most widely-used citation count method exhibits unique characteristics, exhibiting linearity with output count, and failing to capture the underlying knowledge growth trends. In contrast, the sum of all outputs correlates nonlinearly with citation count, more accurately capturing knowledge evolution over time. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that any evaluation or ranking of researchers or institutions according to their output or impact should be done with caution and a deep understanding of the methods being employed. Furthermore, we believe that any such evaluation or ranking should be done in a holistic manner, considering multiple aspects, including both quantitative and qualitative indicators, in addition to expert opinions and diverse perspectives. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual intelligence focused on natural language understanding, reasoning, and production. A key limitation in researching these games has been the slow pace of current AI models, which typically take several seconds to make decisions and significantly hinder concurrent operations like multi-step reasoning. To address this issue, a new framework called TextWorldExpress has been developed, allowing text games to process over one million steps per second with limited adjustments to existing models. In experiments with both classical text games and newly created scenarios, our results demonstrated that current state-of-the-art models can achieve near-human performance on expressed versions of the games, while also successfully integrating multi-step reasoning into their decision-making process. Interestingly, our research also uncovered the phenomenon known as performance divergence, where the ratings of expressed games differ noticeably from those of their full-version counterparts. To mitigate this issue, a new protocol called uniform performance ratio (UPR) was introduced to standardize the evaluation of text games by taking multiple factors into consideration. With UPR, our research revealed that models performance on expressed games closely mirrors their performance in single-step evaluation protocols. Moreover, UPR also enabled us to identify the presence of performance divergence, which we attribute to models' over-reliance on lookup tables due to the limited depth of modern neural language models. In an effort to verify the findings of our research, an open-source repository called TextExpressBenchmark has been established, which provides a comprehensive set of text games at various levels of expression complexity for the research community to contribute to. In terms of system requirements, our implementation demands a relatively modest computer configuration consisting of a single core, 2 GB of RAM, and a 64-bit operating system. Nonetheless, it is essential to note that this architecture is computationally intensive and requires significant power output from any machine that hosts it. In the conclusion section, we outline several potential extensions to our research, while also offering our vision for the future of text games in evaluating natural language understanding models. Furthermore, we provide our response to the critique offered by the review committee and outline our plans for continuing this research in the future. Research has shown that the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films can be influenced by the type of surface termination used. Our results from a combination of surface X-ray diffraction, photoemission spectroscopy, and scanning probe techniques show that oxygen terminations disrupt the corrosion of the underlying oxide layer, allowing the formation of a surface state that competes with a bulk state responsible for the metal-insulator transition.
